WHICH CRITERIA APPLY

| Category | Code | Required? | Criteria |
|---|---|---|---|
| Security (Common Criteria) | CC | Always required | CC1-CC9 |
| Availability | A | Optional | A1 |
| Confidentiality | C | Optional | C1 |
| Processing Integrity | PI | Optional | PI1 |
| Privacy | P | Optional | P1-P8 |

- CC1 Control Environment, CC2 Communication and Information, CC3 Risk Assessment, CC4 Monitoring, CC5 Control Activities, CC6 Logical and Physical Access, CC7 System Operations, CC8 Change Management, CC9 Risk Mitigation (including vendors).
- You choose the optional categories based on your commitments to customers and the nature of your service. Typical drivers: uptime SLAs (Availability), contractual confidentiality obligations (Confidentiality), transaction or calculation accuracy (Processing Integrity), and personal information you collect directly (Privacy).

WHY THE 2017 CRITERIA, NOT THE PROPOSED ONES

- On October 28, 2026, the AICPA issued an exposure draft of "Proposed 2027 SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria and Description Criteria". It keeps the five categories, consolidates overlapping criteria and adds AI-related points of focus.
- It is only a proposal. Comments are due January 15, 2027. It is proposed to take effect for engagements beginning on or after December 31, 2027, with early adoption permitted.
- A period starting January 2027 begins before December 31, 2027. Unless you and your auditor agree to early adoption after a final version exists, which is unlikely so early, you are examined against the current criteria. Do not apply the proposed criteria to this engagement.
- A separate February 2026 exposure draft on attestation standards (AT-C 105/205/210, proposed effective June 15, 2029) does not change the TSC.

PRACTICAL POINTS FOR A 2027 TYPE 2

1. Lock the scope with your auditor before the period starts: the categories, the system boundary (services, infrastructure, data flows, subservice organizations) and the exact period (6-12 months is typical; first-time Type 2 reports are often 3-6 months, but the auditor decides).
2. Controls must be designed and in place on day one of the period, because a Type 2 tests operating effectiveness across the whole window. Quarterly controls (such as access reviews) need all four quarters evidenced in a 12-month period. Annual controls (risk assessment, policy review, pen test, DR test) must fall inside the period.
3. Cost of adding categories: each one adds controls, evidence and test sample work. Add what customers need, not everything.
4. If your 2027 period will carry into 2028, watch the final criteria and ask your auditor early about transition.

Which Trust Services Criteria apply to a SOC 2 Type 2 with a period starting January 2027

Short answer: unless AICPA has finalized and made effective a replacement set, the 2017 Trust Services Criteria (TSP Section 100) with the 2022 revised points of focus apply. I can't confirm any new criteria are effective for a period starting in January 2027. Verify with your auditor and the AICPA site.

Which categories apply
- Security (Common Criteria CC1.1 to CC9.2) is mandatory in every SOC 2.
- Availability (A1.1 to A1.3), Confidentiality (C1.1 to C1.2), Processing Integrity (PI1.1 to PI1.5) and Privacy (P1 to P8) are optional. You include them based on your commitments to customers, your system, and what customers expect to see.

How to choose
- Availability: include it if you have uptime SLAs or customers depend on the service being available.
- Confidentiality: include it if you hold confidential customer or business information under contract or NDA.
- Processing Integrity: include it if the accuracy, completeness and timeliness of processing is central to the service, for example payments, calculations or data pipelines.
- Privacy: include it if you collect, use and retain personal information as a service function and want assurance on the notice, choice, access and disclosure principles. It is distinct from a GDPR assessment.
- Most SaaS companies choose Security plus Availability and Confidentiality. Fewer add Processing Integrity or Privacy.

Other things that apply to a Type 2 examination
- The system description is measured against the DC 200 description criteria (2018, with 2022 updated implementation guidance).
- Type 2 tests operating effectiveness over a period, typically 3 to 12 months. A first-time report often covers 3 to 6 months, and later reports cover 12 months. Controls must be designed and implemented before the period starts.
- Complementary user entity controls (CUECs) and subservice organization treatment (carve-out or inclusive) must be identified.
- Standards: AT-C 105 and AT-C 205 govern the engagement.

Period-related watch points for January 2027
- If a revised criteria set is issued, AICPA normally sets a transition period. A period beginning in January 2027 would most likely still be assessed under the 2017 criteria, but confirm the effective-date language, particularly the rule that applies to periods ending on or after a given date.
- Ask the auditor to state in the engagement letter which criteria version will be cited.
- Set your scope (categories, system boundary, subservice organizations) before the period starts and do not change it mid-period without telling the auditor.

Action list
1. Decide on categories and document the rationale.
2. Confirm criteria version and any transition guidance in writing with the auditor.
3. Complete a readiness assessment in Q4 2026.
4. Have controls operating before January 2027 so there is evidence from day one of the period.

Today your audit uses the 2017 Trust Services Criteria with the 2022 Revised Points of Focus, and your AI systems are examined through the existing criteria.

HOW THE PROPOSAL TREATS AI

- On October 28, 2026, the AICPA's Assurance Services Executive Committee issued the exposure draft "Proposed 2027 SOC 2 Trust Services Criteria and Description Criteria" (dated October 27, 2026).
- It keeps the five categories (Security, Availability, Processing Integrity, Confidentiality, Privacy) and consolidates overlapping criteria.
- AI appears as points of focus, which are guidance within criteria. There is no standalone "AI criterion" and no separate AI category.
- Comments are due January 15, 2027. It is proposed to apply to engagements beginning on or after December 31, 2027, with early adoption permitted. The wording can change before it is final, so do not build to the draft.

WHAT APPLIES TO YOUR AUDIT TODAY

Until the AICPA adopts a final version, the 2017 TSC with the 2022 points of focus are the operative criteria. Do not apply the proposed criteria to a current engagement. That does not mean AI is out of view. An auditor can test AI systems that are in scope under the existing criteria. Where they typically land:

| Area | Criteria | What to be ready to show for AI systems |
|---|---|---|
| Governance and accountability | CC1, CC2, CC3 | Named owner for AI systems; AI use and acceptable-use policy; AI risks in the risk register (model failure, data leakage, misuse, bias or accuracy risks relevant to your commitments) |
| Access | CC6 | Access to models, training data, prompts, logs and API keys limited and reviewed; MFA; secrets management |
| Monitoring and incidents | CC7 | Logging of model and agent activity; alerting; AI-related incidents handled under the IR plan |
| Change management | CC8 | Model, prompt and configuration changes ticketed, reviewed, tested and approved; rollback plan; retraining or model version changes treated as changes |
| Third parties | CC9.2 | Model providers and AI APIs in the vendor inventory and tiered; SOC 2 reports and CUECs reviewed; contract terms on data use and retention |
| Confidentiality | C1 | Customer data classification; whether customer data is sent to third-party models, used for training, or retained; disposal |
| Processing integrity | PI1 | If outputs support commitments to customers, how accuracy, completeness and timeliness of AI-driven processing are checked (validation, reconciliation, human review, error handling) |
| Privacy | P1-P8 | Notice and consent cover AI processing of personal information; retention and deletion apply to prompts and logs |

Also make sure your system description accurately explains where AI sits in the service, which components are in scope and which subservice organizations (for example a model provider) are carved out or carved in.

WHAT TO DO

1. Confirm scope with your auditor: which AI components and providers are inside the boundary, and which categories you include (PI1 and C1 matter most if AI touches customer data or outputs).
2. Build an AI inventory (systems, models, providers, data used, owner) and tie each item to controls above.
3. Make sure AI changes pass through your normal change process. Gaps there are the most likely exception.
4. Add AI providers to vendor management and complete the CUEC mapping.
5. Document controls the way you would any other: owner, frequency, evidence, test procedure. Evidence must be generated during the period.
6. Watch the exposure draft. Consider commenting by January 15, 2027. Controls above are low-regret, since they fit both the current and the proposed criteria.

AI inside SOC 2 scope: the proposed criteria refresh and what applies today

Caveat: I can't verify the contents of any AICPA proposed criteria refresh. I don't have reliable detail on how a draft would treat AI, so I will not invent its wording. Please read the actual exposure draft, if one exists, and confirm its status with your auditor.

What applies to your audit today
- The 2017 Trust Services Criteria with the 2022 points of focus are the operative standard. They do not mention AI explicitly. They are technology-neutral, so your AI systems are in scope to the extent they are part of the system described in your DC 200 system description and affect your service commitments.
- The criteria are applied to AI through your existing controls. A practical mapping:
  - CC1 to CC2 (control environment, communication): AI governance roles, acceptable use policy, ethics and accountability, training.
  - CC3 (risk assessment): include AI-specific risks such as model errors, bias, hallucination, data leakage, prompt injection, and dependence on third-party model providers. Include fraud risk and change in risk from new technology.
  - CC4 (monitoring): monitoring of model performance, drift, abuse and incidents.
  - CC5 to CC6 (control activities, logical and physical access): access to models, training data, prompts, API keys, vector stores and inference endpoints. Least privilege and segregation between environments. Encryption in transit and at rest.
  - CC7 (system operations): logging, anomaly detection, incident response including AI incidents, vulnerability management for ML libraries and models.
  - CC8 (change management): model versioning, validation before release, rollback, approval for prompt or model changes, testing of fine-tuned models.
  - CC9 (risk mitigation, vendors): due diligence and contracts for LLM and AI vendors, including data use and retention terms, no training on customer data, subprocessors.
  - Confidentiality (C1): handling of customer data sent to models, retention and deletion, training data restrictions.
  - Processing Integrity (PI1): accuracy, completeness and validity of AI outputs where your commitments depend on them. Human review where appropriate.
  - Privacy (P series): purpose limitation, consent, and rights handling if personal data is used in training or inference.
  - Availability (A1): capacity and resilience of model-serving infrastructure and fallback when providers fail.
- System description: describe the AI components, data flows, third-party models as subservice organizations (carve-out or inclusive), and the commitments made about AI to customers. Make the description accurate, since auditors test what you say.

Where the proposed refresh may matter
- Any refresh is not effective until finalized. Until then it is not an audit requirement. Auditors may still ask forward-looking questions or add AI-related procedures under their own methodology, which is not the same as a criteria change.
- You can use a draft as a guide for control design, but do not represent your report as conforming to it.

What to do
1. Inventory AI systems and data flows in scope.
2. Add AI risks to your risk assessment and map controls to the existing criteria.
3. Update policies: AI acceptable use, AI vendor management, model change management, data handling.
4. Treat model providers as vendors and obtain their SOC 2 reports and subservice organization assurances.
5. Collect evidence: model change tickets, evaluation results, access reviews, monitoring alerts, vendor reviews.
6. Ask the auditor how they will test AI-related controls and whether they expect any specific description disclosures.
7. Consider complementary frameworks, for example ISO 42001 or NIST AI RMF, if customers ask for AI-specific assurance. These are not part of SOC 2.

Does the 2026 AT-C exposure draft change SOC 2 criteria?

Caveat: I can't verify the specific content of a 2026 AT-C exposure draft. Confirm details against the AICPA document itself. The structural distinction below is what I am confident about.

The key distinction: two different layers
1. Trust Services Criteria (TSP Section 100). These are the criteria, meaning the subject matter standards your controls are evaluated against: Security, Availability, Confidentiality, Processing Integrity and Privacy. They are developed by the AICPA Assurance Services Executive Committee (ASEC). The current version is the 2017 criteria with the 2022 revised points of focus.
2. Attestation standards (AT-C sections, such as AT-C 105 general concepts, AT-C 205 examination engagements, and AT-C 320 for user-entity ICFR reporting). These are set by the Auditing Standards Board (ASB) and govern how the practitioner performs the engagement: acceptance and planning, evidence, reporting, management representations, and report wording.
There is also a third item, the AICPA SOC 2 Guide, which is guidance on applying both.

So an AT-C exposure draft, by its nature, changes practitioner requirements. It does not change the Trust Services Criteria or the controls you must have. Your control set stays mapped to the 2017 TSC.

What an AT-C change could affect for you
- Report format or wording, for example the practitioner's opinion, the basis for opinion, or required paragraphs.
- Practitioner procedures that may change auditor workload or timing, such as evaluating the work of others, use of data, or evaluating information produced by the entity (IPE).
- Management's written assertion and representation letter content.
- Effective dates, which usually apply to reports or periods ending after a stated date. Exposure drafts are not effective until finalized.

Here is a 2027 SOC 2 readiness timeline. It is built on the 2017 Trust Services Criteria with the 2022 Revised Points of Focus, which remain the operative criteria. The proposed 2027 criteria are tracked as a watch item and do not drive the plan.

CONTEXT THAT SHAPES THE PLAN

- On October 28, 2026, the AICPA issued an exposure draft of the proposed 2027 TSC (draft dated October 27, 2026). It keeps the five categories, consolidates overlapping criteria and adds AI-related points of focus without new AI-specific criteria.
- Comments are due January 15, 2027. Proposed effective date: engagements beginning on or after December 31, 2027, with early adoption permitted.
- So a 2027 audit period is examined against the current criteria. Controls built to them should carry forward. Do not re-map to proposed criteria.
- The separate February 2026 attestation standards draft (AT-C 105/205/210, proposed effective June 15, 2029) does not change the TSC.

ASSUMPTIONS (adjust if wrong)

- First SOC 2, with Type 1 optional, then a Type 2 with a 6-month observation window. If you already have a report, skip to the Type 2 steps.
- Scope: Security (required) plus categories your customers need.
- Audit firm is a licensed CPA firm engaged by end of Q1.

TIMELINE

Q4 2026 (now to December): decisions
- Confirm report type, categories, system boundary and target report date with leadership. Name an executive sponsor and a compliance owner.
- Shortlist and engage a CPA firm. Request their readiness approach and sample request list. Confirm they will examine against the 2017 TSC with 2022 points of focus.
- Start a gap assessment against CC1-CC9 and any chosen categories, using RAG status and remediation entries (control area, gap, remediation, owner, date, evidence needed).

January 2027
- Finish gap assessment. Prioritize the commonly flagged gaps: undocumented or unreviewed policies, no formal risk assessment, no access reviews, untested incident response plan, inconsistent change management, no vendor program.
- Kick off remediation with owners and dates.
- Optional: decide whether to comment on the exposure draft by January 15, 2027.
- Sign the audit engagement letter if not yet done.

February to March 2027: build the foundation
- Write and approve the core policy set (information security, access control, incident response, change management, risk assessment, vendor management, BC/DR, data classification, acceptable use, encryption, vulnerability management, plus privacy notice if in scope). Each one has an owner, version, approval and annual review date.
- Run the first formal risk assessment and create the risk register with owners and treatment decisions.
- Distribute policies and capture acknowledgments. Start security awareness training and background check evidence.
- Build a vendor inventory with tiers. Collect SOC 2 reports for critical vendors and map CUECs.
- Build the control matrix (ID, criterion, type, owner, frequency, evidence, test procedure).

April to May 2027: implement and operate
- Implement technical controls: MFA, SSO, endpoint protection, logging and alerting, vulnerability scanning, backup and restore tests, change approval in version control.
- Run the first access review (all in-scope systems, with documented decisions and tickets for changes). Run a first vulnerability scan cycle. Run an incident response tabletop.
- Set up automated, dated evidence exports so evidence is contemporaneous.
- If AI systems are in scope, add them to inventory, change control, vendor review and risk register now. These are low-regret under both current and proposed criteria.

June 2027: readiness and Type 1 (optional)
- Auditor-led or internal readiness review. Fix remaining gaps. Freeze control design before the observation window begins.
- Type 1 as of a date (design only), if customers need something early. Skip it if time is tight.

July to December 2027: Type 2 observation window (6 months, example)
- Monthly: evidence checks and a compliance review meeting.
- Quarterly: access review (Q3 and Q4 evidence), risk register review, vulnerability and patch reports, vendor review progress.
- Within the window: annual items (pen test, DR test, policy review, risk assessment refresh) must land inside the period.
- Sample-based evidence: changes, terminations, incidents. Keep tickets complete.
- Track and fix exceptions as they occur and document them.

Watch items during 2027
- AICPA final TSC publication: once published, ask your auditor how it affects any engagement spanning December 31, 2027 and whether early adoption is on offer. Do not adopt on your own.
- If your period starts on or after December 31, 2027, expect the new criteria to be discussed. Ask the auditor in Q3.

Q1 2028
- Auditor fieldwork, then draft and final report. Management assertion and system description reviewed by you. Plan for exceptions and management responses.
- Share the report under NDA with customers. Plan the next period to run continuously.

KEY RISKS TO THE TIMELINE
- Starting the observation window before controls have been operating long enough to be evidenced.
- Audit firm availability in Q1 2028. Book early.
- Controls on paper that do not match practice.
- Late-finding gaps in vendor and access evidence.

Short answer: nothing changes for your specific package on September 30, 2026 in terms of a hard rejection — but the date matters a lot, and you need to understand exactly why.

Under CR26 (the FedRAMP Consolidated Rules for 2026), a machine-readable mandate (RFC-0024/NOTICE-0009) takes effect at 2PM ET on September 30, 2026, but it applies specifically to two triggers:

1. NEW Rev5 initial-certification packages — packages that are submitted for the first time — must be machine-readable with no grace period, starting at that moment. This explicitly includes packages that are already "In Process" for agency authorization as of that date. If your Moderate authorization is a new/first-time initial certification package and it is still in process on September 30, 2026, it falls into this bucket and will need to be machine-readable (OSCAL or another FedRAMP-approved standardized format) from that point forward — Word/Excel alone will no longer satisfy the intake requirement for that package.

2. Existing Rev5-certified providers (i.e., CSPs that already hold an authorization) are NOT required to convert immediately. Instead, they must submit a full machine-readable package at their next annual assessment completed after September 30, 2026.

The distinction that matters for you is whether your Moderate authorization is best characterized as a "new initial-certification package" (even though it's mid-process) versus an "existing certified provider" going through routine ConMon/annual assessment. Based on your description — "mid-process on a Rev5 Moderate agency authorization" — this sounds like an initial authorization effort, not an existing authorized system's annual assessment cycle. If that's correct, you fall under the no-grace-period rule (LMR-GEN-ICR): your package, even though already in process, must become machine-readable at the September 30, 2026 cutoff. There is no allowance for "we started before the deadline."

Practical implications:
- Approved formats are NIST OSCAL or any public-domain standardized format that 5+ certified CSPs agree to maintain and that FedRAMP has validated. OSCAL is the safe, de facto default.
- CR26 JSON schemas and a validator have been published — use them now to start converting your SSP, SAP/SAR inputs, POA&M, and CIS/CRM content into structured, machine-readable form rather than waiting.
- You still need to be able to produce human-readable renditions on request (for 3PAO reviewers, agency AOs, or auditors who prefer PDF/Word views) — machine-readable is the authoritative format, not the only format.
- Non-compliance consequence: public notification of non-compliance until 2PM ET September 30, 2027, followed by certification revocation if not remedied. That's a serious downstream risk if you slip past the cutoff without a compliant package.

What I'd recommend doing this week:
1. Confirm with your 3PAO and the FedRAMP PMO whether your package is being treated as "new initial certification, in process" (subject to the no-grace-period rule) or something else — get this in writing.
2. Start OSCAL conversion now for the SSP, POA&M, and CIS/CRM — these are the highest-effort artifacts to convert and the ones most likely to slip.
3. Validate against the published CR26 JSON schemas and the FedRAMP validator before September 30.
4. Keep Word/Excel versions as your working drafts if that's easier for your authors, but plan the final submission format as OSCAL, not Office documents.
5. Loop in your agency AO now — a mid-process package hitting this deadline is exactly the scenario that causes last-minute scrambles; give them visibility early.

One caveat: FedRAMP 20x, if you were on that pathway instead, is explicitly exempt from this specific mandate (it has its own machine-readable model), but since you describe a traditional Rev5 agency authorization, that carve-out doesn't apply to you. Use official fedramp.gov guidance and your 3PAO's read on your specific package status to confirm before the cutoff — this is a fast-moving regulatory area and the PMO may issue package-specific guidance.

Background: FedRAMP has been pushing, for several years, toward machine-readable authorization packages built on OSCAL (Open Security Controls Assessment Language) rather than the traditional Word/Excel SSP, SAP, SAR, and POA&M templates. The PMO has repeatedly signaled that Word/Excel-based submissions are a transitional format and that OSCAL-native (JSON/XML/YAML) packages are the long-term requirement, first for new authorizations and eventually across the board, including for agencies operating the FedRAMP Rev5 baseline. Dates announced for "final" cutovers to OSCAL-only submission have shifted more than once as the PMO calibrated for 3PAO and CSP tooling readiness, so if you've seen September 30, 2026 cited, it's most likely tied to one of these transition milestones (e.g., a deadline for new packages, or for existing packages to convert at their next significant change request or annual assessment).

What this likely means for you if the date is real and applies to your effort:
1. New submissions after that date may be required to be in OSCAL format, meaning your reviewing agency and/or the FedRAMP PMO (if you're going through JAB or seeking a P-ATO) may reject or delay processing of a purely Word/Excel package.
2. If you are mid-process — meaning you already have documents in flight with your agency reviewer — you should immediately ask your agency ISSO/AO point of contact and your 3PAO whether your existing package is grandfathered, whether you need to convert before final authorization, or whether the deadline only affects new starts.
3. Even if there's a grace period, agencies are increasingly asking for OSCAL exports as a courtesy or requirement earlier than mandated, because it feeds their own GRC tooling (e.g., emass, Xacta) more efficiently.

What I'd recommend doing regardless of the exact date:
1. Get your OSCAL conversion plan started now. Converting a mature Word/Excel SSP and control implementation narrative into valid OSCAL is not trivial — it requires mapping every control implementation statement, parameter, and responsibility split (CSP vs. inherited vs. customer) into structured, machine-parseable format. Start this in parallel with your existing authorization work rather than waiting for a deadline to force it.
2. Talk to your 3PAO now about their OSCAL tooling maturity — many 3PAOs are still building capability here, and if yours isn't ready, that becomes your critical path.
3. Ask your agency sponsor directly what format they will accept for the SAR, SSP, and POA&M at each remaining review gate. Some agencies have been pragmatic and accepted Word/Excel through completion of the current authorization cycle, with an OSCAL conversion required only at the next annual assessment or significant change.
4. Watch for official FedRAMP PMO announcements — these come via FedRAMP.gov blog posts, the FedRAMP Rev5 transition guidance, and (more recently) the FedRAMP 20x initiative materials, which are explicitly trying to make machine-readable, API-first submission the default going forward.
5. Budget schedule and cost contingency: OSCAL conversion for a Moderate package with dozens of controls and hundreds of parameters is a real effort — plan for weeks, not days, especially if your control narratives are inconsistent or if inheritance from your IaaS provider isn't cleanly documented.

Bottom line: treat any specific date you've heard as provisional until confirmed directly with the FedRAMP PMO or your agency AO, but don't wait for confirmation to start your OSCAL readiness work — the direction of travel is unambiguous, and being caught flat-footed on format at the finish line of a Moderate authorization would be a costly, avoidable delay.

For an existing Rev5 FedRAMP Moderate certified provider (i.e., you already hold authorization and are in steady-state continuous monitoring, not pursuing a brand-new initial certification), the machine-readable mandate does not hit you on September 30, 2026 itself. That date and time (2PM ET, September 30, 2026) is when the "no grace period" rule kicks in for NEW Rev5 initial-certification packages [LMR-GEN-ICR] — including ones already in process. That is a different trigger than yours.

As an existing, already-certified provider, the applicable rule is [LMR-GEN-OAR]: you must submit a full machine-readable package at each annual assessment completed after September 30, 2026. In plain terms:

- Identify your next annual assessment completion date on the calendar (this is your 3PAO-led annual security assessment, tied to your ConMon cycle, not just a POA&M update).
- If that annual assessment is completed before September 30, 2026, you can submit it in your current format (Word/Excel or whatever you use today) — the mandate doesn't reach back to catch it.
- If your annual assessment is completed on or after September 30, 2026, that specific assessment cycle's package must be fully machine-readable. This is not just the new/changed findings — it's described as a "full machine-readable package," so treat it as your SSP, POA&M, CIS/CRM, and related artifacts all needing to exist in structured format at that point, not just a delta submission.

So the precise answer to "when exactly" is: at your next annual assessment that completes on or after September 30, 2026 — not a fixed calendar date that applies uniformly to all existing providers. Two Moderate CSPs with different annual assessment schedules will hit this requirement at different times depending on when their assessment cycle lands relative to the cutoff.

What to do now, regardless of exactly where your annual assessment falls:
1. Pin down your annual assessment completion date precisely with your 3PAO and ISSO — "roughly Q4" isn't precise enough given a hard cutoff.
2. If your assessment date is close to September 30, 2026 (within a couple months either side), treat this as high risk of ambiguity — confirm with your AO/PMO point of contact how "completed" is being interpreted (submission date vs. AO acceptance date vs. 3PAO sign-off date), since that interpretation determines which side of the line you land on.
3. Start OSCAL conversion work now regardless of your exact date. Converting an SSP, POA&M, and CIS/CRM workbook into OSCAL is not a last-month task — treat it as a project with its own timeline, ideally starting 6+ months ahead of your annual assessment.
4. Use the published CR26 JSON schemas and FedRAMP validator to check your converted artifacts before submission; don't wait for the 3PAO to catch format issues.
5. Maintain human-readable renditions in parallel — these are still required "on request" even once you're machine-readable-primary, so don't throw away your Word/Excel authoring workflow entirely; you may need to keep generating readable exports for agency AOs who still prefer them.
6. If you miss the mandate for your qualifying annual assessment, know the consequence structure: public non-compliance notification runs until 2PM ET September 30, 2027, after which certification revocation follows if you're still non-compliant. That's a full year of runway to fix a miss, but don't treat it as slack — reputational exposure during the notification period is itself a real cost with agency customers.

Bottom line: your compliance deadline is defined relative to your own annual assessment cycle, not a single fixed date. Get precise about when that assessment "completes" under the PMO's definition, and start your OSCAL conversion work well ahead of that date rather than waiting for September 30, 2026 as if it were your deadline — it isn't, unless your annual assessment happens to land on or after it.

First, the "machine-readable" requirement historically refers to producing your authorization artifacts (SSP, SAP, SAR, POA&M, and the control implementation summary/CIS) in OSCAL format instead of, or in addition to, Word and Excel. Second, more recently, FedRAMP 20x has introduced a broader push toward continuous, API-driven validation of security posture rather than periodic point-in-time documentation review — this is a related but distinct initiative from the OSCAL mandate and has its own track record of pilot phases with a limited cohort of CSPs before wider rollout.

1. Annual Assessment (Annual Security Assessment Report cycle) — many agencies and the PMO have signaled this is the natural checkpoint to require OSCAL-formatted deliverables, since you're already refreshing your SAR and POA&M at that time.
2. Significant Change Request (SCR) — if you're filing an SCR for a major architecture change, that's another natural forcing function where reviewers may ask for OSCAL artifacts as part of re-review.
3. Continuous monitoring (ConMon) deliverables — monthly/quarterly ConMon packages (vulnerability scan summaries, POA&M updates) are increasingly expected to be submitted in structured, ingestible formats compatible with agency GRC platforms.
4. A hard PMO-wide cutover date — the PMO has discussed sunset dates for pure Word/Excel acceptance, but historically these dates have been pushed back as tooling and 3PAO readiness lagged. Treat any specific calendar date circulating in your organization as provisional.

- Don't wait for a hard deadline to become non-negotiable to start. OSCAL conversion of a mature, already-authorized package is a substantial lift: every control implementation statement, responsibility (CSP/inherited/shared/customer), parameter value, and POA&M entry needs to be represented in structured schema-valid form. - Budget for a parallel run: many CSPs maintain Word/Excel and OSCAL versions simultaneously during transition to avoid disrupting active agency relationships while building automation muscle.

Bottom line: there is a real, PMO-driven direction toward mandatory machine-readable packages for existing Rev5 CSPs, tied most concretely to your next annual assessment or significant change request cycle rather than a single universal calendar date — confirm the specific date with FedRAMP PMO/your AO, and start the conversion work now rather than treating this as a future problem.

Under CR26 (the FedRAMP Consolidated Rules for 2026), FedRAMP has restructured its baseline labeling scheme around four Certification Classes, A through D, replacing the old FIPS 199-based Low/Moderate/High/LI-SaaS labels. The class labels change naming, not the underlying control requirements — a Class C system still maps to what used to be the Moderate baseline's requirements (NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5, 323 controls/enhancements), for example.

The four classes, per notice NTC-0004:

- Class A (Pilot/Transitional): A new baseline introduced specifically under FedRAMP 20x. It's an entry point into the federal market via external frameworks — initially SOC 2 Type II — routed through something called Program Certification. Class A has no legacy equivalent; it didn't exist before CR26. Holders get a 2-year window during which they must obtain a full Class B, C, or D certification through complete assessment — Class A is explicitly transitional, not a permanent end-state.
- Class B: Replaces the old LI-SaaS and Low baselines combined. Covers systems handling non-sensitive federal information where a breach would cause limited harm.
- Class C: Replaces the old Moderate baseline. This is the most common class — the majority of federal cloud deployments, including systems handling CUI (Controlled Unclassified Information), fall here.
- Class D: Replaces the old High baseline. Reserved for federal information where compromise would have severe or catastrophic effects — law enforcement, financial, and health data are typical examples.

Legacy-to-class mapping for translating older documents or conversations: LI-SaaS/Low → Class B, Moderate → Class C, High → Class D. Class A is genuinely new and doesn't correspond to any prior baseline. During the CR26 transition period, old and new labels remain linked so CSPs already authorized under legacy labels retain their authorization status without needing to immediately relabel.

Pipeline status as of mid-September 2026 (today is September 14, 2026):

- Class A: Open since August 3, 2026. This pipeline has been accepting applications for about six weeks at this point.
- Classes B and C: Open since August 31, 2026 — roughly two weeks old as of today. If you're pursuing either of these, you're in the very early wave of applicants under the new structure.
- Class D: Not yet open for general applications. A pilot is expected in late 2026, with a formal, non-pilot option anticipated in early 2027. If you need a High-equivalent authorization today, you are likely still working through the legacy Rev5 Agency Authorization path rather than a Class D pipeline, since Class D isn't operationally available yet.

Other relevant timing context that affects how you should think about these pipelines right now:
- CR26 itself was finalized June 25, 2026, with optional early adoption from July 4, 2026, and becomes mandatory January 1, 2027. So we're currently in the voluntary adoption window — you can choose CR26/20x pathways now, but the legacy Rev5 process is still fully valid until the mandatory date.
- FedRAMP 20x is now positioned as the primary, preferred authorization pathway going forward, built on Key Security Indicators (KSIs), machine-readable evidence, and modular API-driven submissions rather than the traditional static SSP/SAP/SAR document set.
- Legacy FedRAMP Ready was retired (relabeled "Legacy FedRAMP Ready") on July 28, 2026 — no new Ready submissions are being accepted. If you hold Rev5 Ready status, you need to convert by the later of your annual-assessment expiration or November 17, 2026, since the status disappears completely by December 31, 2027.
- JAB P-ATO is fully suspended — the FedRAMP PMO is now the sole authorizing body across all pathways.

Practical takeaway: if you're evaluating which class to pursue, ask what data sensitivity you handle (maps to B/C/D) and whether you're trying to get a foothold via an existing SOC 2 Type II (maps to Class A as a transitional strategy). Given Class D isn't open yet, a High-impact system today still needs the legacy Rev5 High agency-authorization route. Caveat up front: my knowledge of FedRAMP 20x is grounded in its early framing (roughly through late 2025), and I do not have verified, up-to-the-day visibility into "where the pipelines stand as of mid-September 2026." Treat the status portion of this answer as directional context to sanity-check against the current FedRAMP.gov 20x page, PMO announcements, and any direct conversations with the FedRAMP PMO or GSA — not as a confirmed status report.

What FedRAMP 20x is, conceptually: It's the FedRAMP PMO's initiative to fundamentally modernize how cloud services get authorized, moving away from the traditional multi-hundred-page SSP/SAP/SAR/POA&M document cycle with lengthy 3PAO assessments and toward a faster, more automated, continuously validated model. The stated goals include: dramatically reducing time-to-authorization (from many months to weeks), relying on machine-readable evidence (OSCAL, automated key security indicators/KSIs) rather than narrative documents, and enabling continuous validation rather than periodic point-in-time assessment.

On "certification classes" — FedRAMP 20x has been organized around a small number of pilot phases/cohorts rather than a fixed, published taxonomy of permanent "classes" in the way Low/Moderate/High impact levels are a fixed taxonomy under Rev5. As of my knowledge, the structure has looked roughly like this:
- Phase One (Low Impact SaaS pilot): The PMO ran an initial pilot focused on Low-impact SaaS offerings, using a streamlined set of Key Security Indicators (KSIs) instead of the full control catalog narrative, with a small cohort of participating CSPs providing real-world feedback.
- Phase Two / Moderate expansion: The intent was to extend the 20x approach to Moderate impact SaaS and eventually broader IaaS/PaaS offerings, again through cohort-based pilots rather than a general open enrollment, with lessons from Phase One feeding into the KSI catalog and automation tooling.
- Ongoing refinement: KSIs, automated validation ("continuous assessment"), and the underlying technical architecture (APIs for evidence submission, OSCAL-native artifacts) were expected to mature through iterative pilot rounds, with the PMO explicitly stating this was experimental and subject to change based on pilot results, rather than a finished, generally available program.

Because this was explicitly a rolling pilot program rather than a fixed set of "classes" with permanent definitions, I would not assume any specific class names or numbers I might guess at (e.g., "Class A/B/C") are accurate without checking the current FedRAMP 20x page — the PMO has used evolving terminology (KSIs, phases, cohorts) rather than a stable classification scheme, and by September 2026 this may have been reorganized, renamed, or formalized into something closer to an official framework alongside or replacing Rev5.

What I'd recommend to assess "where the pipelines stand" today:
1. Check FedRAMP.gov directly for the 20x program page, which typically lists active pilot cohorts, participating CSPs, and phase status.
2. Look for PMO blog posts or GSA press releases from 2026 summarizing pilot results — these usually disclose how many CSPs completed a given phase, common KSI validation gaps found, and next-phase timing.
3. Ask your 3PAO — 3PAOs participating in 20x pilots are a good source of ground-truth on how mature the automated assessment tooling actually is versus how it's being marketed.
4. Watch for signals about whether 20x is on track to formally supersede parts of Rev5 for specific impact levels/service models, or whether it remains a parallel, optional track for CSPs willing to be early adopters.
5. If you're making a go/no-go decision on participating, ask GSA directly about cohort application windows, since pilot participation has historically been limited and by invitation/application rather than open enrollment.

Bottom line: FedRAMP 20x is a genuine, PMO-driven modernization effort built on KSIs, automation, and phased/cohort-based pilots rather than a settled certification taxonomy — but the specific "classes" and pipeline status as of mid-September 2026 need to be verified against current FedRAMP PMO sources, since this program was explicitly evolving in real time even as of my training data.

For a new cloud SaaS targeting federal customers in late 2026, my recommendation is: default to pursuing FedRAMP 20x / CR26 Certification Classes rather than a legacy Rev5 agency authorization package, but the right answer depends on a few specifics I'd want to confirm with you first.

Why 20x/CR26 is the better starting point for a new entrant right now:

1. It's now the primary, preferred pathway. Under CR26 (finalized June 25, 2026, mandatory January 1, 2027), FedRAMP 20x is explicitly positioned as the go-forward authorization model — continuous authorization built on Key Security Indicators (KSIs), machine-readable evidence, and modular API-driven submissions, rather than the traditional static SSP/SAP/SAR document set. A brand-new CSO built today has no legacy investment in the old SSP/POA&M Word-template process, so there's little reason to start there when the newer model is what FedRAMP wants everyone to move toward anyway.

2. There's a real, currently-open pipeline for a new entrant. Certification Class A opened August 3, 2026 — it's specifically designed as an entry point into the federal market via an existing external framework (initially SOC 2 Type II) through Program Certification. If you already have, or can obtain, a SOC 2 Type II, Class A gives you a comparatively fast on-ramp. Classes B and C opened August 31, 2026, so as of "late 2026" both pipelines are live and accepting new applicants. As a new SaaS company, Class A → then B/C within your 2-year transition window is a plausible, sequenced strategy.

3. Legacy Rev5 is entering wind-down. New Rev5 applications stop being accepted after June 11, 2027, and Rev5 fully sunsets December 31, 2028. Legacy FedRAMP Ready — historically a common way for a new CSP to signal readiness to agency sponsors — was already retired (relabeled Legacy FedRAMP Ready) on July 28, 2026, with no new submissions accepted. Starting a brand-new Rev5 legacy package now means investing in a track that has a visible expiration and reduced sponsor interest, plus you'd need an agency sponsor for the legacy Agency Authorization path, which is often the hardest part for a new, unproven vendor.

4. Machine-readable requirements favor 20x-native tooling anyway. The OSCAL/machine-readable mandate that hits Rev5 packages hard (no grace period for new Rev5 initial certifications from September 30, 2026) explicitly does NOT apply to FedRAMP 20x, which has its own machine-readable model built in from the start. Building your compliance program around 20x-native, API-driven evidence from day one avoids retrofitting OSCAL conversion into a legacy document set later.

Where I'd still want more information before finalizing this recommendation:
- What's your target Certification Class based on the sensitivity of federal data you'll handle? If you're aiming for anything High-equivalent (Class D), that pipeline isn't open yet — pilot expected late 2026, formal option early 2027 — so a High-impact new SaaS may have no choice but to work the legacy Rev5 High agency-authorization path in parallel while waiting for Class D to mature.
- Do you have an agency sponsor lined up, or are you relying on marketplace/self-driven entry? Class A's SOC 2-based entry doesn't require a sponsoring agency the way legacy Agency Authorization does, which is often a major advantage for a new vendor without existing federal relationships.
- Do you already have or can you quickly obtain a SOC 2 Type II? If not, factor in the time to get one before Class A becomes practically available to you.
- What's your actual timeline to first federal revenue? Since CR26 becomes mandatory January 1, 2027 anyway, even a legacy Rev5 start today would likely need to transition to CR26 classes relatively soon, so there's limited benefit to starting legacy unless you have a specific sponsor already committed to the old process.

Bottom line: for most new SaaS entrants in late 2026, start with FedRAMP 20x, targeting Class A (if you have or can get SOC 2 Type II) as a bridge to Class B or C within the 2-year window, rather than initiating a new legacy Rev5 package. Reserve the legacy Rev5 path for cases where you need a High-equivalent authorization immediately and can't wait for Class D to open, or where you already have a specific agency sponsor insisting on the traditional process. Confirm current pipeline status and eligibility criteria directly with FedRAMP PMO/fedramp.gov before committing significant budget, since class definitions and pipeline timing are still evolving through the CR26 rollout.

Short answer: for most new SaaS companies targeting federal customers in late 2026, I'd lean toward pursuing Rev5 through the traditional sponsorship path (agency or JAB/FedRAMP PMO) as your primary, de-risked route, while evaluating FedRAMP 20x opportunistically if you qualify for and can get into an active pilot cohort — but this depends heavily on your risk tolerance, timeline, target agency, and impact level. Note also that my visibility into the exact state of 20x as of late 2026 is limited (see caveats below), so validate this against current FedRAMP PMO guidance before finalizing your strategy.

Key considerations:

1. Certainty and maturity of the path. Rev5 is the established, well-understood process: a defined control baseline (NIST SP 800-53 Rev5), known documentation requirements (SSP, SAP, SAR, POA&M), known 3PAO assessment process, and known timelines (typically 12-18+ months for agency authorization, often longer for JAB). Every agency ATO officer, every 3PAO, and most GRC tooling vendors know how to work within this framework. FedRAMP 20x, by contrast, has been a pilot program with limited cohorts, evolving requirements (Key Security Indicators, automated continuous validation), and no guarantee that agencies broadly recognize or will accept a 20x-based authorization the same way they accept a Rev5 P-ATO or agency ATO today. For a new company that needs revenue certainty and predictable time-to-market, betting the whole go-to-market plan on an unproven, still-evolving pilot track carries real execution risk.

2. Impact level and service model fit. If you are a Low-impact SaaS offering, 20x's pilot programs have specifically targeted that segment, so if you qualify, can get into a cohort, and your target agency is comfortable with a 20x-based package, it may genuinely be faster and cheaper than a full Rev5 Low authorization. If you're Moderate impact (which covers a large share of commercial SaaS handling federal data) or if you're IaaS/PaaS rather than SaaS, the 20x pipeline has been less mature for your category as of my knowledge, making Rev5 the more realistic near-term path regardless of ambition.

3. Your specific agency sponsor's posture. If you already have a specific agency champion who wants to sponsor you, ask them directly which path they're comfortable authorizing under. Many agency ISSOs and AOs are still most comfortable with Rev5 packages because that's what their internal risk acceptance processes, GRC tools, and legal reviews are built around. An agency sponsor's willingness (or lack of it) to accept a 20x-based authorization should be a primary input to your decision, more than the PMO's marketing of 20x's speed advantages.

4. Timeline reality check. FedRAMP authorization of any kind is rarely fast for a brand-new company, especially one without existing FISMA or FedRAMP-adjacent experience. Whichever path you choose, budget 12+ months minimum, factor in 3PAO selection and contracting lead time (often 2-3 months just to onboard a 3PAO), and expect that your engineering and security teams will need meaningful investment in continuous monitoring capability regardless of framework.

5. Hedge your bet where possible. Some CSPs have pursued Rev5 as their primary authorization path while simultaneously engaging with FedRAMP 20x pilots for a subset of low-risk offerings or as an early-adopter learning exercise, positioning themselves to move faster into 20x-native processes once those mature and gain broader agency acceptance. If your company has the resources, this dual-track approach reduces the risk of picking the "wrong" long-term horse without sacrificing near-term revenue-enabling authorization.

Recommendation: Start conversations now, in parallel:
- With FedRAMP PMO/GSA about current 20x cohort eligibility and timelines for your impact level and service model.
- With your target agency sponsor about which path they're prepared to authorize under, since agency acceptance is the actual gating factor regardless of PMO marketing.
- With 3PAOs about capacity and cost for either path, since 3PAO availability is often the real bottleneck.

Default to Rev5 as the resourced, funded, primary plan unless you get concrete signals — from both GSA and your agency sponsor — that a 20x path is open, appropriate for your impact level, and will be accepted as a valid authorization by the agencies you're actually trying to sell to. Don't let program novelty or marketing momentum around 20x cause you to under-resource the proven path.

FedRAMP POA&M remediation and continuous monitoring (ConMon) work together as a single ongoing risk-management cycle once you're authorized. Here's how it fits together.

POA&M basics
The Plan of Action & Milestones (SSP Appendix O) is the living document that tracks every known security weakness — from initial 3PAO assessment findings, annual assessment findings, or vulnerability scans — and your plan to fix each one. It's not a one-time deliverable; it's updated monthly for the life of your authorization.

Each POA&M row needs, at minimum: a unique item ID, the affected NIST 800-53 Rev 5 control(s), a weakness name and description, point of contact, resources required, remediation plan, original detection date, scheduled completion date, milestone change history, status (Open/Closed/Risk Adjusted/Vendor Dependency), risk rating, and flags for false positive / deviation approval / operational requirement. One finding per row — don't bundle multiple vulnerabilities together, since that obscures tracking and remediation evidence.

Remediation SLAs (from the FedRAMP Continuous Monitoring Performance Management Guide)
- Critical (where scanners distinguish it from High): treat as ≤30 calendar days, prioritized immediately — effectively High-or-stricter.
- High: 30 calendar days from identification.
- Moderate: 90 calendar days from identification.
- Low: 180 calendar days from identification.

These clocks start at identification, not at when you get around to triaging the finding, so timely intake and risk-rating of new findings matters as much as the fix itself. Missing these SLAs is one of the most common ConMon findings agencies flag, so track dates carefully and don't let milestone dates slip without documented, approved changes.

Three ways an item can resolve besides a straight fix:
1. Vendor Dependency (VD): the fix depends on a third party (OS vendor, SaaS tool, IaaS provider). You must document the vendor, a tracking ID (CVE or vendor ticket), and expected fix date; your 3PAO validates VDs at annual assessment, and you still need compensating controls in the meantime.
2. Deviation Request (DR): three subtypes — False Positive (the finding isn't real, with evidence), Risk Adjustment (real but lower actual risk due to mitigating factors, quantified), and Operational Requirement (can't fix without breaking functionality, requires documented business justification and compensating controls). All DRs require agency AO approval before you can mark them as such.
3. Closed with evidence: when you close an item, attach the actual evidence of remediation — a clean scan result, a configuration screenshot, a dated confirmation — not just a status change.

Continuous Monitoring cadence
Monthly:
- Submit vulnerability scan results to your agency AO(s).
- Update the POA&M — open findings, remediation progress, new milestone dates.
- Update your asset inventory (IIW) for new/removed assets, including ephemeral cloud-native resources like auto-scaling instances and containers.
- Submit the ConMon Monthly Executive Summary.

Annually:
- Full security assessment by your 3PAO using the Annual Assessment Controls Selection Worksheet (which pulls from four tabs: the Rev 5 control list, conditional controls, CSP-specific controls based on system changes/ConMon activity, and inherited controls from leveraged FedRAMP systems). No control can go untested for more than three years, so selection isn't arbitrary — it cycles through your full baseline over time plus anything flagged by recent activity.
- Updated SSP and appendices.
- Tested Incident Response Plan and Contingency Plan (tabletop minimum; functional exercise preferred, and generally expected for High/Class D).
- Updated SAR and POA&M reflecting the annual assessment's findings — every SAR finding must appear as a POA&M row; agencies cross-reference these directly.

Two things that will actively hurt you in ConMon if overlooked:
- Stale POA&M items — no milestone updates, missed dates without an approved deviation — can trigger suspension of your ATO. Agencies treat a stale POA&M as a signal that the CSP isn't actively managing risk, not just an administrative lapse.
- The Security Inbox requirement (effective January 5, 2026): all authorized CSPs must maintain a dedicated Security Inbox, with no CAPTCHAs or access barriers, so government can reach you quickly with urgent vulnerability directives. This should be referenced in both your Incident Response Plan and your Continuous Monitoring Plan (Appendix M).

Practical advice: build your POA&M tracking into whatever GRC tool or system you already use for scan management so that identification dates, SLA clocks, and milestone updates are captured automatically rather than reconstructed manually each month — reconstructing dates after the fact is exactly what produces the "stale POA&M" and "missed SLA" findings that agencies flag most often. And keep your SSP control narratives, POA&M, and CIS/CRM workbook internally consistent — a control marked "Implemented" in the SSP but appearing as an open weakness in the POA&M is a common inconsistency finding during annual assessment.

Here's how a GRC consultant typically walks a client through POA&M remediation timelines and continuous monitoring (ConMon) expectations under FedRAMP. This is based on the well-established Rev5/traditional FedRAMP framework; if your organization is operating under a FedRAMP 20x pilot, some mechanics (e.g., automated KSI validation replacing parts of manual ConMon) may differ, so confirm specifics against your governing ConMon plan and PMO guidance.

POA&M basics: The Plan of Action and Milestones is the living document that tracks every known weakness or deficiency in your system — findings from the initial assessment, vulnerability scans, penetration tests, incident-driven findings, and control deviations — along with remediation plans, responsible parties, and target completion dates. FedRAMP requires you to maintain and submit updated POA&Ms on a recurring basis (typically monthly) to your authorizing agency or the PMO, and reviewers actively track whether you're closing items within required timeframes.

Standard remediation timelines (these are the widely cited FedRAMP targets, derived from vulnerability severity):
- Critical vulnerabilities: remediate within 30 days of detection.
- High vulnerabilities: remediate within 30 days of detection (in earlier guidance sometimes bucketed with critical; current FedRAMP guidance has trended toward treating Critical and High similarly, often both at 30 days, though some references use a tighter window for Critical — verify the exact current SLA in your ConMon plan and the FedRAMP Continuous Monitoring Strategy Guide).
- Moderate vulnerabilities: remediate within 90 days of detection.
- Low vulnerabilities: remediate within 180 days of detection, or per your organization's risk-based justification.

These clocks start from the date of detection (typically the scan date), not the date the finding is written up or reported, which is a common compliance pitfall — organizations that delay internal triage effectively shorten their own remediation window without realizing it.

Deviation requests: If you cannot remediate within the standard window — due to vendor patch unavailability, business-critical system dependencies, compensating controls, or operational constraints — you must submit a formal risk adjustment/deviation request to your AO, with justification, compensating controls, and a revised target date. These aren't automatic; the AO can reject the deviation and require faster remediation, and a pattern of repeated deviation requests without real progress is a common trigger for authorization concerns or agency escalation.

POA&M submission cadence: Monthly POA&M updates are the norm, submitted alongside your monthly ConMon deliverables. Each submission should show: new findings added, findings closed with evidence, status changes on open items, and updated target dates for anything slipping. Agencies and 3PAOs specifically scrutinize aging open items — findings sitting open well past their target date without documented deviation are a red flag in annual assessments and can jeopardize your ATO.

Continuous monitoring deliverables more broadly, beyond POA&M, typically include:
- Monthly vulnerability scan results (infrastructure, database, web application) and a summary of scan-to-POA&M reconciliation.
- Monthly or quarterly significant change requests for any architecture, control, or personnel changes that affect your security posture.
- Annual security assessment — essentially a mini re-assessment by your 3PAO covering a representative control sample, updated SSP, updated SAR, incident response test results, and contingency plan test results.
- Annual FedRAMP Annual Assessment package submission to your authorizing agency, which is the formal checkpoint where continued authorization is affirmed or challenged.
- Incident reporting — actual security incidents must be reported to US-CERT/CISA and your agency within specified timeframes (historically as fast as 1 hour for confirmed incidents under federal incident reporting requirements, though exact thresholds depend on incident category), separate from the routine POA&M cycle.

Practical recommendations:
1. Build internal SLAs tighter than the FedRAMP minimums (e.g., target 21 days for Critical/High) so that normal internal friction doesn't blow your compliance deadline.
2. Automate scan-to-POA&M ingestion where possible; manual reconciliation is the most common source of missed findings and stale entries.
3. Track POA&M aging as a standing metric in your internal risk dashboard, not just at submission time, so leadership sees overdue items before the agency does.
4. Treat deviation requests as an exception process requiring real justification and compensating controls, not a routine way to manage a backlog — auditors and AOs notice patterns of habitual deviation requests.
5. Rehearse your annual assessment readiness continuously rather than scrambling annually — your ConMon discipline throughout the year is what actually determines how smooth (or painful) the annual assessment turns out to be.

Bottom line: FedRAMP's POA&M and ConMon regime is built around risk-tiered remediation SLAs (roughly 30/90/180 days for Critical-High/Moderate/Low), monthly reporting discipline, and an annual re-assessment checkpoint — the organizations that struggle are almost always the ones that let internal triage delay the remediation clock or that treat deviation requests as routine rather than exceptional.
Prompt: We run a consumer app with several location-related settings. What does the September 2026 Google decision mean for how we design them?
With Skill
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 5/5 assertions passed (100%)
✅Cites the decision: the Irish DPC fined Google Ireland €403,000,000 (final September 21, 2026) as lead supervisory authority
✅Identifies the processing: location data across Web & App Activity, Location History and Location Accuracy
✅States the findings across the ladder: unlawful/unfair processing, transparency failures (Arts. 12/13), accountability gaps, and retention longer than necessary — Arts. 5, 6, 12, 13
✅Mentions the 6-month compliance order (and treats any appeal as reported, not confirmed)
✅Draws design lessons: each location feature needs its own lawful basis, specific transparency and retention limits — bundled 'improve your experience' framing across settings is the failure pattern
**Direct answer:** The Irish DPC's decision against Google Ireland (21 September 2026, EUR 403,000,000) tells you to treat every location-related setting as its own processing operation, each needing its own lawful basis, its own specific transparency and its own retention limit. Bundled, vague "improve your experience" framing across several toggles is the failure pattern.

**What the DPC found (verify against the published decision before relying on detail)**
The DPC acted as lead supervisory authority under Art. 60, following an own-volition inquiry opened in February 2020 after BEUC-coordinated complaints. It examined three settings: Web & App Activity, Location History and Location Accuracy. It found:
- Unlawful and unfair processing for Web & App Activity and Location History (Arts. 5(1)(a), 6).
- Insufficient transparency for all three (Arts. 5(1)(a), 12, 13).
- An accountability gap for Location Accuracy (Art. 5(2)).
- Retention longer than necessary for Web & App Activity and Location History (Art. 5(1)(e)).
It ordered compliance within six months. Google is reported to be appealing, but I can't confirm that, so treat the decision as not yet final.

**Design implications for your app**

1. **Map each setting to a distinct purpose and lawful basis (Arts. 5(1)(b), 6).**
   - Do not let one consent or one "location on" switch cover several purposes such as navigation, personalisation, analytics and advertising.
   - If you rely on consent, it must be specific, informed, unambiguous and as easy to withdraw as to give (Art. 7; Recital 32). Granularity matters. Where separate purposes are bundled, consent is unlikely to be valid.
   - If you rely on contract (Art. 6(1)(b)), it only covers location processing that is objectively necessary for the service the user asked for. Personalisation and ad profiling rarely meet that test.
   - If you rely on legitimate interests, you need a documented LIA. Under EDPB Guidelines 1/2024 the interest must be real and present, the processing necessary, and the balancing honest. Precise or historical location is sensitive in practice because it reveals home, work, health-related visits and religious or political attendance. That weighs heavily against you and can bring Art. 9 into play through inference.

2. **Make transparency setting-specific (Arts. 12, 13).**
   - The notice, and the in-product text at the toggle, should say what each setting collects (GPS, Wi-Fi, cell, IP-derived), what it is used for, who receives it and how long it is kept.
   - Explain what actually changes if the user turns it off.
   - Do not describe two settings that behave differently in one sentence.

3. **Set and enforce retention per setting (Art. 5(1)(e)).**
   - Define a period for each location data type and implement automatic deletion or aggregation. Include backups and analytics copies.
   - Document the rationale for each period. "Until the user deletes it" is hard to defend as a default.

4. **Show accountability (Art. 5(2), Art. 24).**
   - Keep records of consent (Art. 7(1)), the LIA and the RoPA entry (Art. 30) for each setting.
   - Maintain a data-flow map that shows where each location signal goes. The Location Accuracy finding suggests regulators will ask you to prove how a setting works, not just describe it.

5. **Apply privacy by default and design (Art. 25).**
   - Default to off for non-essential location collection.
   - Offer a coarse-location option where it serves the feature.
   - Don't use dark patterns. Equal prominence for accept and reject is a standing enforcement priority.

6. **Check the device layer.** If you read location from the device, the ePrivacy Directive Art. 5(3) as transposed nationally may require consent for accessing information on the terminal, in addition to GDPR. The ePrivacy Regulation was withdrawn in February 2025, and the Digital Omnibus proposal to fold these rules into GDPR is not yet law.

7. **Run a DPIA (Art. 35)** if you track location systematically at scale or combine it with other data. Location tracking is a recognised high-risk indicator in regulator DPIA lists. Children's data raises the bar further (Art. 8).

- For each, record the purpose, lawful basis, notice text, retention period and downstream recipients.
- Remove or merge settings you can't justify separately.
- Test whether the user-visible description matches what the code does.

**Caveats:** Whether a given setting needs consent or can rest on another basis depends on your facts and Member State law, and you should confirm that with counsel.

What follows is how I would approach location-setting design under GDPR and ePrivacy, based on the established law and guidance that any such decision would sit within. Treat it as a design framework, not an analysis of that ruling.

1. Location data is personal data, and often sensitive in effect
Precise location (GPS, Wi-Fi, Bluetooth beacons) is personal data under Art. 4(1). It is not a special category by default, but regulators treat it as high-risk. It can reveal religion (place of worship), health (clinics), sexual orientation or political views, and the EDPB and CJEU (Meta v Bundeskartellamt, C-252/21) accept that inferences from data can bring Art. 9 into play. Location history also feeds DPIA triggers (large-scale tracking, vulnerable users, innovative tech).

2. Consent under ePrivacy and GDPR
- Accessing the device's location, or storing or reading information on the terminal, engages Art. 5(3) ePrivacy Directive, which requires consent in most cases. Where location comes from a telecom operator, Art. 9 ePrivacy also requires consent.
- Consent must meet GDPR standards (Arts. 4(11), 7): freely given, specific, informed, unambiguous, as easy to withdraw as to give.
- The OS permission prompt is not enough on its own. It does not tell users who processes the data, for what purposes, or for how long. Pair it with an in-app explanation before the prompt.

3. Design implications for multiple location settings
- Granularity: separate settings for precise, approximate and none. Default to the least invasive that delivers the feature. Many features (weather, local content) work with city-level data.
- Purpose separation: "location for the core feature", "location for personalisation", "location for ads or analytics" and "location for product improvement" should be separate, unbundled choices. Consent for one purpose cannot be assumed for another.
- No dark patterns: equal prominence for accept and decline, no pre-ticked boxes, no repeated nagging after refusal, no degraded service where location is not necessary (Art. 7(4), EDPB guidelines on deceptive design patterns).
- Background versus foreground: "while using" and "always" are materially different. Require a separate, specific opt-in for background collection and remind users periodically that it is on.
- Consistency across surfaces: if a user turns off location in one account setting but a different setting (ad personalisation, "web and app activity", history) still lets inferred or IP-derived location be used, regulators will see that as misleading. The settings must map to actual data flows. Check that IP-based, Wi-Fi-based and inferred location are all covered by what you tell users.
- Withdrawal and deletion: turning a setting off should stop collection immediately, and you need a way to delete stored history. Auto-delete defaults (for example 3 months) support storage limitation under Art. 5(1)(e).
- Transparency: explain in plain language what each setting does, who receives the data (including ad partners and SDKs), and retention. Layer notices and just-in-time prompts (Arts. 12-14).
- Children: if minors use the app, apply Art. 8, default off, and heightened scrutiny.

4. Governance steps
- Do a DPIA on location features.
- Map every SDK and third party that receives location, and set data processing agreements or joint-controller arrangements.
- Keep consent records (what was shown, when, which version).
- Apply data minimisation and privacy by default (Art. 25). The default state of every location setting should be the most protective one.
- Audit whether settings labels match behaviour. In practice, the major enforcement risk is a gap between what the UI says and what systems do.
- Check international transfers if location data leaves the EEA.

5. Practical next steps
1. Inventory every location signal and purpose.
2. Rebuild settings around purpose-specific, granular, default-off choices.
3. Test the UI for dark patterns with a user-research review.
4. Update the privacy notice and the record of processing.
5. Review the actual decision when you share it, and adjust for any specific holding on consent granularity, default states, or how settings must reflect data flows.

**Direct answer:** A supervisory authority (SA) is not required to fine you. Under Art. 58(2), a fine (Art. 83) is one corrective power among several, and the choice depends on the case. EDPB Guidelines 04/2026 (adopted at the September 2026 plenary, consultation open until 13 November) set out a five-step methodology for deciding whether to fine at all. The guidelines are still in draft, so treat the detail as provisional and check the published text.

**The corrective-powers toolkit (Art. 58(2))**
From lightest to heaviest, an SA can:
- Issue a warning that intended processing is likely to infringe (Art. 58(2)(a)).
- Issue a reprimand (Art. 58(2)(b)).
- Order you to comply with data subject requests (Art. 58(2)(c)).
- Order you to bring processing into compliance, in a specified way and period (Art. 58(2)(d)).
- Order notification of a breach to data subjects (Art. 58(2)(e)).
- Impose a temporary or definitive limitation or ban on processing (Art. 58(2)(f)).
- Order rectification, erasure or restriction (Art. 58(2)(g)).
- Withdraw certifications (Art. 58(2)(h)).
- Impose an administrative fine, in addition to or instead of the above (Art. 58(2)(i); Art. 83).
- Order suspension of data flows to a third country (Art. 58(2)(j)).

Art. 83(2) says a fine can be imposed "in addition to, or instead of" other measures, and that it must be effective, proportionate and dissuasive in each case (Art. 83(1)).

**Factors that push towards a fine (Art. 83(2))**
- **Nature, gravity and duration** of the infringement, and the number of data subjects and damage suffered. Long-running, large-scale processing is the typical fine case.
- **Intentional or negligent character.** Deliberate or reckless conduct, such as ignoring clear guidance or prior warnings, weighs heavily.
- **Categories of data.** Special category data, children's data and location data raise gravity.
- **Core obligations breached.** Lawfulness, transparency, consent, data subject rights and international transfers (the Art. 83(5) tier, up to EUR 20M or 4% of worldwide turnover) are fined more readily than procedural lapses (the Art. 83(4) tier, up to EUR 10M or 2%).
- **Failure to mitigate** or to cooperate with the SA (Art. 83(2)(c), (f)).
- **Previous infringements** and repeat behaviour. Uber has been fined four times by the Dutch AP.
- **Late or poor breach notification** (Art. 83(2)(h)).
- **Financial benefit gained** from the infringement (Art. 83(2)(k)).

**Factors that favour an order or lesser measure**
- A first-time, isolated or short-lived infringement with limited impact.
- Prompt self-detection, notification and remediation.
- Genuine cooperation with the SA.
- Documented accountability: a DPO, a RoPA, a DPIA and training (Art. 83(2)(d)).
- Adherence to approved codes of conduct or certifications (Art. 83(2)(j)).
- Genuinely unclear legal questions where no clear guidance existed.
- Small organisations for whom a fine would be disproportionate, where the SA judges an order sufficient. National practice varies.

**Recent enforcement context**
Fines in 2026 show the pattern for serious cases. The Dutch AP fined Uber EUR 824.99M (21 August 2026) for fully automated driver deactivations with no meaningful human review (Art. 22) and inadequate transparency. The Irish DPC fined Google EUR 403M (21 September 2026) over location data, finding unlawful processing, transparency failures, accountability gaps and excessive retention, with a six-month compliance order. Both involved large-scale, long-running, core-principle breaches. In each case the SA paired the fine with, or kept the option of, corrective orders, so a fine does not replace the duty to fix. Both are reported or expected to be appealed.

At the other end, the CEF 2025 erasure action produced mostly guidance and follow-up orders, not fines. The CEF 2026 action will cover transparency (Arts. 13-14).

**Practical implications**
- Fixing quickly does not guarantee you avoid a fine, but it is one of the strongest mitigating factors.
- Keep evidence of your accountability measures before an inquiry starts. An SA won't credit controls it cannot see.
- Notify breaches on time (Art. 33) and cooperate (Art. 31).
- Respond to SA information requests fully and promptly. Obstruction is itself an infringement and an aggravating factor.
- Cross-border cases run through the one-stop-shop (Art. 60) and may involve the EDPB dispute mechanism (Art. 65), which tends to increase fine levels.
- National procedural law and SA culture differ. Some SAs lean towards orders and reprimands, others towards fines.

I can't predict a specific outcome. It turns on facts and on which authority handles the case.
