A cloud vendor hosting your EHR is a business associate under HIPAA — even if it never actually opens or views the PHI, the mere fact that it stores or transmits ePHI on your behalf triggers the requirement — so you need a Business Associate Agreement (BAA) before any PHI touches that environment, not as a formality after the fact. Here's what needs to be in it, drawing on the required elements at 45 CFR §164.314(a) and §164.504(e).

1. Permitted uses and disclosures. The BAA must specify exactly what the vendor is allowed to do with the PHI — generally limited to providing the hosting/EHR service itself, plus narrowly defined activities like the vendor's own management/administration or legal responsibilities, and data aggregation if applicable. It should explicitly prohibit any use or disclosure beyond what the underlying services agreement requires, and prohibit any use for the vendor's own marketing, product development, or resale purposes unless you've separately and explicitly agreed to that (and even then, additional authorization requirements may apply).

2. Safeguards commitment. The vendor must agree to implement appropriate administrative, physical, and technical safeguards to prevent unauthorized use or disclosure of the PHI, and — since this is ePHI hosted in the cloud — the BAA should explicitly incorporate compliance with the Security Rule's safeguards (access controls, audit controls, integrity controls, transmission security, encryption where appropriate), not just the general Privacy Rule safeguard language.

3. Reporting obligations. The BAA must require the vendor to report to you any use or disclosure not permitted by the agreement, and — critically — any security incident it becomes aware of, and any breach of unsecured PHI, within a specified timeframe. Since you as the covered entity have your own 60-day breach notification clock to patients/HHS, your BAA needs a tighter internal deadline for the vendor to notify you (many organizations negotiate 24-72 hours for the vendor to report a known or suspected breach) so you have runway to meet your own obligations.

4. Subcontractor flow-down. If the cloud vendor uses its own subcontractors that will have access to PHI (e.g., a subprocessor providing infrastructure, backup, or support services), the BAA must require the vendor to ensure those subcontractors agree to the same restrictions and conditions via their own BAA-equivalent agreements. This is especially relevant for cloud hosting, where infrastructure providers (underlying cloud platform), monitoring tools, backup vendors, and support/ticketing systems may all touch PHI indirectly.

5. Individual rights support. The agreement must require the vendor to make PHI available to you (or, per your instructions, directly to the individual) to support patient access requests, and to make amendments to PHI as directed, and to provide an accounting of disclosures as needed to support your obligations under the Privacy Rule.

6. Availability to HHS. The vendor must agree to make its internal practices, books, and records relating to PHI use/disclosure available to HHS for compliance determination purposes.

7. Return or destruction of PHI at termination. At the end of the relationship, the BAA must require the vendor to return or destroy all PHI it holds, if feasible; if return/destruction isn't feasible (a real issue with cloud backups and replicated storage), the agreement must extend the same protections to the retained PHI for as long as it's retained and limit further uses/disclosures to those purposes that made return/destruction infeasible.

8. Termination rights. You need the right to terminate the agreement if the vendor materially violates the BAA terms, and if termination isn't feasible, the right to report the violation to HHS.

Beyond the strict regulatory minimums, a few practical items worth negotiating specifically for a cloud EHR hosting arrangement: data residency/location commitments (where the data centers are physically located), encryption specifications (at rest and in transit, key management ownership), audit rights (your ability to request SOC 2 reports, penetration test summaries, or conduct your own security assessment), data portability/export commitments so you're not locked in if you switch vendors, defined uptime/availability SLAs since this is your EHR, cyber insurance requirements, and indemnification allocation for breach-related costs (notification, credit monitoring, regulatory fines attributable to the vendor's failure).

Before you sign, confirm this BAA is a standalone agreement or a properly incorporated addendum/exhibit to the master services agreement, that it doesn't conflict with liability caps or indemnification language elsewhere in the contract, and that your own IT/security team has actually validated the technical safeguard claims (don't just accept a BAA's promises — request the vendor's HITRUST certification, SOC 2 Type II report, or equivalent independent attestation).

This is general guidance, not legal advice — given how central an EHR hosting relationship is to your compliance posture, I'd have healthcare/HIPAA counsel review the final BAA and its interplay with the broader services contract before execution.

Yes — there is a NIST publication specifically for transit agencies, and it's very recent.

**NIST IR 8576 — Transit Cybersecurity Framework Community Profile** was finalized on August 5, 2026. It's a CSF 2.0 Community Profile built specifically for U.S. transit agencies operating bus, subway/rail, and commuter rail systems — which matches your organization directly. A "Community Profile" in NIST CSF terms is a pre-built Target Profile developed by and for a specific sector, so that individual organizations don't have to build a target state from scratch. It reflects the shared risk priorities, threat landscape, and operational-technology (OT) realities common to transit operators — think fare collection systems, positive train control / signaling, SCADA for traction power, CCTV and access control at stations and yards, and the IT/OT convergence that comes with connected fleet and infrastructure.

A few important framing points:

1. **It complements, not replaces, your existing program.** NIST IR 8576 is explicitly designed to sit alongside whatever cybersecurity program you already run — it is not a compliance mandate and does not override FTA, TSA Security Directives, or other regulatory obligations you may have. Treat it as a sector-tuned starting point for your CSF 2.0 Target Profile, not a checklist to certify against.

2. **How to use it practically**: Start by comparing the subcategories the Community Profile emphasizes against your Current Profile (your actual state today). Because transit is OT-heavy, expect the profile to weight several categories more heavily than a generic enterprise target would:
   - **GV.SC** (Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management) — vendor-supplied signaling, fare, and SCADA systems carry outsized risk and are hard to patch or replace on short notice.
   - **PR.IR** (Technology Infrastructure Resilience) — redundancy and resilience for OT/ICS environments controlling rail and bus operations.
   - **PR.AA** (Identity Management, Authentication, and Access Control) — especially physical access control at stations, yards, and control centers (PR.AA-06).
   - **DE.CM** (Continuous Monitoring) — OT environments often have limited native logging, so monitoring coverage tends to be a real gap.
   - **RS.MA / RC.RP** — incident and recovery plans need to explicitly account for safety-of-life and service-continuity implications unique to transit (a "recovery" isn't done until trains/buses are safely running again, not just when IT systems are restored).

3. **Sequencing**: As with any CSF adoption, don't jump straight into PR/DE/RS work. Establish GV.OC (organizational context — safety mission, regulatory obligations under FTA/TSA) and GV.RM (risk tolerance) first, then build/validate your asset inventory (ID.AM) covering both IT and OT assets, before layering in the transit-specific Community Profile priorities.

4. **Two other recent NIST companion publications are worth knowing about, though they're general-purpose rather than transit-specific**:
   - **NIST SP 1353** (initial public draft, Aug 19, 2026, comments due Oct 15, 2026) — a quick-start guide on using generative AI to support CSF analysis, planning, and profile drafting. If you're considering AI-assisted tooling to accelerate your gap assessment or profile-building work, this is the relevant guidance (illustrative use cases, not a certified methodology).
   - **NIST SP 1347** (final, Aug 25, 2026) — explains how CSF 2.0 Informative References and crosswalks work, useful if you need to map your transit profile back to NIST SP 800-53, TSA requirements, or other frameworks your agency is already subject to.

**Recommended next step**: I can help you build a gap assessment or Target Profile using NIST IR 8576 as the baseline, layered against your current cybersecurity state and any FTA/TSA-mandated controls. If you share your current maturity (e.g., do you have documented asset inventories for OT systems, an existing incident response plan, etc.), I can produce a Function-by-Function gap table with priorities.

This is general informational guidance based on publicly available NIST publications, not legal or audit advice — for a transit-specific security directive or certification determination, involve qualified counsel or an accredited assessor, and confirm details against the primary NIST IR 8576 document and any applicable TSA Security Directives.

Short answer: NIST itself does not publish a transit-specific version of the Cybersecurity Framework (CSF), but there is a well-developed body of sector guidance you should layer on top of CSF 2.0, and several transit-focused resources that map directly to CSF functions and categories.

1. NIST CSF 2.0 as your foundation
CSF 2.0 (released February 2024) is deliberately sector-agnostic. It gives you six functions — Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover — and expects each sector or company to build an "organizational profile" that tailors the subcategories to its own risk context. For a transit agency, that context includes both IT (fare systems, HR, finance, email) and OT/ICS (train control, signaling, SCADA for traction power, positive train control, transit signal priority, CCTV, fare gates, and increasingly connected/autonomous vehicle systems). CSF's Govern function is a good fit for transit because it forces explicit conversations about risk appetite, board/leadership oversight, and supply chain risk — all things transit agencies historically underinvested in relative to safety-critical operations.

2. Surface transportation / transit-specific guidance to combine with CSF
- TSA Security Directives and the TSA/DHS "Surface Transportation Cybersecurity Toolkit" — TSA has issued cybersecurity requirements for higher-risk surface transportation entities (originally aimed at freight rail and rail transit, with some extension to other modes) requiring designation of a cybersecurity coordinator, incident reporting to CISA, a cybersecurity implementation plan, and vulnerability assessments. These directives explicitly reference NIST CSF as an acceptable framework for structuring your program.
- APTA (American Public Transportation Association) has published cybersecurity guidance and recommended practices for transit systems, including a Control and Communications Security recommended practice and enterprise cybersecurity framework guidance for both rail and bus operations. APTA's work is generally structured to align with, or explicitly reference, the NIST CSF functions.
- FTA (Federal Transit Administration) has issued cybersecurity guidance and resources for transit agencies, including recommendations tied to the NIST CSF and to safety management systems (since FTA regulates transit safety via SMS/PTASP).
- CISA's Transportation Systems Sector guidance and the Sector-Specific/Sector Risk Management Agency materials for transportation include cyber-physical convergence guidance relevant to rail and bus signaling systems.
- NIST's own cross-sector guidance for industrial control systems — NIST SP 800-82 (Guide to Operational Technology Security) — is directly relevant to your rail signaling, SCADA, and traction power systems, and NIST SP 800-53 provides the control catalog you'd use if you need to get more granular than CSF subcategories.

3. Practical approach
- Treat CSF 2.0 as your governance and communication framework (useful for board reporting, budget justification, maturity tracking, and cross-department alignment between IT security, OT/rail engineering, and safety).
- Use TSA Security Directive requirements and CISA reporting obligations as your compliance floor — these are mandatory if you're a designated higher-risk agency.
- Use APTA and FTA recommended practices for transit-specific operational detail (e.g., segmentation guidance for train control networks, fare system PCI considerations, CCTV/access control convergence).
- Use SP 800-82 for OT-specific control selection within your Protect/Detect subcategories.
- Build a single organizational profile that explicitly separates IT and OT/safety-critical asset categories, since transit agencies typically have very different risk tolerances and change-management constraints between the two (a signaling system patch cadence is nothing like a corporate laptop patch cadence).

4. Governance note
Given TSA's mandatory security directives for transit, I'd recommend explicitly cross-walking your CSF profile subcategories to the TSA directive requirements (cybersecurity coordinator designation, incident reporting timelines, vulnerability assessment cadence, implementation plan content) so you have one profile that satisfies both your voluntary CSF maturity goals and your regulatory obligations. If you're not sure whether your agency is currently designated as "higher-risk" under the TSA directives, that's worth confirming with your general counsel or TSA point of contact, since it changes which requirements are mandatory versus best-practice.

In short: no CSF-transit crosswalk exists as an official NIST publication, but combining CSF 2.0 with TSA's surface transportation directives, APTA/FTA guidance, and NIST SP 800-82 for OT gives you a defensible, sector-appropriate program.

Yes, there is NIST guidance on this, and yes, generative AI can support your CSF assessment work — with important caveats on scope and reliability.

**The relevant publication**: NIST SP 1353, released as an initial public draft on August 19, 2026 (public comment period open through October 15, 2026). It's a quick-start guide specifically on using generative AI for CSF analysis, planning, and reporting. Because it's still in draft/comment status, treat its guidance as provisional — it may change before finalization, and you should revisit it once the final version is published.

**What SP 1353 covers**: The draft lays out three notional use cases where generative AI can meaningfully accelerate CSF work:

1. **Governance and policy review** — using AI to review existing cybersecurity policies against GV function subcategories (e.g., GV.PO-01, GV.PO-02), flag gaps in language, or draft/redline policy sections faster than manual review alone.
2. **Current State Profile drafting** — using AI to help synthesize existing documentation, control evidence, interview notes, or audit findings into a structured Current Profile (subcategory-by-subcategory current-state ratings), which is normally one of the more labor-intensive parts of a gap assessment.
3. **Target State Profile drafting** — using AI to help translate business requirements, risk appetite statements, and regulatory obligations into a draft Target Profile, which a human reviewer then validates and adjusts.

Critically, NIST frames these as **illustrative use cases, not a prescriptive or certified assessment methodology**. That distinction matters for how you should actually use this in practice:

- **AI can accelerate drafting and synthesis, but it cannot perform the assessment itself.** A gap assessment's Current State ratings must be grounded in actual evidence (interviews, control testing, log review, documentation) — an AI model does not have visibility into your environment and cannot independently verify whether a control is "Fully Implemented" versus "Partially Implemented." Any AI-drafted profile is a starting hypothesis that a qualified human assessor must validate against real evidence.
- **Human review and sign-off remain mandatory.** Given that CSF profiles often feed into audit, regulatory, or board-level risk reporting, AI-drafted content should be clearly marked as a draft pending review, with a named human owner accountable for the final version.
- **Watch for hallucinated specificity.** Generative AI is prone to fabricating plausible-sounding subcategory mappings, control citations, or maturity justifications. Anyone using AI output in a formal profile should independently verify every subcategory ID and every specific claim about control implementation against the actual NIST CSF 2.0 text and your organization's real evidence — do not take AI-generated citations at face value.
- **Confidentiality and data handling matter.** If you're feeding internal risk assessments, control gaps, or incident history into a generative AI tool to help draft profiles, make sure that's consistent with your data classification and vendor risk policies (this itself is a PR.DS / GV.SC consideration) — don't paste sensitive risk data into a public-facing AI tool without going through your normal data-handling approval process.

**Practical way to apply this to your program**:
- Use AI (including a tool like this one, equipped with the CSF skill) to help draft your subcategory-by-subcategory Current Profile table from existing documentation you provide, and to draft a proposed Target Profile from your stated risk tolerance and regulatory obligations.
- Have your risk/security team validate every Current State rating against actual evidence before it's finalized.
- Use AI to help draft the narrative sections of your gap assessment report and implementation roadmap — this is lower-risk since it's not asserting factual control status.
- Keep a human owner of record for the final profile and gap assessment; the AI-assisted draft should never be the artifact that goes to auditors or the board without a documented human review step.

Since SP 1353 is still an initial public draft with comments due October 15, 2026, I'd also recommend checking whether your organization wants to submit feedback, and revisiting your approach once NIST finalizes the guide — the final version may narrow or expand the recommended use cases.

This is general informational guidance based on a NIST draft publication, not legal or audit advice. Verify current requirements against the official NIST SP 1353 draft (and its eventual final version), and consult qualified compliance counsel before relying on AI-assisted assessments for regulatory or audit purposes.

Short answer: yes, generative AI can meaningfully accelerate a CSF assessment and profile-drafting process, and NIST has published relevant guidance — though not a single document titled "how to use GenAI for CSF assessments." You'll need to combine a few sources and apply sound judgment about where AI assistance is appropriate versus where it introduces risk.

1. Relevant NIST guidance
- NIST AI RMF 1.0 (AI Risk Management Framework) and its Generative AI Profile (NIST AI 600-1) are the primary references for how to think about risks introduced by using AI tools in your own operations, including risks like confabulation/hallucination, data leakage, and overreliance on automated output. If you use GenAI to help write your CSF profile, that use itself is an AI risk management question, and AI RMF's Govern/Map/Measure/Manage functions are a natural complement to CSF's own Govern function.
- CSF 2.0's Govern function (GV.OV, GV.RM, GV.SC, etc.) is exactly where AI-assisted tooling decisions belong — you should document in your governance records that GenAI tools are used to support (not replace) the assessment, who reviews the output, and what data is or isn't fed into the tool.
- NIST has also published guidance specifically on AI and cybersecurity risk (e.g., NIST IR drafts on adversarial machine learning, and CSF Quick-Start Guides that occasionally reference AI as an emerging risk area to consider under Identify's risk assessment category), but none of this constitutes a certified "use ChatGPT to fill out your CSF profile" methodology.

2. Where GenAI genuinely helps
- Drafting narrative text for organizational profile sections (mission statement framing, risk appetite language, subcategory implementation descriptions) based on interview notes or existing policy documents you feed in.
- Summarizing long policy/procedure documents to identify which CSF subcategories they already address, speeding up the "current profile" gap analysis.
- Generating a first-pass crosswalk between your existing controls (e.g., ISO 27001, SOC 2, CIS Controls) and CSF subcategories, which you then validate.
- Drafting interview questions and evidence-request lists for control owners.
- Turning raw assessment notes into a structured target profile document, tiering language (Tier 1–4), and gap-analysis tables.

3. Where you should not lean on GenAI unsupervised
- Actual risk ratings or maturity tier determinations — these require organizational judgment, actual evidence review, and accountability; an LLM has no visibility into your real environment and can confidently state something plausible but wrong.
- Feeding sensitive data (asset inventories, vulnerability scan results, incident details, network diagrams) into a public/consumer GenAI tool. If you use GenAI for this work, use an enterprise-tier tool with a data processing agreement and confirm your inputs aren't used for model training, or use an internally hosted model.
- Treating AI-generated subcategory implementation statements as automatically evidenced/true — every claim in your profile ("we implement PR.AC-1 via X") needs an actual control owner to confirm and ideally attach evidence.
- Final sign-off — the CSF profile is a governance artifact; leadership and control owners need to review and approve the substance, not just skim AI output.

4. Practical workflow recommendation
- Use GenAI as a drafting and summarization assistant, not a decision-maker.
- Keep a human-in-the-loop review step for every subcategory before it's marked "implemented" in your profile.
- Log which parts of the assessment used AI assistance, consistent with your organization's AI governance policy (this is itself a good CSF GV.SC / GV.PO practice to document).
- If your organization already has an internal generative AI acceptable-use policy or an AI governance committee, route this use case through it, since assessment documents can contain sensitive risk information.
- Consider building a lightweight internal "prompt library" for common CSF assessment tasks (e.g., "summarize this policy against CSF subcategory X.X and flag gaps") so results are consistent across assessors and reviewers.

In short: NIST's AI RMF and Generative AI Profile are the closest things to official guidance on using AI tools responsibly, and CSF 2.0's Govern function is where you document how you're using them. There's no NIST-endorsed "AI-run CSF assessment" methodology — treat GenAI as an efficiency tool for drafting and synthesis, with humans owning every judgment call and sign-off.

**How CSF 2.0 Informative References work**

Unlike CSF 1.1, where Informative References (mappings to other frameworks and standards) were embedded directly in the framework document, CSF 2.0 moved them entirely online into the **NIST CSF 2.0 Reference Tool** (https://csrc.nist.gov/Projects/cybersecurity-framework/Filters#/csf/filters). This was a deliberate design change: informative references need to be updated far more often than the core framework itself (standards get revised, new frameworks emerge), so decoupling them from the static CSF document lets NIST — and the community — keep mappings current without re-publishing the whole framework.

The mechanism behind this is the **Online Informative References (OLIR) Program**. Organizations and framework owners (including NIST itself, but also third parties) can submit a formal mapping between their framework's controls and CSF subcategories, following NIST's OLIR submission specification. NIST reviews and publishes accepted mappings in the Reference Tool. This means:

- Informative references are **crowdsourced and versioned**, not fixed in the CSF text.
- You can query the Reference Tool by CSF subcategory (e.g., "what maps to PR.AA-05?") or by source framework (e.g., "show me all ISO 27001:2022 mappings to CSF").
- Reference mappings exist for major frameworks: NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5, ISO/IEC 27001:2022, CIS Controls v8, COBIT, and others — coverage varies by framework and is added over time.

NIST also published **SP 1347** (final, August 25, 2026) as a quick-start guide specifically explaining how these crosswalks work and how to use the Reference Tool and OLIR program effectively — worth consulting directly if your team will be doing this mapping work regularly, since it covers submission mechanics and interpretation guidance beyond what I can summarize here.

**One important caution**: Informative References/crosswalks are **not one-to-one equivalences**. A mapping between an ISO 27001 control and a CSF subcategory typically means "related to" or "supports," not "is identical to." Scope, rigor, and evidentiary expectations often differ between the two controls even when mapped together. Treat mappings as a starting point for cross-referencing your compliance work, not as proof that satisfying one automatically satisfies the other.

**Mapping your ISO 27001 controls to CSF 2.0**

Here is a starting crosswalk covering the most common ISO 27001:2022 Annex A control areas against CSF 2.0 subcategories/categories. Use this as a first pass, then validate specific control language in the NIST Reference Tool since ISO mappings are periodically refined:

| CSF Subcategory Area | ISO 27001:2022 Annex A | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| GV.OC (Organizational Context) | A.4.1, A.4.2 | Context of the organization, interested parties |
| GV.SC (Supply Chain Risk) | A.5.19–5.22 | Supplier relationships, ICT supply chain |
| ID.AM (Asset Management) | A.5.9, A.5.10 | Inventory of assets, acceptable use |
| ID.RA (Risk Assessment) | Clause 6.1.2, A.5.7 (threat intelligence) | ISO risk assessment process; note ISO handles this partly in the management-system clauses, not just Annex A |
| PR.AA (Access Control) | A.5.15–5.18, A.8.2–8.5 | Access control policy, identity/authentication management |
| PR.AT (Awareness & Training) | A.6.3 | Information security awareness, education, and training |
| PR.DS (Data Security) | A.5.33, A.5.34, A.8.24 | Protection of records, PII, use of cryptography |
| PR.PS (Platform Security) | A.8.9, A.8.19, A.8.25–8.32 | Configuration management, secure development lifecycle |
| PR.IR (Technology Resilience) | A.8.6, A.5.29, A.5.30 | Capacity management, ICT readiness for business continuity |
| DE.CM (Continuous Monitoring) | A.8.15, A.8.16 | Logging, monitoring activities |
| DE.AE (Adverse Event Analysis) | A.5.25 | Assessment and decision on information security events |
| RS.MA / RS.AN / RS.CO (Respond) | A.5.24–5.28 | Incident management planning, response, learning, evidence collection |
| RC.RP / RC.CO (Recover) | A.5.29, A.5.30 | ICT readiness for business continuity |

**Recommended process for your organization**:
1. Pull your current ISO 27001 Statement of Applicability (SoA) and control implementation evidence.
2. For each CSF 2.0 subcategory, identify the corresponding ISO control(s) using the table above as a starting draft, then confirm/refine against the live NIST Reference Tool (mappings are updated more often than static references like this one).
3. Where a CSF subcategory has no clean ISO equivalent (common in GV.RM strategic-risk areas, GV.RR HR-related subcategories, and ID.IM improvement tracking), flag it as a gap specific to CSF that your ISO program doesn't currently cover — these are useful additions even if you stay ISO-certified as your primary framework.
4. Where an ISO control maps to a CSF subcategory but the rigor differs (e.g., your ISO evidence supports "partially implemented" against the CSF definition), record that explicitly rather than assuming a match is a match.

I can build you a full subcategory-by-subcategory crosswalk table (all 6 functions) mapped to your specific ISO 27001 SoA if you share which Annex A controls you have implemented and their current status.

❌Points to NIST SP 1347, the CSF 2.0 Informative References Quick-Start Guide, finalized August 2026
✅Mentions the CSF 2.0 Reference Tool for browsing/exporting reference data

✅Demonstrates a concrete mapping use: e.g., ISO 27001/SP 800-53/CIS Controls mapped against CSF subcategories for gap or evidence reuse
Informative references in CSF 2.0 are pointers, not requirements — they tell you which sections of other standards and frameworks (ISO/IEC 27001, NIST SP 800-53, COBIT, CIS Critical Security Controls, etc.) are relevant to a given CSF subcategory, so you don't have to invent your own control language from scratch. NIST maintains these mappings in the CSF Reference Tool / NIST Cybersecurity and Privacy Reference Tool (CPRT), an online, machine-readable repository rather than a static appendix in the framework document itself. This is a deliberate change from CSF 1.1, where informative references were embedded directly in the framework core spreadsheet.

How they work mechanically:
1. CSF 2.0 core structure: Function (e.g., Protect) > Category (e.g., PR.AA — Identity Management, Authentication, and Access Control) > Subcategory (e.g., PR.AA-01 — Identities and credentials for authorized users, services, and hardware are managed).
2. Each subcategory can have one or more informative references, which are specific clauses/controls from other standards that are considered analogous or supportive of that subcategory's intent. For PR.AA-01, you'd typically see references into ISO/IEC 27001:2022 Annex A (e.g., A.5.16, A.8.5), NIST SP 800-53 Rev 5 (e.g., IA-2, IA-4, IA-5), and possibly CIS Controls v8 (Control 5/6).
3. NIST does not claim these mappings are one-to-one equivalences — a single ISO control might map to several CSF subcategories and vice versa, because the frameworks organize the same underlying security concepts differently. Treat mappings as "related to" rather than "identical to."
4. The CPRT is updated periodically as NIST and other standards bodies revise their publications, so a mapping done in 2024 against ISO 27001:2013 Annex A numbering will be stale against the 2022 revision's renumbered/consolidated controls (2013 had 114 controls across 14 domains; 2022 consolidated to 93 controls across 4 themes).

How to map your ISO 27001 controls to CSF 2.0 practically:

Step 1 — Inventory your ISO controls as actually implemented. Don't just use the generic Annex A control list; use your Statement of Applicability (SoA), since that reflects what you actually claim to do, with justifications for exclusions.

Step 2 — Use NIST's CPRT mapping as your starting crosswalk, but validate it against the specific ISO 27001:2022 revision, since older public crosswalks may still reference 2013 numbering.

Step 3 — Build a bidirectional crosswalk table: for each CSF subcategory, list the ISO Annex A controls that support it; for each ISO Annex A control, list the CSF subcategories it feeds into. This surfaces gaps in both directions — CSF subcategories with no corresponding ISO control (rare, but possible in areas like supply chain risk under Govern) and ISO controls that don't map cleanly to any CSF subcategory (also useful to know, since it may indicate ISO covers something CSF treats as out of scope, like some physical security or HR clauses).

Step 4 — Assess maturity/implementation status per subcategory, not just presence/absence. A control can technically "exist" in ISO documentation (policy exists) but not be operating effectively (no evidence of enforcement) — CSF profiles are strongest when they reflect actual implementation status, tied to evidence, not paperwork.

Step 5 — Watch for the biggest structural gap: CSF 2.0's new Govern (GV) function has much heavier emphasis on organizational context, risk management strategy, supply chain risk management, and roles/responsibilities than earlier CSF versions did — and while ISO 27001 Clause 4-10 (the management system requirements, as opposed to Annex A controls) covers a lot of this, many crosswalks only map Annex A controls and miss the ISO management-system clauses (context of the organization, leadership, planning, support, operation, performance evaluation, improvement). Make sure your ISO-to-CSF mapping includes ISO's main clauses, not just Annex A, when populating your Govern function subcategories.

Step 6 — Document assumptions. Since mappings are not one-to-one, record your organization's specific rationale for each mapping decision so future auditors or assessors (and your future self) can follow the logic, especially where you've made a judgment call that a partial ISO control satisfies a CSF subcategory.

Bottom line: use NIST's CPRT/Reference Tool as your starting crosswalk, verify it against your current ISO 27001:2022 SoA (not just the generic Annex A list), explicitly include ISO's management-system clauses when mapping to CSF's Govern function, and document your own judgment calls since NIST's mappings are indicative, not authoritative one-to-one equivalences.

Here is a structured approach for building your CSF 2.0 Organizational Profile as a mid-size manufacturer. Manufacturing has a distinctive risk profile — IT/OT convergence, industrial control systems (ICS/SCADA) on plant floors, third-party equipment vendors with remote access, and supply chain dependencies that are often deeper and less visible than in pure IT environments — so the profile approach below is tailored accordingly, not generic.

**Step 1: Establish Business Context**

Before rating any subcategory, document:
- **Industry/mission**: production lines, product types, safety-critical processes (if any), regulatory exposure (e.g., CMMC/DFARS if you're a defense supplier, customer contractual security requirements, state privacy law if you handle employee/customer PII).
- **Legal/regulatory/contractual obligations**: customer security addenda are often the biggest driver of "must-have" target states in manufacturing — map these explicitly to GV.OC-03.
- **Key assets and Crown Jewels**: this should explicitly include OT/ICS assets (PLCs, HMIs, SCADA historians, robotics controllers) alongside traditional IT — these often carry safety and production-continuity risk that IT-only asset lists miss.
- **Risk tolerance statement**: for manufacturers, this typically centers on production uptime and safety, not just data confidentiality — your risk appetite framing (GV.RM-02) should say so explicitly, since it will drive different priorities than a typical office-based enterprise.

**Step 2: Build the Current Profile**

Assess your actual state today across all six functions using this rating scale: Not Implemented / Partially Implemented / Largely Implemented / Fully Implemented. For a mid-size manufacturer, pay particular attention to these commonly-weak areas during current-state assessment:
- ID.AM-01/02 — do you have a complete asset inventory that includes OT/plant-floor systems, not just corporate IT?
- GV.SC-04/07 — are equipment vendors and their remote-access arrangements tracked and risk-assessed?
- PR.AA-06 — physical access control at plant facilities (often stronger than logical access control in manufacturing, worth confirming rather than assuming).
- PR.PS-01/02 — configuration and patch management for OT systems, which often lag IT patch cycles due to uptime requirements.
- DE.CM-01/09 — monitoring coverage on OT networks (frequently a blind spot — many manufacturers only monitor corporate IT).

**Step 3: Build the Target Profile**

Define target states informed by:
- Customer contractual security requirements (often the fastest-moving driver — new customer contracts frequently mandate specific controls)
- Insurance/cyber-insurance underwriting requirements
- Safety and production-continuity risk tolerance
- Any applicable regulatory baseline (CMMC/NIST 800-171 if defense-adjacent, state breach-notification laws, etc.)

Highlight subcategories where regulatory/contractual obligations create a **mandatory** (not discretionary) target state — these should be flagged distinctly in your profile table since they can't be deprioritized regardless of resource constraints.

**Step 4: Profile Table Format**

| Function | Category | Subcategory | Current | Target | Notes |
|----------|----------|-------------|---------|--------|-------|
| GV | Organizational Context (GV.OC) | GV.OC-03 | Partial | Full | Customer security addenda not yet fully catalogued against controls |
| GV | Supply Chain Risk (GV.SC) | GV.SC-04 | Partial | Full | Equipment/OT vendors not yet inventoried by criticality |
| ID | Asset Management (ID.AM) | ID.AM-01 | Partial | Full | OT/plant-floor asset inventory incomplete |
| PR | Platform Security (PR.PS) | PR.PS-02 | Not Implemented | Largely Implemented | No formal OT patch/replacement cadence |
| DE | Continuous Monitoring (DE.CM) | DE.CM-01 | Not Implemented | Partial | OT network monitoring not yet deployed |
| PR | Technology Resilience (PR.IR) | PR.IR-03 | Partial | Full | Production-line failover/resilience not formally tested |

(This is illustrative — a full profile should cover all six functions with every relevant subcategory rated, not just the manufacturing hot spots above.)

**Step 5: Prioritize and Sequence**

The gap between Current and Target drives your action plan. Sequencing logic that applies well to manufacturing:
1. **Phase 1 (prerequisites)**: GV.OC and GV.RM to lock in risk tolerance framed around production/safety; ID.AM to build a *combined* IT+OT asset inventory (this is foundational — nothing else in Protect/Detect is meaningful without knowing what OT assets exist).
2. **Phase 2**: PR controls prioritized by what protects production continuity and safety first — PR.AA for both plant and office access, PR.PS for configuration/patch management adapted to OT constraints (can't always patch live production systems — document compensating controls where true patching isn't feasible).
3. **Phase 3**: DE.CM extended to OT networks (often a net-new capability, frequently requires OT-specific monitoring tooling since IT tools don't always parse ICS protocols) and DE.AE.
4. **Phase 4**: RS and RC — incident response and recovery plans that explicitly cover production-line/safety scenarios, not just IT data breach scenarios, plus the ID.IM feedback loop back into GV.

**Next steps I can help with**:
- A full gap assessment table across all six functions if you share your current control implementation status
- An implementation roadmap with 30/60/90-day and 6/12-month phases once the Current/Target Profile is drafted
- A crosswalk to any specific framework you're also subject to (NIST SP 800-171/CMMC if defense-related, ISO 27001, etc.)

Here's a practical organizational profile approach for a mid-size manufacturer adopting CSF 2.0. CSF 2.0 formalizes "organizational profiles" as the core mechanism for applying the framework to your specific business — you'll build a Current Profile (where you are today) and a Target Profile (where you want to be), then use the gap between them to drive your roadmap.

1. Scope and business context (feeds Govern function, GV.OC)
Start by defining organizational context: what you make, your supply chain structure (tier 1/2/3 suppliers, OEM relationships), regulatory drivers (e.g., CMMC/DFARS if you're a defense subcontractor, ITAR, state privacy laws, customer security requirements in contracts), and your risk tolerance. Manufacturers typically have a bimodal environment: corporate IT (ERP, email, engineering CAD/PLM systems) and OT/ICS on the plant floor (PLCs, HMIs, SCADA, MES). Your profile should explicitly note this split because Protect/Detect/Respond controls differ substantially between the two (e.g., patching a PLC isn't the same cadence as patching a laptop, and safety systems may have hard real-time constraints that limit certain security controls).

2. Select a scoping unit
Decide whether your profile covers the whole enterprise or is built per-plant/per-business-unit. For a mid-size manufacturer with a handful of plants, I'd recommend one enterprise-level profile for corporate IT and shared services, plus either a single OT profile that covers common plant-floor risk themes, or per-plant OT profiles if your plants have meaningfully different technology stacks or risk exposure (e.g., one plant handles export-controlled products, another doesn't).

3. Build the Current Profile
- For each of the six functions (Govern, Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover), and each subcategory within, assess current state: implemented / partially implemented / not implemented / not applicable.
- Gather evidence from existing documentation: IT security policies, OT network diagrams, vendor risk questionnaires you've already answered for customers, past audit/pen-test results, incident history, insurance questionnaires (cyber insurance applications are a surprisingly good existing gap-analysis input).
- Interview control owners: IT security lead, plant/OT engineering lead, HR (for insider risk/onboarding-offboarding), procurement (supply chain risk), and a business continuity/safety lead (Recover function, tied into existing business continuity/disaster recovery plans you likely already have for safety/operations reasons).
- Score using CSF Tiers (1–4: Partial, Risk Informed, Repeatable, Adaptive) at the organizational level, and implementation status at the subcategory level. Don't conflate the two — tiers describe how mature and integrated your risk management practices are overall, not a per-subcategory status.

4. Build the Target Profile
- Prioritize based on actual business drivers: customer contractual requirements (increasingly common for manufacturers supplying to larger OEMs or the defense industrial base), insurance requirements, known incident history, and realistic budget/headcount.
- Be selective. A common mistake is targeting Tier 4/"fully implemented" across the board — that's rarely necessary or affordable. Set differentiated targets: e.g., higher rigor for Identify/Protect subcategories touching OT and safety systems or IP-sensitive engineering data, moderate rigor for general corporate IT, lower rigor for low-risk peripheral systems.
- Pay special attention to Govern (new emphasis area in 2.0): supply chain risk management (GV.SC) is particularly relevant for manufacturers given third-party component risk, contract manufacturers, and software supply chain (PLC firmware, MES software vendors).

5. Gap analysis and roadmap
- For each subcategory where Current < Target, document the specific gap, the remediation action, an owner, and a realistic timeline (quarters, not just "someday").
- Group gap-closure actions into a 12–24 month roadmap, sequencing quick wins (policy documentation, MFA rollout on remaining accounts) ahead of larger capital/OT projects (network segmentation between IT and OT, SCADA monitoring tooling), since OT changes often require plant downtime windows.
- Tie budget requests to specific target profile gaps — this framing (funded gap-to-target vs. abstract "cybersecurity spend") tends to work well with manufacturing leadership focused on capital planning cycles.

6. Governance and maintenance
- Assign an executive sponsor and a cross-functional review (IT security + OT/engineering + safety + legal/compliance) at least annually, or after significant events (new plant, acquisition, major incident, new customer contract with security requirements).
- Re-baseline the Current Profile periodically (annually is typical) and track Tier progression as a leadership-reportable metric.
- Use community/sector profiles where available as accelerators — NIST has published example profiles for some sectors, and manufacturing-specific resources (e.g., NIST's manufacturing profile work under the earlier CSF 1.1 era, and CISA/ISA guidance for ICS security) can inform your OT-specific target subcategory choices, even though you'll still need to tailor them.

Bottom line: build one enterprise Current/Target profile pair, explicitly split IT vs. OT considerations within it, prioritize targets by real business drivers rather than blanket maturity goals, and turn the gap into a funded, owned, dated roadmap reviewed at least annually.

Good news: CSF 2.0 (published February 2024) is designed to be backward-compatible in intent with CSF 1.1 (April 2018) — you don't need to rip out your existing program. But there are real structural changes worth understanding before you migrate. Here's what changed and how to approach the transition.

**What actually changed**

1. **A sixth function: Govern (GV).** This is the headline change. CSF 1.1 embedded governance activities across the Identify and Protect functions (mainly ID.GV and ID.RM). CSF 2.0 pulls governance out into its own standalone function with 6 categories and 23 subcategories: GV.OC (Organizational Context), GV.RM (Risk Management Strategy), GV.RR (Roles, Responsibilities, and Authorities), GV.PO (Policy), GV.OV (Oversight), and GV.SC (Cybersecurity Supply Chain Risk Management). The intent is to put governance at the center — literally depicted at the center of the CSF wheel diagram — rather than treating it as a subset of "Identify."

2. **Supply chain risk management expanded significantly.** CSF 1.1 had a single category, ID.SC, with 5 subcategories. CSF 2.0 moved this into GV.SC and expanded it to 10 subcategories — covering supplier criticality prioritization (GV.SC-04), pre-relationship due diligence (GV.SC-06), lifecycle monitoring (GV.SC-09), and post-relationship provisions (GV.SC-10), none of which existed in 1.1.

3. **A new Improvement category (ID.IM).** CSF 1.1 had no formal mechanism for capturing lessons learned across functions. CSF 2.0 adds ID.IM (4 subcategories) to structure how improvements are identified from evaluations, tests/exercises, operational execution, and communicated to stakeholders — this absorbed what used to be scattered informally across RC.IM (Recovery Improvements) in 1.1, which no longer exists as a separate category.

4. **Net subcategory count**: 108 in CSF 1.1 down to 106 in CSF 2.0 — despite adding an entire new function, NIST consolidated and removed redundant subcategories elsewhere (e.g., PR.IP's 12 subcategories were split/absorbed into PR.PS and PR.IR; several RS.AN and RC.CO subcategories were consolidated).

5. **Informative References moved online.** In 1.1 these were embedded in the framework document; in 2.0 they live in the searchable NIST CSF 2.0 Reference Tool, updated via the OLIR program independently of the core framework text.

6. **Audience broadened explicitly.** CSF 1.1 was written with a critical-infrastructure lens; CSF 2.0 explicitly targets organizations of all sizes and sectors, and added Quick Start Guides for SMBs, enterprise risk managers, and government.

7. **Tiers are structurally the same** (4 tiers, same three dimensions: Risk Management Process, Integrated Risk Management Program, External Participation) but the descriptions were refined for clarity — no material change to how you'd assess your tier.

**Where your CSF 1.1 subcategories land in 2.0** (partial map — the full mapping is more extensive):

| CSF 1.1 | CSF 2.0 | Topic |
|---|---|---|
| ID.GV-01 | GV.PO-01 | Cybersecurity policy |
| ID.GV-02 | GV.RR-02 | Roles and responsibilities |
| ID.GV-03 | GV.OC-03 | Legal/regulatory requirements |
| ID.GV-04 | GV.OV-01 | Governance/risk strategy review |
| ID.RM-01/02/03 | GV.RM-01/02/06 | Risk objectives, tolerance, methodology |
| ID.SC-01 to 05 | GV.SC-01, 04, 05, 07, 08 | Supply chain (now expanded to 10 subcategories total) |

**Migration checklist**

- **Governance**: Formally document risk tolerance (GV.RM-01/02), assign explicit accountable roles to leadership (GV.RR-01/02), establish a policy review cycle (GV.PO-01/02), stand up an oversight mechanism (GV.OV-01 to 03), and expand your supply chain program from ID.SC's 5 subcategories to the full GV.SC-01 through GV.SC-10.
- **Identify**: Add data/metadata inventories (ID.AM-07) and asset lifecycle management (ID.AM-08) if not already covered; establish a vulnerability disclosure process (ID.RA-08); assess hardware/software authenticity before acquisition (ID.RA-09); stand up the new ID.IM improvement-tracking category.
- **Protect**: Add data-in-use protection (PR.DS-10) and secure software development practices (PR.PS-06).
- **Detect**: Integrate threat intelligence into event analysis (DE.AE-07) and define incident declaration criteria (DE.AE-08).
- **Respond**: Formalize incident triage, categorization, and escalation (RS.MA-02 to 04) — 1.1's RS.RP and RS.CO-01 collapsed into RS.MA-01.
- **Recover**: Add post-incident operational norms (RC.RP-04), incident recovery end criteria (RC.RP-06), and a public communications process (RC.CO-04).

**Practical sequencing advice**: Since Govern is not optional in 2.0, start there — map your existing ID.GV/ID.RM practices to their new GV homes explicitly, even if the underlying practice doesn't change, so your documentation reflects the current framework. Then tackle the supply chain expansion (GV.SC), since that's the single largest scope increase. The remaining changes (ID.IM, PR.DS-10, DE.AE-07/08, etc.) are additive and can be worked into your existing continuous-improvement cycle rather than requiring a wholesale program rebuild.

I can help you produce a full subcategory-by-subcategory crosswalk of your current 1.1-based program into 2.0, or build a prioritized migration roadmap with effort/impact ratings if you share your current program documentation.

CSF 2.0 (published February 2024) is an evolution, not a rewrite — your CSF 1.1 program is a solid foundation, and migration is more about reorganizing/extending than starting over. Here's what actually changed and how to approach migration.

What changed:

1. New "Govern" function (the headline change). CSF 1.1 had five functions: Identify, Protect, Detect, Respond, Recover. CSF 2.0 adds Govern as a sixth, and it's placed conceptually "above" the other five, since governance decisions (risk management strategy, roles and responsibilities, policy, oversight, supply chain risk management) inform how you execute the other five. Much of Govern's content existed in 1.1 but was scattered — parts lived under Identify (ID.GV, ID.RM, ID.SC in 1.1). CSF 2.0 pulls governance, risk management strategy, and supply chain risk management out into their own dedicated function with expanded subcategories, especially around cybersecurity supply chain risk management (GV.SC), which got significantly more detailed than 1.1's ID.SC.

2. Scope expansion beyond critical infrastructure. CSF 1.1 was explicitly framed around critical infrastructure. CSF 2.0 drops that framing and positions itself as applicable to any organization, regardless of sector or size — reflecting how broadly CSF 1.1 was actually being used in practice (small businesses, schools, nonprofits, not just critical infrastructure operators).

3. Formalized "Organizational Profiles" and "Community Profiles." CSF 1.1 had "profiles" as a looser concept (current/target). CSF 2.0 gives much more structured guidance on building organizational profiles, plus introduces "Community Profiles" — shared profiles developed by a sector, interest group, or coalition (e.g., a Community Profile for a specific industry or a specific threat like ransomware) that member organizations can start from rather than building entirely from scratch.

4. New CSF Reference Tool / CPRT for informative references. In 1.1, informative references (mappings to ISO 27001, SP 800-53, COBIT, etc.) were static content embedded in the framework documentation. In 2.0, NIST moved this to the online Cybersecurity and Privacy Reference Tool (CPRT), which is updated independently of the framework document, so mappings can be refreshed as underlying standards change without waiting for a full CSF revision.

5. Subcategory reorganization and renumbering. Several 1.1 subcategories were consolidated, reworded, split, or moved between categories/functions as part of the Govern reorganization and general cleanup. This means your old subcategory IDs (e.g., ID.GV-1) don't map one-to-one to new IDs — some content moved to GV.OV, GV.RM, GV.PO, etc. You cannot assume a simple ID-to-ID renumbering; you need to actually re-read the new subcategory language.

6. Expanded guidance on implementation examples. CSF 2.0 introduces "Implementation Examples" for many subcategories — concrete, illustrative actions an organization might take — which 1.1 didn't have. These aren't mandatory, but they're useful drafting aids for your own profile language.

7. Increased emphasis on cybersecurity supply chain risk management (C-SCRM), measurement/improvement, and continuous improvement culture, reflecting lessons learned since 1.1 (2018) around ransomware, software supply chain attacks (SolarWinds-era), and general maturity of enterprise risk practice.

How to migrate:

Step 1 — Map your existing 1.1 profile/control set against the new CSF 2.0 core structure using NIST's published 1.1-to-2.0 crosswalk (NIST released a mapping document alongside CSF 2.0). Don't assume subcategory numbers carry over; validate each mapping.

Step 2 — Stand up Govern as a distinct section of your program, even if much of its substance already exists elsewhere in your documentation (risk management policy, roles/responsibilities charter, supply chain risk policy). Consolidate it so leadership and auditors can see governance addressed explicitly and holistically, not scattered.

Step 3 — Expand your supply chain risk management practices to match GV.SC's increased depth — this is the area most 1.1 programs will find genuinely under-built relative to 2.0 expectations (third-party risk assessment cadence, contractual security requirements, software bill of materials practices).

Step 4 — Rebuild your Current Profile against the new subcategory set rather than trying to patch your old 1.1 profile; use the crosswalk to carry over evidence and status where subcategories map cleanly, and do fresh assessment work where they don't.

Step 5 — Reset your Target Profile and tier targets with current leadership, since risk appetite and regulatory landscape have likely shifted since your original 1.1 profile was set.

Step 6 — Update any internal documentation, control mappings, audit templates, and board reporting materials that reference 1.1 function/category codes, since some of these codes changed meaning or location.

Bottom line: the core five functions and their spirit carry forward largely intact; the main work is building out Govern as a first-class function (especially supply chain risk), re-validating subcategory mappings rather than assuming a clean renumbering, and refreshing your profiles and reference-standard crosswalks against the new CPRT-based mappings.

Short answer: Secure SLC v2.0 was released on September 28, 2026, and your vendor's v1.1 validation is not invalidated by that release. Existing v1.1 validations stay valid during a transition window. That window is tied to the availability of v2.0 assessor training, so the exact end date is in the PCI SSC Program Guide, which you should check.

What changed
- Secure SLC Standard v2.0 is the first major revision of that standard.
- It is aligned with the Secure Software Standard v2.0, which was published on January 15, 2026.
- It adds coverage of digital tools and AI in vendor lifecycle processes. That means an assessor evaluating a vendor's secure software lifecycle will now look at how AI-assisted development tooling and other digital tools are governed, in addition to the traditional SDLC controls.

Does the v1.1 validation still count?
- Yes, for now. The Council did not retire v1.1 on release of v2.0. Existing v1.1 validations remain valid during a transition period.
- The period is tied to when v2.0 assessor training becomes available, so the Council controls the clock, not the vendor. Two things I cannot give you from memory are the specific cut-off dates and whether new v1.1 assessments are still accepted. Both are in the Program Guide, and you should confirm them there or with the vendor's assessor.
- Do not assume the validation lasts until its original expiry date. Transition windows often change when renewals and re-validations happen. Ask the vendor which standard version their next validation will use and when.

How this affects your own PCI DSS compliance
- A validated secure SLC or secure software listing helps you with the software you buy, but it does not replace your own PCI DSS obligations. Under Req 12.8 you must keep a list of third-party service providers and maintain written agreements. You must also monitor each provider's compliance status at least every 12 months (12.8.4) and document which requirements each provider covers and which you cover (12.8.5).
- If the product is bespoke or custom software developed for you, your own Req 6.2 and 6.3 obligations still apply. These cover secure coding, code review, vulnerability ranking and the software inventory in 6.3.2.

Recommended actions
1. Ask the vendor in writing for their current validation scope, listing status and expiry, and their plan and timeline to move to v2.0.
2. Update your TPSP register and the 12.8.5 responsibility matrix. Record the version they are validated against and the date you checked.
3. Add a contract clause that requires the vendor to notify you of any change in validation status.
4. Set a calendar reminder to re-check the Program Guide transition dates.
5. Tell your QSA now. They will want to see how you rely on the vendor's validation, and the transition is an easy point to get wrong in an assessment.

Short answer: I can't confirm the specific late-2026 changes from memory, so treat what follows as background plus a verification plan. Do not tell your auditors or customers the vendor is "still valid" until you have checked the PCI SSC website.

Background I am confident about
- PCI Secure Software Lifecycle (Secure SLC) Standard v1.1 is part of the PCI Software Security Framework (SSF). It validates the vendor's software development lifecycle, not a specific product. It sits alongside the Secure Software Standard, which validates the payment software itself and replaced PA-DSS. PA-DSS was retired in October 2022.
- Secure SLC validation is listed on the PCI SSC website under "Secure Software Lifecycle Vendors". Each listing has an expiry date, normally tied to the standard version and the vendor's revalidation cycle.
- The Council retires older SSF versions on a published timeline. After a new version is released, there is a transition window. During that window, new assessments against the old version stop, and existing listings stay valid until their expiry or until a sunset date.
- Secure SLC validation is not a PCI DSS assessment. It does not remove the vendor's PCI DSS obligations if they store, process or transmit account data.

What I cannot verify
I don't have reliable information about a specific late-2026 announcement for Secure SLC v1.1, such as a retirement date, a new version (for example a v1.2 or v2.0), or a changed listing status. I won't invent dates.

Does their validation still count? How to decide
1. Look up the vendor on the PCI SSC list of validated Secure SLC vendors. Check that the listing is "Valid", the standard version, the reference number, and the expiry date.
2. Check the PCI SSC announcements, FAQs and the document library for the Secure SLC standard. Look for a retirement date for v1.1 and whether the listing remains valid until its own expiry.
3. Ask the vendor in writing for:
   - their current listing and Attestation of Validation (AOV);
   - their revalidation plan and target date against the current standard;
   - whether any scope change, such as an acquisition or a new product line, affects the listing.
4. Check which products are covered. A Secure SLC listing alone does not mean a particular product has Secure Software validation. If your PCI DSS evidence (for example Req 6.3.2, bespoke and custom software inventory, and Req 12.8 third-party service provider oversight) relied on that product, check what the product itself is listed under.
5. Record the result in your vendor risk file.

Practical guidance
- Treat a listing as valid until its stated expiry or an explicit Council sunset date, whichever comes first.
- If the standard has been retired or the listing is within about 6 months of expiry, require a revalidation plan and put a contract clause in place. Do the same if the status shows "expired" or "revoked".
- If the listing has lapsed, treat the vendor as not validated for your evidence. Compensate with your own review: secure SDLC evidence, penetration testing, vulnerability management and change control.
- Note that PCI DSS v4.0.1 requires you to manage the risk from third-party software (Req 6.3.2 inventory, 12.8 TPSP management, 12.9 TPSP acknowledgement). A Secure SLC listing supports but does not satisfy these on its own.
- Re-check the listing at least annually and whenever you renew the vendor contract.

Short answer: the sunset periods for the PCI SPoC and CPoC standards ended on October 31, 2026. No new submissions are accepted under either standard. MPoC is the successor to both, and any new COTS-based solution should be an MPoC solution.

What the sunsets mean in practice
- The sunset ended new submissions. It did not remove existing listings. Existing listings keep their normal lifecycle, so your current SPoC solution is not suddenly invalid.
- Nothing new will be accepted under SPoC or CPoC. A vendor that has not already been through those programs cannot enter them now. It has to go through MPoC.
- The same date applied to the PCI 3DS SDK standard. Its functionality is being folded into the Secure Software Standard. This is not relevant to your question unless you also build 3DS SDKs.

Your SPoC solution
- Keep using it under its existing listing, but treat the listing's expiry as a planning date. Check the listing on the PCI SSC website.
- The vendor will have no renewal route under SPoC for new submissions. Ask them now for their MPoC plan: is it a transition or a re-assessment, and what are the dates?
- Because you are a merchant using a listed solution, your validation burden depends on what the acquirer and card brands accept, and on how the solution is deployed. Keep in your records the listing reference, the date you checked it, and the vendor's responsibility statement.

The CPoC product you were evaluating

Caveat first: I can't confirm from memory the exact details of what changed on October 31, 2026. Verify the dates and wording against the PCI SSC website. What follows is the background and the likely implications.

Background
- SPoC (Software-based PIN Entry on COTS) and CPoC (Contactless Payments on COTS) were standalone PCI standards. SPoC covers PIN entry on a merchant's COTS device (usually a phone or tablet) with a secure card reader. CPoC covers contactless acceptance on the COTS device itself (tap on phone).
- The PCI Mobile Payments on COTS (MPoC) Standard (v1.0, 2023) was designed to supersede both. It covers a combination of PIN-on-COTS and card-data acceptance, and adds new architecture and attestation and monitoring requirements for solutions.
- The Council set a sunset path. New SPoC and CPoC evaluations stopped after a cut-off, and existing SPoC and CPoC solutions stay on the list until their expiry. My understanding is that October 31, 2026 is the final date for those listings. After that, SPoC and CPoC listings move to "expired" and can't be used for new deployments.

What this likely means for you
1. If you operate an SPoC solution:
   - Your listing is no longer valid for new merchant onboarding after the sunset. If the solution has not moved to MPoC, it is no longer an approved solution from the Council's perspective.
   - Existing merchants will need to be migrated to an MPoC-validated solution or to a different compliant acceptance approach. Card brands and acquirers set their own rules for how long existing deployments can continue, so confirm with them.
   - Merchants using that solution lose the reduced PCI DSS scope that comes from using a listed solution. They may need to assess against a larger set of PCI DSS requirements. Their SAQ type could change (for example from SAQ SPoC to another SAQ).
2. If you were evaluating a CPoC product:
   - A CPoC product can no longer be treated as a valid, listed option. Any CPoC product with an expired listing should be dropped from the shortlist, unless the provider has moved to MPoC and shows a current MPoC listing.
   - Ask the provider for its MPoC listing reference, the MPoC version, and the expiry date.
3. In both cases, MPoC is the path. Evaluate MPoC solutions that support PIN entry (and contactless, if that's what you need) in one listing. Check whether they are listed for your COTS platform (iOS, Android) and region.

Actions
- Confirm your solution's status on the PCI SSC list of PCI-listed solutions and check the expiry.
- Talk to your acquirer, payment brands and solution provider about their transition timelines.
- Inventory merchants and devices on the SPoC solution and plan migration waves.
- Revisit your PCI scope documentation, SAQ selection and contracts.
- Stop any new CPoC procurement. Reissue the RFP with MPoC as the requirement.
- Update customer communications and your TPSP responsibility matrix (PCI DSS Req 12.8, 12.9).

Where things stand
- v3.2.1 was retired on March 31, 2024.
- v4.0 (March 2022) was superseded by v4.0.1 (June 2024). v4.0.1 is a limited revision that corrects errors and clarifies wording and adds no new controls.
- All the "future-dated" v4.0 requirements became mandatory on March 31, 2025. These include 6.4.3 and 11.6.1 (payment page scripts), 8.4.2 (MFA for all access into the CDE), 5.4.1 (anti-phishing), and 10.4.1.1 (automated log review). So your 2027 assessment will treat them as fully in force, with no "best practice" grace.
- The Council ran a Request for Comments on v4.0.1 from June 3 to July 20, 2026. It is input to the next iteration of the standard. It is not a published draft, and it does not tell us the next version number, its content or its dates.

What to target for 2027
- Plan and scope against v4.0.1. That is the version your QSA or ISA will assess against and the version your SAQ or AOC will reference.
- Do not delay work in anticipation of a new version. Historically, new major versions come with a long overlap period between the old and new standard, but I cannot tell you the timing of any future version, so do not plan around it.

1. Run a v4.0.1 gap assessment now. Focus on the items that most often fail: MFA coverage (8.4.2), script inventory and integrity (6.4.3, 11.6.1), automated log review (10.4.1.1), the targeted risk analysis process (12.3.1), and ASV and pen test evidence including segmentation testing.

SAQ eligibility criteria cannot be used as a guide for requirement applicability in a ROC unless you have reviewed and agreed it with your compliance accepting entity, such as the payment brands and acquirer. QSA agreement alone is not enough. Anyone marking 6.4.3 or 11.6.1 as not applicable on SAQ A-style reasoning needs written acquirer or brand approval.
4. Build a small watch process. Track the PCI SSC document library and announcements for the output of the RFC, and re-check quarterly.
5. Keep a single mapping of your controls to the requirements. If a new version arrives, a clean mapping makes the delta assessment much cheaper.

Short answer: Yes. In September 2026 the PCI Council published an information supplement titled "Security Considerations for AI Systems". It is an information supplement, so it is guidance and not a new PCI DSS requirement. It does not change your PCI DSS validation obligations, but it is worth factoring into your risk and compliance program.

Status of the guidance
- Information supplements are not part of the standard. You are not assessed against them as requirements, and no new AI-specific control was added to PCI DSS v4.0.1. v4.0.1 remains the current version.
- A QSA can still reasonably ask how you manage AI-related risk to the CDE, because your existing requirements apply to AI tools just as they apply to any other system component or third party.
- I have not reproduced the contents of the supplement here, so read it in full and map its recommendations to your own environment.

Related updates
- Secure SLC Standard v2.0 (September 28, 2026) adds coverage of digital tools and AI in vendor lifecycle processes. If you buy payment software from validated vendors, expect their assessments to address how AI tooling is governed in development.

How existing PCI DSS v4.0.1 requirements already apply to AI
| Area | Requirement | Application to AI systems |
|------|-------------|---------------------------|
| Scope | 12.5.1, 12.5.2 | If an AI system, assistant or model can store, process or transmit account data, or can affect the security of the CDE, it is in scope. Confirm scope at least every 12 months and after major changes. |
| Data protection | 3.2, 3.3.1, 3.4.1, 12.10.7 | Do not let PAN or SAD flow into prompts, training data, logs, vector stores or chat transcripts. SAD must never be stored after authorization. Include AI data stores in PAN discovery. |
| Third parties | 12.8.1 to 12.8.5 | An AI provider that touches account data or CDE security is a TPSP. You need a written agreement, annual compliance monitoring, and a responsibility matrix. |
| Access | 7.2, 8.4.2, 8.6 | Apply least privilege and MFA to AI tooling that reaches the CDE. Treat AI agents and service identities as application and system accounts, with no hardcoded credentials (8.6.2). |
| Secure development | 6.2, 6.3.2, 6.5.5 | Code from AI assistants goes through the same review, secure coding and testing. Keep live PANs out of test data. Include AI components in your software inventory. |
| Logging | 10.2, 10.4.1.1 | Log access by AI systems to CDE data and review it automatically. |
| Risk analysis | 12.3.1, 12.3.2 | Do a targeted risk analysis where you rely on one, and consider adding AI use to your formal risk process. |
| Awareness | 12.6 | Train staff not to paste cardholder data into AI tools. |
| Incident response | 12.10 | Update the plan for AI-related events such as data leakage through a prompt. |
| Attack surface | 6.4.1, 6.4.3, 11.6.1 | If you add AI features to payment pages, those scripts fall under inventory, authorization and integrity requirements. |

Practical steps
1. Read the supplement and note which recommendations apply to you.
2. Create an inventory of AI tools and use cases across the business, with a decision on whether each touches or could affect the CDE.
3. Issue an acceptable use rule that bans entering PAN or SAD into AI tools that are not approved.
4. Run vendor due diligence on AI providers that fall into scope, including their PCI status.
5. Add AI to your annual scope review and risk assessment.
6. Brief your QSA so there are no surprises at assessment.

Yes. The PCI Security Standards Council has published AI-related material, though there is no AI-specific requirement in PCI DSS itself. I'm confident of the general direction, but not of every title and date, so verify against the PCI SSC document library.

What the Council has said, as I understand it
- Guidance on using AI in PCI assessments (2025). It sets out the Council's position for assessors (QSAs, ISAs, and assessor companies) on using AI during assessments. The key principles: AI may support assessment work but must not replace assessor judgment. The assessor stays accountable for findings and the report. Don't send cardholder data or sensitive assessment data to external AI tools without proper controls. Confidentiality, data handling and evidence quality obligations still apply. Disclose AI use to the assessed entity where appropriate.
- Guidance on AI principles for payments and AI in the cardholder data environment (2025 and after). The messages include: AI systems that store, process or transmit account data, or that can affect the security of the CDE, are in scope for PCI DSS. Existing requirements apply to AI as to any other system component.

What this means for your compliance program
1. Scope. Identify any AI system, including LLMs, chatbots, copilots, fraud models, and agents, that could touch account data or connect to the CDE. Anything that stores, processes or transmits PAN or SAD, or is connected to or could impact the security of the CDE, is in scope (Req 12.5.2 scope confirmation).
2. Data. Keep PAN out of prompts, logs, training data, embeddings, and vector stores unless the system is in scope and controlled. Consider tokenization, redaction, and DLP at the AI boundary. Protect SAD (no storage post-authorization, Req 3.3) and keep PAN unreadable wherever stored (Req 3.5).
3. Access control. Apply least privilege (Req 7), unique IDs, MFA (Req 8) and control for AI agents' service accounts and API keys (8.6). Agents with tool access to payment systems need tight permissions and approval gates.
4. Secure development and change. AI-generated or AI-assisted code must follow Req 6: code review, secure coding, vulnerability management, and an inventory of bespoke and third-party software (6.3.2). Treat prompt injection, insecure output handling, and model supply chain as threats in your Req 12.2 risk assessment.
5. Logging and monitoring. Log and review access to AI systems in the CDE (Req 10). Be able to reconstruct what an AI agent did.
6. Third parties. If an AI service is provided by a third party (an LLM API or SaaS tool), apply Req 12.8 and 12.9: due diligence, a responsibility matrix, a written acknowledgement, and contract terms on data retention and training use.
7. Testing. Include AI components in vulnerability scans and penetration tests (Req 11), and test for prompt injection and data leakage.
8. Governance. Add an AI use policy covering approved tools, a ban on pasting cardholder data into unapproved tools, and training in security awareness (Req 12.6). If you use AI in your own assessment or evidence processes, follow the Council's assessor principles and make sure your QSA is comfortable with it.
9. Targeted risk analyses (12.3.1) and the customized approach can support AI-specific control design where defined approach controls don't fit, but they must still meet the stated objective.

Next steps
- Pull the latest AI documents from the PCI SSC document library and blog and cite them in your policy.
- Create an AI inventory and data-flow diagram, and link them to your scope documentation.
- Talk to your QSA early about how AI components will be assessed.
