ANPD institutional status and the consultation

Caveat first: this area moved quickly through 2025 and 2026, and my knowledge of late-2026 developments is incomplete. What follows is my best understanding, with the points to verify flagged.

1. Where the ANPD came from
The Autoridade Nacional de Proteção de Dados was created by the 2018 LGPD amendments and started life in 2020 as a federal body linked to the Presidency (later the Ministry of Justice), with a transitional legal nature. The LGPD itself (Art. 55-A) said that nature could be transformed into an indirect federal public administration entity (an autarchy, "autarquia de natureza especial") by the Executive, within two years of the structure being set up. That transformation was formalised in 2022 (Provisional Measure 1,124/2022, converted into Law 14.460/2022), making the ANPD an autarquia especial with technical, decision-making and administrative autonomy, linked to the Ministry of Justice and Public Security.

2. The more recent change: regulatory agency
In 2025 the government moved to reshape the ANPD again. Provisional Measure 1,317/2025, issued in September 2025 alongside the passage of the child digital protection statute (Law 15.211/2025, the "ECA Digital"), converted the ANPD into a regulatory agency, renamed in some texts as the Agência Nacional de Proteção de Dados, with a broader mandate that includes overseeing and sanctioning compliance with the ECA Digital for digital services directed to or likely used by children and adolescents. The restructuring brought new positions, a regulatory-agency career framework and more budget. Please verify whether the provisional measure was converted into law in full, amended, or lapsed, and what its current official name and organisational structure are, as that is the point most likely to have changed.

3. Governance
The ANPD is led by a Board of Directors (Conselho Diretor) of five directors appointed by the President and approved by the Senate, with fixed terms. It has a National Council for Personal Data and Privacy Protection (CNPD) with multistakeholder membership, an internal Ombudsman and a Corregedoria. Its operational areas include the General Coordination of Inspection (Fiscalização), Regulation, and Technology and Research. It is also the Brazilian counterpart in the Global Privacy Assembly and cooperation networks, and it has an adequacy-related track with the EU. The European Commission adopted an adequacy decision for Brazil's regime in early 2026 (verify); that is relevant to your EU-Brazil flows, and it complements Brazil's own international transfer rules.

4. What is "the consultation"?
Without knowing which one you heard about, there are a few candidates and I do not want to guess confidently:
- ANPD public consultations (consulta pública) and "tomada de subsídios" (calls for input) are a routine part of its regulatory agenda. Recent ones have covered topics such as the DPO (encarregado) role, international data transfers, security incident reporting, high-risk processing and DPIAs (RIPD), artificial intelligence, data subject rights, anonymisation, and children's data.
- Implementation of the ECA Digital: the ANPD has run consultations on technical standards, age assurance and parental supervision, and on how the new statute interacts with LGPD Art. 14.
- The Regulatory Agenda for 2025-2026: the ANPD consults on its priorities, which include AI, biometric data, and children and adolescent protection.
- A possible legislative consultation or public hearing in Congress on the Brazilian AI bill (PL 2338/2023) or on the ANPD's expanded role.
If you can tell me the topic or paste the notice, I can be specific. The right place to check is the gov.br/anpd site (section "Participação social") and the Participa + Brasil platform where consultations are published with dates, documents and submission forms.

5. Why it matters to you
- Consultations are your chance to shape binding rules. ANPD resolutions (such as Res. CD/ANPD 2/2022 for small agents, 4/2023 on sanctions, 15/2024 on incident reporting, 18/2024 on the DPO, 19/2024 on international transfers) came out of this process.
- Submissions are generally public, and industry associations (Câmara-e.net, ABES, Brasscom, FEBRABAN and others) file joint positions that you can join.
- Final texts usually lag consultations by several months, so use the consultation draft as a reliable preview and begin compliance planning.

6. Recommended actions
- Subscribe to ANPD newsletters and monitor the Diário Oficial da União.
- Map which open consultations affect your processing (children, transfers, AI, biometrics).
- Prepare a short, evidence-based submission through your trade association or counsel.
- Confirm the current legal status (agency, name, directors) before citing it in any contract or regulatory filing.

Obligations for a social platform popular with Brazilian teenagers (October 2026)

You are subject to LGPD (Art. 3, offering services to people in Brazil, regardless of where you are established), the Digital ECA (in force since 17 March 2026), and ANPD's growing enforcement focus on minors. The ByteDance/TikTok fine of R$153.7 million (DOU, 25 August 2026) is the template for what ANPD treats as a serious failure: feeds operated without an adequate legal basis for children's and adolescents' data.

1. Legal basis and the best-interest standard (Art. 14)

- Crianças (under 12): specific, prominent consent from a parent or guardian is required (Art. 14, section 1). The controller must make reasonable efforts to verify it (section 5).
- Adolescents (12 to 17): processing must observe their best interest (Art. 14 caput; ANPD Enunciado 1/2023). This is not a consent-only regime. Consent is not automatically the right basis, and any Art. 7 basis can be used if the best-interest test is met. Whichever basis you pick, document the reasoning.
- Do not treat a teenager's tick-box as a safe harbour. For feeds, recommendation, profiling and advertising, ask whether the processing actually serves the adolescent's interest. The TikTok decision turned on the legal basis for feed operation, so that is where scrutiny lands.
- Legitimate interest for engagement-maximising or ad-targeting uses of minors' data is hard to defend. Do a documented balancing test, and expect it to be tested.
- Sensitive data inferred from behaviour (health, sexual life, religion, biometrics) needs an Art. 11 basis.

2. Transparency (Art. 9, Art. 14, section 6)

Notices must be clear, accessible and suited to the audience's age and understanding. That means plain language and layered or visual formats, in Portuguese, aimed at a teenager. Include controller identity, the encarregado's contact, purposes, bases, sharing, retention, rights, and profiling.

3. Digital ECA and ANPD supervision

- ANPD is now an autonomous agency (Lei 15.352/2026) and supervises Digital ECA duties.
- Order CD/ANPD 122/2026 (11 August) requires semiannual transparency reports from platforms with more than 1 million registered minor users. The first report covered January to June 2026 and was due by 17 September. The next is due by 1 February 2027, then 1 August 2027, and so on. If you are above the threshold and did not file, treat it as a live compliance gap. If you are near it, build the reporting process now.
- Consulta Pública 1/2026 (until 26 October 2026) proposes to extend the sanctioning regime to Digital ECA duties and internet application providers, with interim measures without prior hearing and daily fines capped at R$50M. This is a proposal. Until it is adopted, Resolution 1/2021 and Resolution 4/2023 apply. Consider filing comments.

4. Operational controls

| Area | What to have |
|---|---|
| Age assurance | Proportionate, privacy-preserving age checks, not data-hungry verification (necessity principle, Art. 6, III) |
| Parental consent | For under-12s: verifiable, specific, withdrawable, logged |
| Defaults | Privacy by design and default (Art. 46, section 2): private profiles, no public location, limited contact from strangers |
| Profiling and ads | Strong limits on behavioural advertising to minors, human review for automated decisions (Art. 20) |
| RIPD (Art. 38) | A documented impact assessment for recommendation systems, profiling and any sensitive inferences |
| Data minimisation | Collect only what each feature needs, and set retention limits |
| Rights | Channels usable by teens and by parents or guardians, with identity checks proportionate to risk |
| Encarregado | Published contact (Art. 41), able to handle minors' issues |
| Security (Art. 46) | Higher standard for minors' data. Art. 48 notification within 3 working days for relevant-risk incidents |
| Transfers | If you send data to a US parent or vendors, ANPD standard clauses (Resolution 19/2024) are mandatory |

5. Exposure

Fines up to 2% of Brazilian revenue, capped at R$50M per infraction (Art. 52), though TikTok's R$153.7M shows several infractions can stack. You also face deletion orders, blocking, and possible suspension, plus civil claims and action from the Public Prosecutor or consumer bodies.

6. Priorities for the next 90 days

1. Map every processing activity touching under-18s and record its basis.
2. Run an RIPD on feed ranking and ad targeting.
3. Confirm your Order 122/2026 position.
4. Review age-assurance and parental-consent flows.
5. Rewrite notices for teen readability.
6. Decide on a consultation response by 26 October.

Which data do you currently collect from teens, and do you run personalised feeds or ads? With that I can produce a gap table.

Obligations for a social platform popular with Brazilian teenagers

Caveat: Brazil's child-protection rules changed substantially in 2025-2026, and I may be missing late-2026 implementing details. Verify specifics with Brazilian counsel and the ANPD's published guidance.

1. Two overlapping regimes
(a) LGPD Art. 14: processing of children's (under 12) and adolescents' (12 to 17) personal data must be in their "best interest". For children, specific and prominent consent from at least one parent or guardian is required. ANPD Statement/Enunciado CD/ANPD 1/2023 clarified that adolescents' data can rest on any LGPD legal basis (Arts. 7 or 11) provided the best-interest principle is observed, so you are not forced into consent for teens, but legitimate interest and contract must be defended with the best-interest lens.
(b) The ECA Digital (Law 15.211/2025, in force from March 2026, subject to verification): a statute applying to digital products and services directed at, or likely to be accessed by, children and adolescents, regardless of where the provider is located. A teen-popular social platform is squarely in scope.

2. Core ECA Digital-type duties (verify against current text and regulations)
- Best interest and integral protection by design and by default: risk assessment and mitigation for content, contact, conduct and commercial risks, with the highest privacy settings by default.
- Age assurance: reliable mechanisms to verify or estimate age, going beyond self-declaration, while respecting data minimisation. Do not collect more data than needed to determine age, and avoid reusing age-check data.
- Parental supervision: for accounts of users under 16, linkage to a parent or guardian account is generally required, with parental tools for time limits, spending, contacts, and privacy settings.
- Restrictions on profiling and targeted advertising to minors: the statute prohibits profiling-based targeted advertising directed at children and adolescents and the use of manipulative design.
- Loot boxes in games for minors are banned; dark patterns and engagement-maximising features (autoplay, infinite scroll where harmful) are restricted.
- Content duties: prompt removal of content that violates minors' rights, such as sexual exploitation and abuse, on notice and in some cases proactively; reporting channels; cooperation with authorities and mandatory notification of serious child abuse content.
- Transparency: periodic reports on moderation and risk mitigation for larger services, accessible, age-appropriate terms and privacy notices.
- A legal representative in Brazil for foreign providers is a recurring requirement; confirm.
- Sanctions: warnings, fines of up to R$50 million or 10% of Brazilian revenue (whichever is lower per the text as I recall it), suspension and prohibition of activities.
- Regulator: the ANPD, restructured as a regulatory agency, is the supervising authority for ECA Digital compliance.

3. LGPD obligations that apply on top
- Legal basis and purposes documented for each processing activity involving teens; avoid reliance on consent where the teen cannot freely give it.
- Transparency: privacy notice written in simple, clear, age-appropriate language, with visual and audiovisual aids (LGPD Art. 14, para. 6).
- Data minimisation: do not condition participation on providing more data than strictly necessary (Art. 14, para. 4).
- DPIA/RIPD: processing of minors' data at scale and any profiling or recommendation systems will almost certainly be "high risk" under ANPD criteria (Res. CD/ANPD 2/2022 notion of high-risk processing), so prepare and maintain a Relatório de Impacto.
- Data subject rights (Art. 18): operational channels exercisable by teens or through parents.
- DPO (encarregado): appointed and publicly identified (Res. CD/ANPD 18/2024).
- Security and incident reporting: 3 business days to notify ANPD and affected data subjects of incidents posing relevant risk (Res. CD/ANPD 15/2024); incidents involving minors are a risk aggravator.
- International transfers: standard contractual clauses under Res. CD/ANPD 19/2024 for any offshore hosting or parent-company access.
- Records of processing (ROPA).

4. Other relevant Brazilian rules
- ECA (Law 8.069/1990) and the Marco Civil da Internet (Law 12.965/2014), including its notice-and-takedown regime and the Supreme Court's 2025 ruling expanding platform liability under Art. 19.
- Consumer Code (CDC) on abusive and manipulative practices.
- Advertising self-regulation (CONAR) guidance on child-directed advertising, and the Brazilian Constitution's principle of absolute priority for children.

5. Practical roadmap
1. Scope and classify: confirm that the ECA Digital and LGPD Art. 14 apply, and identify teen cohort sizes by age band.
2. Gap assessment against safety-by-design: default settings, recommender systems, DMs from strangers, geolocation, live features, in-app purchases.
3. Age assurance design: pick a proportionate method, DPIA it, and avoid retaining age-verification evidence.
4. Parental tooling and under-16 account linking.
5. Advertising: switch off behavioural advertising to known minors, and exclude likely-minor segments.
6. Governance: DPO, ROPA, RIPD, a child-safety risk assessment, a moderation and takedown SLA, reporting channels, Brazilian legal representative.
7. Documentation: keep evidence to qualify for mitigating factors in the ANPD's dosimetry framework.
8. Monitor ANPD regulations, guides and consultations on age assurance and parental supervision.

Bottom line: treat teen users as the highest-risk cohort. Build high-privacy defaults, real age assurance, no behavioural ads to minors, strong takedown processes and a documented best-interest assessment.

Lawfully transferring personal data from Brazil to your US parent

Short answer: for a US recipient, the practical route is the ANPD standard contractual clauses (Resolution CD/ANPD 19/2024), adopted without modification. There is no adequacy decision for the US, and the January 2026 Brazil-EU mutual adequacy does not help here.

1. Why a transfer mechanism is needed

Sending personal data to a US parent, or even giving it remote access, is an international transfer under Arts. 33 to 36. LGPD allows it only through one of the Art. 33 mechanisms. Being part of the same corporate group does not exempt the transfer.

2. Your options

| Mechanism | Fit for a US parent | Comment |
|---|---|---|
| Adequacy (Art. 33, I) | Not available | ANPD has issued no adequacy decisions. The EU/EEA is treated as adequate from January 2026, but that does not extend to the US |
| ANPD standard contractual clauses (Art. 33, II(b); Res. 19/2024) | Best fit | Mandatory for contract-based transfers. The grace period ended 23 August 2025. Adopt without modification |
| Specific contractual clauses (Art. 33, II(a)) | Possible | Needs ANPD approval, so slow, and rarely worth it |
| Binding corporate rules / global corporate standards (Art. 33, II(c)) | Possible for intragroup flows | Require ANPD approval and a mature group programme. Good long-term if you have many group transfers |
| Specific, highlighted consent (Art. 33, VIII) | Fallback only | Must be specific to the transfer, informed of its international nature and risks. Fragile and revocable, so not suitable for routine HR or customer data |
| Other Art. 33 grounds | Narrow | Legal cooperation, vital interests, legal obligation, contract performance at the subject's request, or exercise of rights in proceedings. These cover specific cases, not a general parent-subsidiary flow |
| ANPD authorisation (Art. 33, IX) | Case-by-case | Rarely used |

Practical recommendation: sign the ANPD SCCs between the Brazilian entity and the US parent.

3. Using the ANPD standard clauses

- Take the text exactly as published. Resolution 19/2024 does not allow altering the clauses. You complete the annexes and options only.
- Fill the annexes: parties, controller or processor roles, description of the transfer, purposes, data categories (flag sensitive and children's data), recipients and onward transfers, security measures, and retention.
- Role mapping matters: if the parent processes as your processor, the clauses must fit that. If it is a controller in its own right, document that.
- Keep it ready for ANPD. You may be asked to show the executed clauses, and the transfer must also comply with the rest of LGPD.
- Add an Art. 38 RIPD where the data is high-risk, and keep a documented transfer-impact view of the destination's laws on government access.

4. The rest of the transfer still has to be lawful

The transfer mechanism covers only the transfer. You also need:
- An Art. 7 or 11 basis for the underlying processing, and a purpose that covers sharing with the parent (purpose limitation, Art. 6, I).
- Data minimisation: send only what the parent needs, and consider pseudonymisation or anonymisation.
- Transparency (Art. 9): tell data subjects that data goes to the US parent, the purpose, and the mechanism used (ANPD SCCs for the US).
- Records: reflect the transfer and mechanism in your RoPA.
- Security (Art. 46) at both ends, plus onward-transfer controls for the parent's own vendors.
- Rights: the parent must support Art. 18 requests routed through you.
- Incident clause: parent must alert you promptly so you can meet the 3-working-day Art. 48 notification.

5. Common errors to avoid

- Relying on a modified or custom DPA instead of the unmodified ANPD SCCs.
- Reusing EU SCCs. They are not accepted as a substitute for ANPD's clauses.
- Assuming "EU adequacy" covers a US parent just because your group is EU-linked.
- Relying on bundled consent in a privacy policy.
- Forgetting remote access from the US, which also counts as a transfer.
- Missing the SCC deadline. ANPD lists international transfers as an enforcement priority, and exposure is up to 2% of Brazilian revenue, capped at R$50M per infraction.

6. Steps

1. Inventory the data flows to the US (including support, analytics, HR, and cloud).
2. Define the roles of each party.
3. Execute the ANPD SCCs.
4. Update the privacy notice and RoPA.
5. Document your minimisation and risk reasoning.
6. Review annually, and watch ANPD for any adequacy decisions.

If you tell me the data categories and whether the parent acts as controller or processor, I can sketch the annex content.

✅Practical advice: audit existing intercompany agreements for ANPD SCC incorporation; don't rely on consent as a transfer workhorse
Lawful transfer of personal data from Brazil to a US parent company

1. The framework
Chapter V of the LGPD (Arts. 33-36) regulates international transfers, and ANPD Resolution CD/ANPD No. 19/2024 (August 2024) operationalised it. Any transfer, including remote access from the US to data stored in Brazil, counts as an international transfer. Intra-group transfers get no exemption. A transfer must satisfy two things: (1) an LGPD legal basis for the underlying processing, and (2) one of the Art. 33 transfer mechanisms.

2. The available transfer mechanisms (Art. 33)
- Adequacy decision by the ANPD. As of my knowledge, the ANPD has not recognised the US as adequate. Brazil has been working on adequacy with the EU in the other direction. Do not rely on adequacy for the US unless an ANPD decision is published.
- Standard contractual clauses (SCCs, "cláusulas-padrão contratuais"). The most practical option for a parent-subsidiary arrangement. Annex II of Res. 19/2024 contains the mandatory text, which must be adopted in full and without alteration, and filled in with the transfer details (parties, purposes, categories, security measures, onward transfers, liability). The deadline to migrate existing contracts to the ANPD SCCs was 23 August 2025.
- Specific contractual clauses, which require prior ANPD approval. Slow and rarely used.
- Binding corporate rules (BCRs, "normas corporativas globais"), which suit multinational groups with many flows but require ANPD approval. Worth considering if you have many Brazilian-US-global flows.
- Seals, certificates and codes of conduct (also subject to ANPD approval).
- Art. 33 exceptions: data subject's specific and highlighted consent with prior information on the international nature of the transfer; performance of a contract at the data subject's request; legal or regulatory obligation; exercise of rights in legal proceedings; protection of life; international legal cooperation; public policy authorisation. These are interpreted narrowly and are poor fits for routine intra-group flows. Consent is fragile because it can be revoked.

3. The recommended route for you: SCCs
Steps:
1. Map the flows. Identify categories of data (employees, customers, marketing, sensitive data), purposes, recipients in the US, onward transfers, retention, and systems.
2. Determine roles. The Brazilian entity is typically the exporter (controller). The US parent may be a controller or an operator. The SCCs have modules for controller-to-controller and controller-to-operator (Section II vs the optional modules); choose the correct one. The parent may be a joint or independent controller if it uses data for its own purposes.
3. Confirm the legal basis for the underlying processing and for sharing with the parent: legitimate interest, contract, legal obligation, or consent. Perform and document a legitimate interest assessment where relevant.
4. Execute the SCCs verbatim, completing the annexes. Choose the governing details the template leaves open (such as dispute resolution, the option for a security-incident notification period, and onward transfer conditions). Add a commercial agreement around them without conflicting with the SCCs. In case of conflict the SCCs prevail.
5. Publish information to data subjects: privacy notice should disclose the international transfer, the countries, the mechanism, and give access to a summary of the SCC terms. Provide the full text on request (Res. 19/2024 requires making SCC text or a summary available in Portuguese).
6. Perform a transfer risk assessment. The Resolution requires the exporter to ensure the SCCs can be honoured, including consideration of destination-country laws and practices such as government access. Document it.
7. Security and governance: encryption in transit and at rest, access controls, minimisation, retention limits and logging for access from the US.
8. Sensitive data, children's data, and employee data call for extra care (RIPD/DPIA).
9. Keep records: ROPA with the transfer entries, signed SCCs, TRA, notices; be ready to produce them to the ANPD on request.

4. Note on the EU-US Data Privacy Framework
The EU-US DPF has no bearing on Brazil-US transfers. Certifying the US parent does not itself satisfy the LGPD, though it can support the risk assessment about US safeguards.

5. Data subject rights and incident duties
Data subjects can still exercise their rights against the Brazilian controller, and the SCCs oblige the importer to assist. Incident notification (Res. CD/ANPD 15/2024) runs on a 3-business-day clock for incidents posing relevant risk, so the SCCs and your internal escalation need to ensure the US parent notifies the Brazilian entity fast enough.

6. Common pitfalls
- Modifying the SCC text: invalid, and a breach of the Resolution.
- Treating cloud storage in the US or support access as not a transfer.
- Relying on consent for HR data in an employment relationship.
- Failing to update existing intra-group agreements by the deadline.
- Not capturing onward transfers by the parent to its processors.
- Ignoring the requirement that the importer be bound by the Brazilian law rights.

7. Timeline
SCC execution and TRA: 4 to 8 weeks for a typical group. BCRs: many months.

Bottom line: sign the ANPD standard clauses unaltered between the Brazilian entity and the US parent, back them with a documented legal basis, transparency and risk assessment, and keep records. Confirm any adequacy or regulatory update with Brazilian counsel.

Responding to unauthorised access to customer data in your Brazilian operation

The key facts: LGPD Art. 48 and Resolution CD/ANPD 15/2024 require notification to ANPD and affected data subjects if the incident may cause relevant risk or harm. The preliminary ANPD notification is due within 3 working days of when you become aware of it. The full report is due within 20 working days of confirmation. Start the clock from awareness, not from the end of your investigation.

Incident timeline

Hour 0 to 24: detect and contain
- Activate the incident response team: security, legal, the encarregado (DPO), communications, and the business owner.
- Contain the access: revoke credentials and tokens, isolate affected systems, block the attack path. Do not wipe systems, because evidence matters.
- Preserve logs, images, and timestamps. Start an incident log recording who knew what and when. Note the exact time of awareness, since it sets your deadline.
- Involve your processors and cloud vendors. Under Art. 39 and Art. 46 they must support you, and you remain responsible for their security.
- Use privileged channels for legal analysis. Keep forensic facts separate from legal conclusions.

Day 1 to 2: assess
Determine:
- What data: identification, CPF, contact, financial, credentials, and above all sensitive data (Art. 11) or children's data, which raise risk.
- How many data subjects, and in which countries (Brazilian residents bring LGPD in under Art. 3).
- Nature of the incident: confidentiality, integrity, or availability. Was data exfiltrated, encrypted, or only viewed?
- Likelihood and severity of harm: fraud, identity theft, discrimination, reputational damage, physical risk.
- Whether data was encrypted or pseudonymised, which can reduce risk.
Record the risk conclusion and reasoning. If you decide not to notify, document why, because ANPD can ask.

Within 3 working days: preliminary ANPD notification
Submit through ANPD's incident channel. Cover what you know, under the Art. 48 content list:
- Nature of the affected personal data
- Information on the data subjects involved
- Technical and security measures used to protect the data
- Risks related to the incident
- Reasons for any delay
- Measures adopted or planned to reverse or mitigate the effects
Where facts are incomplete, say so and commit to a supplementary submission. A partial, timely notice is better than a late complete one.

Notify data subjects
Where the incident may entail relevant risk or harm, notify affected individuals, in clear Portuguese and without undue delay. Say what happened, what data, the likely consequences, what you are doing, what they can do (for example password resets, watching for phishing, credit monitoring), and how to reach the encarregado. Coordinate timing with ANPD, since it may direct you on communications.

Within 20 working days of confirmation: full report to ANPD
Provide the complete account: root cause, final scope, timeline, data categories and counts, mitigation, communications to data subjects, and corrective actions.

Parallel workstreams
- Other regulators and contracts: check sectoral rules (for example Banco Central for financial entities, ANS or ANVISA for health), customer contracts with notification clauses, cyber-insurance notice requirements, and, if you are in a group, parent-level reporting.
- If the data also covers EU residents, GDPR's 72-hour clock to the supervisory authority may apply separately. Run the two assessments in parallel.
- Law enforcement: consider a police report (boletim de ocorrência) and engaging the specialised cybercrime units.
- Communications: a single consistent holding statement. Avoid statements you cannot support.

Remediation and accountability
- Fix the root cause, then review access controls, MFA, logging, vendor oversight, and encryption (Art. 46).
- Update the RIPD, RoPA, and risk register.
- Lessons-learned review, and test the playbook again.
- Keep a complete incident file. Under the accountability principle (Art. 6, X), your documentation is your main mitigating evidence.

Exposure
Failure to notify, late notice, or weak security can lead to warnings, fines up to 2% of Brazilian revenue (R$50M per infraction cap), publicisation, blocking or deletion orders, and civil damages claims under Art. 42. ANPD is now an autonomous agency (Lei 15.352/2026) and has stepped up enforcement, so good cooperation, prompt corrective action, and demonstrable controls (Art. 52, section 1) count in your favour. Large-scale breaches are an ANPD priority.

Immediate checklist
1. Record the awareness timestamp and calendar the 3-working-day deadline.
2. Contain and preserve evidence.
3. Scope the data and the people affected.
4. Decide on notification and document the decision.
5. File the preliminary ANPD notice.
6. Notify data subjects if risk warrants.
7. Prepare the 20-working-day report.

Responding to unauthorized access to customer data in Brazil

Treat this as a live incident. The key Brazilian rule is Art. 48 of the LGPD and ANPD Resolution CD/ANPD No. 15/2024, which set a 3-business-day deadline (from when the controller becomes aware that the incident may cause relevant risk or damage to data subjects) to notify both the ANPD and affected data subjects. The clock starts at awareness of the incident with relevant risk, not at completion of the investigation. Below is the sequence I would follow. This is general guidance, not legal advice.

Hour 0-24: contain and organise
1. Activate the incident response plan and convene a core team: security lead, DPO (encarregado), legal counsel (Brazilian), communications, executive sponsor, and HR or customer care as needed.
2. Contain: isolate affected systems, revoke or rotate compromised credentials and keys, block the attacker's access paths, and disable exploited vulnerabilities. Preserve evidence: take forensic images and logs, and keep chain of custody. Do not wipe systems.
3. Open an incident log with timestamps of detection, decisions, and actions. This record is mandatory under the Resolution (incident register kept for at least five years) and it is your main evidence of diligence.
4. Engage an external forensic firm under legal privilege where appropriate, and notify your cyber insurer, since policies often require prompt notice and pre-approved vendors.
5. Notify the US parent or global security team per intra-group procedure, since global obligations may also be triggered.

Day 1-2: assess scope and risk
- Determine what data, how many data subjects, which categories (identifiers, financial, sensitive, children, credentials), the time window, whether the data was exfiltrated, encrypted or only accessed, and whether it is still exposed.
- Assess whether the incident presents relevant risk or damage to data subjects: Resolution 15/2024 considers it present when the incident involves sensitive data, data of children, adolescents or elderly people, financial data, authentication data, legally protected secrets, or large scale data. Weigh the likelihood of identity theft, fraud, discrimination or other harm.
- Identify whether you are controller or operator. If you are an operator for a client, you must notify the controller immediately so they can meet their own deadlines, and follow the contract.
- Decide on notification. If in doubt about relevance, the safer course is to notify, since late notification is itself a sanctionable infraction.

Within 3 business days: notify
A. ANPD: use the ANPD's electronic incident communication form (through the ANPD's online system). Content: description of the nature and category of data affected; number of data subjects; technical and security measures used; risks; reasons for delay if any; measures taken or planned to mitigate; DPO contact details. If you do not yet have all the facts, submit a preliminary notice and supplement it, as the Resolution allows a complementary communication within 20 business days.
B. Data subjects: communicate directly in clear and simple Portuguese, covering the nature of the incident, the data affected, risks, measures taken, steps they can take to protect themselves (change passwords, monitor accounts), and DPO contact. Use direct channels (email, SMS, app notice). Public notice is acceptable only when direct contact is impossible.
C. Others as applicable: Brazilian sector regulators (Banco Central, SUSEP, ANS, Anatel), the Federal Police or civil police for criminal complaint (boletim de ocorrência) if it is a crime; credit card brands and partners; the CERT.br or CTIR Gov for relevant incidents; your customers if you are a processor; and foreign regulators for non-Brazilian data subjects (GDPR 72-hour, US state laws), since a US parent will have its own deadlines. Align the timelines early.

Days 3-30: investigate, remediate, document
- Complete the root-cause analysis and remediation: patching, MFA, segmentation, monitoring, vendor controls.
- Submit the complementary report to the ANPD if the initial one was partial.
- Offer support to affected individuals where warranted, such as credit monitoring, helplines, and a dedicated FAQ.
- Manage ANPD follow-up. The ANPD may open an inspection or sanctioning process, request information, or order measures including public disclosure. Respond completely and on time, since non-response has been a source of early sanctions.
- Handle claims: expect individual complaints, Procon or consumer-association action, and possible litigation under Art. 42. Preserve documents and coordinate communications.

Communications
Prepare a consistent holding statement, FAQ for customer care, and internal messaging. Avoid speculation, and ensure what you tell customers matches the ANPD notification.

Mitigating factors for sanctions
The ANPD's dosimetry rules (Res. 4/2023) reward prompt notification, cooperation, quick mitigation, and an existing governance and security programme. Documented incident response plan, training, and ROPA all help.

Post-incident lessons
- Update the RIPD (DPIA) and ROPA, run a lessons-learned review, retest controls, and brief the board.
- Test your incident plan annually.

Common mistakes
- Waiting for the full forensic picture before notifying.
- Notifying only the ANPD and not data subjects.
- Failing to retain records.
- Inconsistent statements across jurisdictions.
- Treating the US parent's investigation as a substitute for a Brazilian filing.

Immediate checklist: stop the bleeding, preserve evidence, call counsel and the DPO, determine data and people affected, decide the relevant risk, start the 3-business-day clock, and prepare the ANPD form and the data subject message now.

| FY2027 (report published 2028) | Revised ESRS (mandatory) | Applies to financial years beginning 1 January 2027. |

**3. How to choose for FY2026**

Arguments for the revised ESRS in FY2026:
- Lower datapoint burden, since roughly 320 mandatory datapoints replace more than 1,000.
- No double build. You would otherwise do a 2023-basis report in FY2026 and then rebuild for FY2027.
- Your FY2026 baseline would be comparable with FY2027.

Arguments for staying on the 2023 ESRS for FY2026:
- Your FY2024 and FY2025 reports (wave-one reporters have already published) were built on the 2023 ESRS. Staying put gives continuity of prior-year comparatives (ESRS 1 requires comparatives for quantitative disclosures).
- Your data processes, XBRL tagging and assurance work are already calibrated to that structure.
- The revised standards are not yet in force, so the risk of an early-adoption interpretive question is higher.

My practical suggestion is to run a short mapping exercise before deciding. Take your FY2025 report, map it to the revised mandatory datapoints, and see how much you would drop, what must change, and how comparatives would be handled. Then decide.

2. Run the FY2025-to-revised-ESRS datapoint mapping.
3. Decide the FY2026 basis, document the rationale, and agree it with the board or audit committee and the assurance provider.
4. Plan the FY2027 data and controls build on the revised ESRS.

Short answer: wave-one companies (large public-interest entities with 500+ employees, reporting on FY2024 in 2025) currently apply ESRS Set 1 (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2023/2772). A simplified, revised ESRS is in the pipeline, and the expectation is that it applies from FY2027, with possible optional early use for FY2026. Please verify the exact adoption status before you lock your plans, because this has been moving quickly.

1. Background: why the standards are being revised
The Omnibus I package (sustainability simplification), proposed in February 2025, did two things. First, the "stop-the-clock" directive (Directive (EU) 2025/794) postponed reporting for wave two and wave three companies by two years. It did not delay wave one. Second, the content directive amends CSRD and CSDDD: it raises the scope threshold to more than 1,000 employees and more than EUR 450M net turnover, removes the sector-specific standards, replaces reasonable assurance with limited assurance only, and requires the Commission to revise the ESRS to reduce datapoints and clarify the double materiality assessment. EFRAG was mandated to deliver simplified draft ESRS. Its technical advice went to the Commission at the end of 2025, with a substantial reduction in mandatory datapoints (on the order of 60 percent or more cut in the headline figures cited) and more phase-in relief and flexibility.

2. What you apply, year by year
- FY2025 (reported in 2026): ESRS Set 1 as it stands, together with the Commission's "quick fix" relief. Wave-one companies can continue to use the existing phase-ins (for example, for some Scope 3, biodiversity and own-workforce datapoints) and the extended phase-ins have been aligned with the simplification work. Practically, you continue with the Set 1 structure: ESRS 1, ESRS 2, the topical standards you find material.
- FY2026 (reported in 2027): This is the transition year. The Commission's revised ESRS delegated act is intended to apply for financial years starting 1 January 2027, but the expectation is that companies could optionally apply the simplified standards earlier. Unless and until the delegated act is adopted and survives scrutiny, Set 1 remains the legally binding standard for FY2026. I would plan on Set 1 as the baseline with a documented decision on whether to adopt early.
- FY2027 (reported in 2028): The revised (simplified) ESRS are expected to be the binding standard, provided the delegated act is adopted and passes the Parliament and Council scrutiny period.

3. Legal status of the revised standards
Revised ESRS are not law until the Commission adopts them as a delegated act under Article 29b of the Accounting Directive, and the Parliament and Council have not objected during the scrutiny period (typically four months, extendable by two). EFRAG's technical advice is just advice. The Commission may deviate from it. Consequently, the revised ESRS are currently a draft and carry no legal force. Companies should treat the EFRAG advice as a strong signal of direction, not as something to comply with.

4. Do you remain in scope at all?
Check this first. Under the Omnibus content directive, scope is limited to companies with more than 1,000 employees and more than EUR 450M turnover (for EU companies). Many wave-one companies that were in scope on the 500-employee test will drop out. The transposition rules matter: member states may allow wave-one companies that fall below the new thresholds to be exempted for FY2025 and FY2026, depending on national transposition. Transposition is required by early 2027 or thereabouts, so national law is uneven. If you are out of scope, consider the voluntary standard (VSME) as a way to answer customer and bank requests.

5. Practical recommendations
- Confirm in-scope status using the new thresholds and your member state's transposition position.
- Keep your FY2025 reporting on Set 1; do not rebuild your whole system around draft text.
- Run a gap analysis between Set 1 and the EFRAG simplified draft so that a switch for FY2026 or FY2027 is cheap. The core architecture (double materiality, ESRS 2 general disclosures, E1 climate) is retained, so your climate and workforce data collection investments carry over.
- Make a board-level decision on early adoption for FY2026, and disclose the basis of preparation clearly.
- Track: the Commission delegated act, the scrutiny period, national transposition, and the taxonomy simplification which runs in parallel.

Short answer: no. At 800 employees you are outside mandatory CSRD scope, whatever your turnover. Your response to customer requests should be the voluntary standard, not a bespoke questionnaire for each customer.

**1. Scope analysis**

| Criterion | Requirement under Directive (EU) 2026/470 | You | Met? |
|---|---|---|---|
| Employees | More than 1,000 | 800 | No |
| Net turnover | More than EUR 450 million | EUR 600M | Yes |
| Verdict | Both are required (AND) | | **Out of mandatory scope** |

Directive (EU) 2026/470 was published in the Official Journal on 26 February 2026 and entered into force in March 2026. Mandatory CSRD reporting now applies only to large undertakings with more than 1,000 employees and net turnover above EUR 450 million. The conditions are cumulative. Your EUR 600M turnover clears the financial test, but the headcount test fails, so you fall outside.

Points to check:
- **Headcount basis.** Confirm how employees are counted (average over the year, full-time equivalents). Being near the line matters, and 800 gives you a comfortable margin, but verify the counting method and whether any group entities aggregate.
- **Group structure.** If you are part of a larger group, scope may be assessed at parent or consolidated level, and a group report could cover you. If your parent is itself above 1,000 employees and EUR 450M, you may still be asked to feed data into its report.
- **Transposition.** The scope change must be transposed by Member States by about 19 March 2027, and Germany is still pending. If you operate in a Member State that has not yet transposed, check the local position, though the EU-level direction is clear.
- **Growth.** If you cross 1,000 employees later, you would re-enter scope, so monitor it.
- **Stop-the-clock context.** Directive (EU) 2025/794 had deferred the wave 2 and 3 reporting by two years before the scope cut. Companies like you that were previously expecting to report simply exit mandatory scope.

**2. What to do when large customers ask for data**

Customers that are themselves in scope still need value-chain information for their own reporting. But there is now a legal ceiling on what they can demand from you.

- The voluntary standard, Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1560 (VSME-based; in force 24 September 2026), is the reference vehicle for you.
- It operates as the value-chain cap. Reporters may not demand more from value-chain partners with 1,000 employees or fewer than the content of this standard.

So when a customer sends a long ESG questionnaire, your position is: "Here is our report under the EU voluntary standard." That is a legitimate, EU-recognised response.

**3. Practical steps**

1. **Prepare one voluntary-standard report.** Build a single package aligned to Delegated Regulation 2026/1560 and refresh it annually. Reuse it for every customer request.
2. **Prepare a standard reply.** A short note that you are outside mandatory CSRD scope under Directive (EU) 2026/470, that you report under the voluntary standard, and that under the cap the customer's requests should not go beyond it. Keep it polite and factual.
3. **Triage requests.** For each request, check what is genuinely beyond the voluntary standard. Where it is, you can decline, or agree selectively as a commercial choice.
4. **Review contracts.** Look for supplier clauses that contractually require ESG data. A legal cap on what a reporter can demand does not automatically void contract terms already agreed, so have counsel check any existing flow-down clauses. I would not assume the cap overrides signed contract language without legal review.
5. **Know your own numbers.** Scope 1 and 2 emissions, energy, headcount and basic workforce data are the usual asks. Having them ready helps customers who must estimate their Scope 3 anyway. Customers may use proxy or sector-average data where yours is not available, and they must disclose that estimation approach (ESRS 1, para. 64 per the reference).
6. **Commercial upside.** Good data can be a differentiator in tender processes, even where it is not legally required.

**4. Optional extras**

- Using GRI, CDP or EcoVadis is still fine as a voluntary choice if a customer relationship justifies it.
- Assurance is not required for you. If a customer asks for verified data, that is a commercial decision.
- Keep an eye on the revised ESRS (Delegated Regulation 2026/1563, in force 10 November 2026) in case a customer references them. They bind your customers, not you.

**5. Bottom line**

You are not a CSRD reporter. Verify headcount method and group structure, then centralise your response on the voluntary standard and rely on the value-chain cap when requests exceed it.

You should still prepare for customer data requests, and the EU has deliberately created a ceiling on what they can ask for.

1. The scope test after Omnibus I
Under the amended Accounting Directive, a large undertaking is in CSRD scope if it has more than 1,000 employees on average and either more than EUR 450M net turnover (for EU companies). The old test (250 employees plus two of three size criteria: EUR 50M turnover, EUR 25M balance sheet) is no longer the gate. Both conditions must be met: employees above 1,000 AND turnover above EUR 450M.

At 800 employees you fail the employee limb even though your EUR 600M turnover passes the turnover limb. So, as an EU company, you are out of scope. Points to verify:
- Employee count: it is the average number of employees over the financial year, and the definition in the directive should be counted as full-time equivalents under the national transposition. Check whether group-level numbers (consolidated) push you above 1,000. If you are a subsidiary of a larger group, the group may report on a consolidated basis and you may get an exemption, but the group's own thresholds are what matter.
- Non-EU parent: if you are the EU arm of a non-EU group, the third-country regime applies (EU net turnover above EUR 450M for two consecutive years, with an EU subsidiary or branch meeting thresholds). Reporting under that regime starts later. Your EUR 600M EU turnover may matter there, depending on your structure. You said "turnover in the EU", which suggests this may be relevant, so confirm what entity is the reporting group.
- Listed SMEs: they were removed from scope entirely.
- National transposition: member states must transpose the content directive; until they do, there may be gaps. Stop-the-clock means wave-two and wave-three entities do not report until FY2027 at the earliest anyway, so there is no immediate compliance obligation even in the uncertain cases.
- If you reach 1,000 employees in future, you would come in. Monitor headcount trends.

2. Customers will ask anyway
Many in-scope customers need value chain data (Scope 3, supplier due diligence, social and human rights information). Even though you are not a CSRD reporter, you are in their value chain. Key points:
- The Omnibus introduced a "value chain cap": in-scope companies cannot require from value-chain partners with up to 1,000 employees more than what is in the voluntary standard for SMEs. The Commission has recommended the VSME standard (Commission Recommendation of July 2025) as that benchmark. Since you have 800 employees, you sit within this protection. A customer should not demand more than VSME-level data in a formal request, and the ESRS are meant to reflect that cap.
- In practice commercial pressure will go beyond law: contract clauses, supplier codes, and questionnaires (CDP, EcoVadis, customer portals). The cap is a legal limit on what reporting companies can require under CSRD, but contract negotiation remains commercial.

3. What to do
1. Build a baseline: use the VSME (Basic module, then Comprehensive if customers need governance and strategy detail). It covers GHG emissions Scope 1 and 2, energy, pollution, water, waste, workforce, health and safety, and business conduct.
2. Calculate your GHG inventory (Scope 1 and 2 and, where practical, the main Scope 3 categories) using the GHG Protocol. Having it audited or independently reviewed raises trust.
3. Create a single, standard response pack so that you answer all customers with the same data, rather than answering each questionnaire from scratch. Include a policy summary, targets, certifications (ISO 14001, 50001), and a contact point.
4. Triage requests: for each, ask whether it fits within VSME; where it asks for more, negotiate, ask which legal basis they rely upon, and consider whether the commercial value justifies the effort. CSDDD obligations of customers (supply chain due diligence) are also reduced and delayed, so do not assume everything asked is legally mandated.
5. Protect confidential data: do not hand over detailed commercial data without NDAs.
6. Governance: assign an owner, document data sources, and keep an evidence trail.
7. Consider voluntary reporting: it can be a competitive advantage with banks and customers, and gets you ready if you cross the threshold.

Caveat: my knowledge of national transposition is limited. Check your member state's law and get legal advice on group structure and non-EU parent effects.

Short answer: CSRD sustainability reporting is subject to limited assurance, performed by your statutory auditor or an independent assurance services provider (IASP). The EU-specific limited-assurance standard is still being finalised, and reasonable assurance is no longer on the legislative path.

**1. Who provides assurance (Art. 26a Accounting Directive as amended by the CSRD)**

- Your statutory auditor, or
- An independent assurance services provider (IASP), where the Member State permits this.

The practical choice is often the financial statement auditor, because of the efficiency of working with the same team. Check the position in your Member State, because the national rules on who qualifies as an IASP differ.

**2. What the assurance covers**

- Compliance of the sustainability reporting with the ESRS.
- The double materiality assessment process, including the process to identify material information.
- The sustainability information itself, including the XBRL/iXBRL digital tagging requirement.
- Connection of the sustainability information to the dedicated section of the management report (Art. 19a).

**3. Level of assurance: limited**

Limited assurance has applied from the first reporting year. The conclusion is in negative form ("nothing has come to our attention"), supported by inquiries and analytical procedures, with less extensive evidence than a financial audit.

A change from earlier guidance: older material, including the original CSRD text, said reasonable assurance would be phased in later, with a Commission review by 2028. The Omnibus removed the empowerment for reasonable-assurance standards, so limited assurance remains the regime. If you have an internal roadmap that budgets for a move to reasonable assurance, you can drop that assumption.

**4. Against what standard: current status as of 3 October 2026**

- There is no finalised EU-wide limited-assurance standard yet. In the interim, practitioners use national standards or international ones such as ISAE 3000 (Revised) and ISSA 5000, depending on the Member State's rules. Confirm with your auditor which is being applied in your jurisdiction.
- CEAOB delivered its technical advice to the Commission on 25 September 2026. The advice proposes an EU limited-assurance standard built on ISSA 5000, with EU add-ons and carve-outs.
- The Commission's limited-assurance delegated act is due by 1 July 2027. Until it is adopted, this is advice, not law.

So the honest answer on "against what standard" is: the EU standard is in the pipeline and your auditor will use the framework applicable in your Member State until then. Don't tell the board that the EU standard has been adopted.

**5. Interaction with the Omnibus changes**

- Check whether you are in mandatory scope (Directive (EU) 2026/470: more than 1,000 employees and more than EUR 450 million net turnover). If you are out of scope, assurance is not mandatory and any assurance on voluntary reporting is a commercial choice.
- If you are in scope, what is assured depends on your ESRS basis. For FY2026 you may choose the 2023 ESRS (as amended) or the revised ESRS (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1563, in force 10 November 2026). For financial years beginning 1 January 2027, the revised ESRS apply. The revised ESRS cut mandatory datapoints from over 1,000 to roughly 320, which narrows what the auditor must examine.

**6. Readiness checklist**

1. Named owners for each material ESRS topic and each datapoint.
2. DMA documented: methodology, scoring, stakeholder input, thresholds (ESRS 2 IRO-1).
3. Data lineage from source system to reported figure, with completeness checks.
4. Internal controls over sustainability reporting (ESRS 2 GOV-5), with management review and sign-off.
5. Estimation methods documented for value-chain gaps, including limitations (ESRS 1, para. 64).
6. Prior-year comparatives reconciled, plus a restatement policy.
7. Reporting boundary and any differences from the financial reporting boundary documented.
8. Audit committee oversight.

Engage the assurance provider early. The reference guidance recommends agreeing scope, approach and timeline during gap-assessment, not at the end. If you can, build documentation of high quality from the start, because rebuilding evidence trails retrospectively is hard.

**7. What to ask your auditor**

- Which standard are you applying for our FY2026 engagement, and in which Member State's framework?
- How will you handle our choice between 2023 and revised ESRS?
- Will you review the XBRL tagging, and when is the ESEF sustainability taxonomy expected?
- What changes do you expect when the EU limited-assurance standard is adopted?

This is general compliance information, not legal advice. Check your Member State's transposition and your auditor's current methodology.

Currently that means limited assurance, by a statutory auditor or (where the member state allows) an independent assurance services provider. The Omnibus I amendments removed the planned move to reasonable assurance and replaced it with Commission guidelines. The assurance standard is, for now, whatever your member state has prescribed, with ISSA 5000 as the dominant international benchmark.

1. Legal basis
CSRD amended the Audit Directive and the Accounting Directive. Article 34 of the Accounting Directive requires the sustainability reporting (including the Article 8 taxonomy information and the digital tagging) to be assured. Originally, the Directive called for limited assurance initially, moving to reasonable assurance by October 2028, with the Commission to adopt assurance standards by October 2026. Omnibus I changed this: the move to reasonable assurance has been removed, and the Commission's obligation to adopt binding assurance standards has been replaced with an obligation to issue targeted, non-binding assurance guidelines (expected around 2026) so that limited assurance is delivered consistently.

2. Who can provide it
- The statutory auditor or audit firm that audits your financial statements.
- Member states may allow other statutory auditors or audit firms approved in that state, or an independent assurance services provider (IASP) accredited under conditions equivalent to those for statutory auditors on competence, independence, quality control and oversight. The member state choice matters: some (for example Germany initially) have been restrictive, and some have opened the market to IASPs. If you are multinational, check each state.
- For groups, the group auditor must handle consolidated reporting; component work needs coordination.
- Independence rules apply: the prohibited non-audit services, fee caps and rotation rules for PIEs bite in different ways, so avoid using the same provider for consulting on your sustainability systems and assurance.

3. Against what standard
The Commission has not adopted EU assurance standards. In the meantime, member states apply their own standards or give auditors the choice. In practice:
- ISSA 5000 (General Requirements for Sustainability Assurance Engagements), issued by the IAASB in November 2024, is the global baseline and the most likely template for EU practice. The IAASB standard is effective for periods beginning on or after mid-December 2026 and early adoption is allowed.
- Existing standards such as ISAE 3000 (Revised) and ISAE 3410 (GHG statements) are widely used.
- National standards: Germany's IDW draft standards, France's CNCC/H2A guidance, Netherlands NBA. The Commission's guidelines will aim to converge.
- CEAOB guidelines have been issued as supervisory expectations.

4. What limited assurance covers
The conclusion addresses whether anything has come to the assurer's attention indicating that the sustainability statement does not comply with the Directive's requirements, including: compliance with ESRS (including the process to identify the information reported, the double materiality assessment), compliance with the tagging requirement, and compliance with taxonomy reporting. Limited assurance is a negative-form conclusion with less evidence than reasonable assurance; it is still demanding, especially on the materiality process and the value chain data.

5. Practical consequences for you
- Treat the report as assurance-ready from day one: documented methodology, data owners, controls, and evidence retention. Pursue "internal control over sustainability reporting".
- Run a dry run or readiness review before the first assured cycle.
- Appoint your assurer early: scope, materiality, timing of work on the DMA, and access to value chain evidence should be agreed.
- Audit committee oversight is expected: the committee must monitor the reporting process and the assurance.
- Expect questions on estimates and on the use of phase-ins; make sure the statement explains basis of preparation.
- Budget: assurance fees are a material cost; fee levels vary by provider.
- Wave status: for wave-one companies, FY2024 reports were first assured under national rules; for FY2025 onward, the process continues.

6. What is uncertain
Reasonable assurance is no longer a mandated step, but the Directive allows the Commission to review the issue later. The Commission's guidelines are non-binding, and national divergence persists. Check your state's transposition and the final text of the guidelines.

Before the walkthrough, one threshold question that the skill requires me to ask: are you reporting on the current 2023 ESRS basis or the revised ESRS basis? The answer changes some detail, though not the logic of the DMA.

Status check: the revised ESRS are Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1563, adopted 3 July 2026, published in the Official Journal on 21 September 2026 and in force from 10 November 2026. They apply to financial years beginning 1 January 2027, and for FY2026 in-scope undertakings can choose either basis. Mandatory datapoints fall from over 1,000 to roughly 320.

Also confirm scope first. Under Directive (EU) 2026/470, only large undertakings with more than 1,000 employees and net turnover above EUR 450 million are in mandatory scope. If you are below that, the DMA is optional, and the voluntary standard (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1560) is your vehicle.

**What the revised ESRS change for the DMA**

I am confident of the headline changes: far fewer mandatory datapoints, and former voluntary datapoints moved to EFRAG non-mandatory guidance. I would not claim detailed paragraph-level changes to the DMA methodology without checking the published text of 2026/1563. The skill's methodology below is anchored in ESRS 1 paras. 45 to 56 and ESRS 2 IRO-1 and SBM-3, so verify the paragraph numbers against the revised text before you cite them in a report.

What stays constant: double materiality, impact materiality plus financial materiality, a topic is material if it meets either or both, and the DMA drives what you report.

**The eight-step process**

**Step 1. Understand the context.** Map business activities, business model, geographies and the full value chain (upstream and downstream). Use sector references such as SASB or GRI sector standards. Output: a context document and value-chain map.

**Step 2. Identify actual and potential impacts.** Combine internal sources (operations review, incident data, management interviews) with external sources (stakeholder engagement, benchmarks, peers). Engage affected stakeholders, not only investors: workers, communities, customers, NGOs, financial institutions and regulators (ESRS 1, para. 22). Output: a long list of impacts by topic.

**Step 3. Assess significance of impacts.**
- Negative actual impacts: scale x scope x irremediability.
- Negative potential impacts: add likelihood.
- Positive impacts: scale x scope, with likelihood for potential ones.
Use a consistent 1 to 5 scoring scale, and set and justify your thresholds. The reference example is severity at or above 27 for actual and 50 for potential impacts. That is illustrative only, as there is no prescribed numerical threshold.

**Step 4. Identify financial risks and opportunities.** Physical risks (acute and chronic), transition risks (policy, technology, market, reputation) and opportunities. Consider effects on financial position, performance, cash flows, access to finance and cost of capital, across short (under 1 year), medium (1 to 5 years) and long (over 5 years) horizons.

**Step 5. Assess financial significance.** Rate magnitude and likelihood. The template uses EBITDA bands (below 1%, 1 to 5%, above 5%) and likelihood bands. Again these are company-defined and must be disclosed.

**Step 6. Determine materiality topic by topic.** Apply both lenses. Build a matrix: topic, impact material, financially material, overall, report. A topic that is material on either lens is reported in full. For non-material topics, give a brief justification.

**Step 7. Document and disclose.** ESRS 2 IRO-1 covers the process: scope, methodology, criteria, thresholds, stakeholder engagement, frequency. ESRS 2 SBM-3 covers the output: the material IROs and their interaction with strategy and business model. Keep an impact register and a financial risk and opportunity register for the audit trail.

**Step 8. Validate and update.** At least annually, and on triggers such as a business change, new regulation or an emerging risk. Disclose changes in conclusions.

**Applying it under the revised ESRS: practical points**

1. Run the DMA once and use it to select among the streamlined datapoints. Fewer mandatory datapoints means the DMA matters more as the filter for topical disclosures. ESRS 2 general disclosures remain mandatory regardless of outcome.
2. If you have an existing 2023-basis DMA, do not discard it. Re-validate it, map each material topic and sub-topic to the revised standards, and document any changes in conclusions.
3. Value chain: keep it in scope for impacts and risks. Note the cap, which says reporters cannot demand more from value-chain partners with 1,000 employees or fewer than the voluntary standard contains. That affects how you gather value-chain data after the DMA, not whether the DMA considers the value chain. Use proxies and sector averages where direct data is missing, and disclose the method.
4. Climate (E1) is presumed material for most large companies. Excluding it needs strong evidence.

**Common pitfalls**

- Own operations only, with the value chain ignored.
- Consulting only investors.
- Financial materiality neglected.
- Thresholds not justified.
- DMA done after deciding what to report.
- Over-excluding topics without a brief explanation.
- A static one-off exercise.

**Governance and assurance**

The assurance provider covers the DMA process (limited assurance, Art. 26a), so keep decisions, scoring and stakeholder evidence traceable, and have the board or audit committee approve the outcome.

This is general compliance information, not legal advice. Check the final text of Regulation 2026/1563 for revised paragraph references.

Below is a practical walkthrough of a double materiality assessment (DMA) under ESRS 1 Chapter 3 and IG 1 (the EFRAG implementation guidance), with notes on how the revised, simplified ESRS are expected to change the process. The revised standards are still draft in my knowledge, so I describe the process in terms that survive the changes.

Core idea
A topic is material if it is material from an impact perspective (your actual or potential, positive or negative impacts on people and environment), a financial perspective (sustainability matters that create risks or opportunities affecting your cash flows, access to finance or cost of capital in the short, medium or long term), or both. Either is enough to report.

Step 1: Plan and govern
- Set the scope: the consolidated group, plus the upstream and downstream value chain.
- Appoint an owner and a cross-functional team (sustainability, risk, finance, legal, operations, procurement, HR).
- Get governance sign-off: define who approves the result (board or audit committee) and how the work will be documented for assurance.
- Align with enterprise risk management so that financial materiality uses your existing risk framework.

Step 2: Understand context and map the value chain
- Document business model, activities, geographies, products, business relationships and sectors.
- Map the value chain: raw materials, suppliers, own operations, distribution, customers, end of life.
- Identify the stakeholders: affected stakeholders (workers, communities, consumers, ecosystems) and users of the report (investors, banks, regulators). Plan engagement, including proxies where nature cannot speak for itself.

Step 3: Identify impacts, risks and opportunities (IROs)
- Start from the ESRS list of sustainability matters in AR 16 of ESRS 1 (topics, sub-topics and sub-sub-topics across E1 to E5, S1 to S4, G1) as a long list, then add entity-specific topics.
- Use inputs: due diligence results, supplier audits, incident logs, grievance data, risk register, scenario analysis, industry studies, stakeholder consultations, and sector references.
- Describe each IRO precisely: what, where in the value chain, actual or potential, positive or negative, short/medium/long-term horizon, and for negatives whether it is connected to your business relationships.

Step 4: Assess materiality
Impact materiality:
- Negative impacts: severity (scale, scope, irremediable character) and likelihood for potential impacts. For human rights impacts, severity takes priority over likelihood.
- Positive impacts: scale and scope, and likelihood for potential impacts.
Financial materiality:
- Magnitude of potential financial effects and likelihood of occurrence, using the same scales as enterprise risk management where possible. Consider dependencies on natural, human and social resources.
Set scoring scales (for example 1 to 5), define thresholds and justify them. Thresholds are a judgement; document the rationale and test sensitivity. Avoid netting off or averaging that hides serious impacts. Note that the simplified ESRS direction is to let companies take a top-down, proportionate, "reasonable and supportable" approach, avoid exhaustive bottom-up listing, and drop a requirement to report on the detail of the process beyond what is needed.

Step 5: Validate and decide
- Review the results with management and, if possible, stakeholders; reconcile with risk and strategy.
- Make the final determination for each topic and datapoint. Remember that if a topic is not material, you need not report its disclosure requirements, but climate (E1) requires an explicit conclusion and explanation if you conclude it is not material. Also, ESRS 2 general disclosures are always required.
- Within each material topic, apply information materiality at the datapoint level: omit datapoints not material, but apply the "mandatory datapoints" derived from other EU law (SFDR, Pillar 3, Benchmark Regulation, Climate Law) as ESRS 2 Appendix B lists, unless you state not material.

Step 6: Document and disclose
- Disclose the process (IRO-1), the results (SBM-3), and how the IROs connect to strategy and business model. List the disclosure requirements covered (IRO-2).
- Keep evidence: workshop minutes, scoring, data sources, decisions. The assurer will test the DMA process.

Step 7: Keep it alive
- Repeat annually at light touch with a full review at least every few years or on significant change (new acquisitions, new products, regulation, incidents).
- Link the DMA to risk management, strategy, targets, and controls.

Common pitfalls
- Treating DMA as a survey of stakeholders only.
- Blurring impact and financial perspectives.
- Not covering the value chain.
- Over-reliance on consultants without internal ownership.
- Weak documentation of thresholds.
- Concluding too many or too few topics are material without evidence.
- Ignoring the interplay with the EU taxonomy and the CSDDD.

Timeline: expect 3 to 6 months for a first full DMA at a mid-size group, less for a refresh. Plan for the revised ESRS by running a light gap check of your DMA against the simplified guidance when it is final.

Short answer: it depends on your size. If you have 1,000 employees or fewer, your customers' demands are legally capped by the EU voluntary standard. If you are above 1,000 employees and meet the turnover test, you are a CSRD reporter yourself and must produce your own ESRS disclosures. Either way, you do not owe customers an open-ended "full Scope 3 and supplier ESG" dataset.

**1. Step one: where do you sit?**

Under Directive (EU) 2026/470 (OJ 26 February 2026, in force March 2026), mandatory CSRD reporting applies to large undertakings with more than 1,000 employees and net turnover above EUR 450 million. Transposition is due around 19 March 2027.

- **Above both thresholds:** you are in scope. You must report under the ESRS yourself.
- **At or below 1,000 employees (or EUR 450M turnover or less):** you are out of mandatory scope and you are protected by the value-chain cap.

**2. What customers can require if you are a 1,000-employee-or-below partner**

The voluntary standard, Commission Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1560 (in force 24 September 2026), is the cap. Reporters may not demand more from value-chain partners with 1,000 employees or fewer than its content. So:

- You can point customers to a voluntary-standard report as the full answer to their CSRD-driven requests.
- Requests for a complete Scope 3 inventory, detailed supplier-tier ESG questionnaires or topic-by-topic ESRS datapoints go beyond the cap and can be declined.
- Customers remain free to ask for more as a commercial matter, such as a tender criterion, and you can decide whether to agree. The cap restricts what reporters may require under the CSRD framework. I would not assume it overrides contract terms you have already signed, so have counsel review any existing flow-down clauses.

**3. What you must produce yourself if you are in scope**

You report on your own operations and your upstream and downstream value chain where material (ESRS 1, value chain, paras. 62 to 68). Whether that includes full Scope 3 depends on your DMA:

- ESRS E1-6 requires gross Scope 1, 2 (location-based and market-based) and Scope 3, where climate is material. Climate is presumed material for most large companies.
- Scope 3 is determined by the DMA and category relevance. Scope 3 is required if material. A practical phasing suggested in the reference material is Year 1 categories 1, 3, 6, 7 and 11, then adding 2, 4, 5 and 12, then full coverage.
- Disclose a transition plan (E1-1), targets (E1-4) and energy (E1-5) where applicable.
- Value-chain workers (S2) and business conduct and supplier relationships (G1-2) if material.

The revised ESRS (Delegated Regulation (EU) 2026/1563, in force 10 November 2026, mandatory for financial years beginning 1 January 2027, optional for FY2026) cut mandatory datapoints from over 1,000 to roughly 320. I would not assert exactly how Scope 3 appears in the revised text without checking the published regulation, so verify the Scope 3 requirement in the revised E1 before finalising your plan.

**4. Where value-chain data is not available**

You do not have to obtain primary data from every supplier. You may use proxy data, sector averages and reasonable estimates, provided you disclose which datapoints are estimated, the methodology, accuracy and uncertainty, and the steps to improve it (ESRS 1, para. 64 per the reference). The reference approach, from least to most effort:

| Method | Best for | Data quality |
|---|---|---|
| Spend-based emission factors (EEIO) | Long-tail suppliers | Low to medium |
| Industry sector averages | Where direct data is unavailable | Low |
| Supplier questionnaires (EcoVadis, custom) | Tier-1 suppliers | Medium to high |
| CDP Supply Chain | Large, listed suppliers | High |
| Site audits | High-risk suppliers | Very high |

Prioritise suppliers by spend share, sector and geographic risk, and strategic or sole-source relationships.

**5. If you are the one sending requests down your own supply chain**

The cap works in both directions. As a reporter, you may not ask your own suppliers with 1,000 employees or fewer for more than the voluntary standard. Redesign your supplier questionnaires to match it, and use estimates for the rest.

**6. Recommended actions**

1. Confirm your scope status (headcount, turnover, group structure).
2. Prepare a voluntary-standard report once and reuse it.
3. Draft a standard customer response citing Delegated Regulation 2026/1560 and the cap.
4. Log each request, mark what is in or beyond the voluntary standard, and escalate commercially important exceptions.
5. If you are in scope, run the DMA, then build the E1-6 and value-chain data plan with proxies where needed.
6. Review contracts with counsel.
