Cyber Essentials (CE) is the UK government-backed cyber security certification scheme, and since it's a mandatory requirement on your central government contract, you'll need the basic certificate at minimum (some contracts, especially those involving MoD or sensitive data, require Cyber Essentials Plus - check your tender documents/DOS notice carefully, as it will specify which level).

What it covers
CE is built around five technical control themes:
1. Firewalls - boundary firewalls configured on all devices and networks, default/weak rules removed.
2. Secure configuration - removing unnecessary software, accounts, and default passwords from all devices.
3. User access control - least-privilege access, strong password policies (or biometrics/MFA), admin accounts controlled and MFA-enforced on cloud services.
4. Malware protection - anti-malware software or application allow-listing on all in-scope devices.
5. Security update management (patch management) - all software kept in licensed, supported versions, with security patches applied within 14 days of release for critical/high vulnerabilities.

The process
- Self-assessment questionnaire (SAQ): you complete an online questionnaire (via IASME or a Certification Body) describing your IT estate and how each control is implemented. A qualified assessor reviews it, may ask follow-up questions, and grants certification if it passes.
- No physical audit for basic CE - it's entirely desk-based/questionnaire-based.
- Scope: you can scope the whole organisation (recommended for a first attempt at a government contract, since assessors/customers often expect whole-organisation scope) or a sub-set of your network, but a limited scope must be clearly segregated and justified - this can raise eyebrows with government customers.

Timeline
For a 40-person company with no prior certification, expect 4-8 weeks total: 1-2 weeks to gather an asset inventory (laptops, phones, cloud tenants, servers), 2-4 weeks to close any control gaps (patching backlog, enabling MFA everywhere, tidying admin accounts, ensuring supported OS versions), then 1-2 weeks for the questionnaire submission and assessor review/re-submission cycles. If you're currently unmanaged (e.g., no MDM, mixed personal devices, no centralised patching), budget more time.

Cost
- Certification body fee: roughly £300-£500+VAT for basic Cyber Essentials for a small/medium organisation, though pricing varies by provider and company size band. IASME-licensed certification bodies set their own prices within IASME's guidance.
- Cyber Essentials Plus (if required) is more expensive - typically £1,500-£3,000+ depending on the number of devices, sample size, and whether an assessor visits on-site or does it remotely, because it involves technical testing (vulnerability scanning, sample device checks, internal/external tests) rather than self-assessment.
- Internal cost is usually the bigger number: remediation work (patching, MDM enrolment, MFA rollout), possible new tooling (endpoint protection, patch management), and staff time to complete the questionnaire and gather evidence. For a 40-person company with reasonably modern M365/cloud-based IT, this is often £2,000-£10,000 of internal effort/tooling, but could be higher if you have legacy on-prem servers or shadow IT.

Practical tips for a first-timer
- Start with an asset/scope inventory - you can't secure what you don't know you have.
- Nail down MFA on all cloud admin and user accounts - this is the single most common reason for failed submissions.
- Check for unsupported software/OS versions (e.g., old Windows Server, EOL routers) - CE requires everything to be in vendor support.
- Confirm your certification body is IASME-accredited (the current sole accreditation body for the scheme in the UK).
- If bidding on a live tender, check whether the contract requires certification in place at time of bid or by contract award - deadlines matter, and remediation plus assessor turnaround can take longer than expected.

Overall: for a straightforward, cloud-based 40-person business, basic Cyber Essentials is very achievable in under two months at a total cost (certification + tooling + labour) usually in the £3,000-£12,000 range, though it can be less if your IT is already well-managed.

This is a very common profile for a modern small business, and the good news is the scoping rules for exactly this setup (BYOD, fully remote, cloud-only infrastructure) are well defined under the current Cyber Essentials question set (Danzell / Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3, mandatory for assessment accounts created from 27 April 2026). Here's how it breaks down.

**Microsoft 365 and AWS: both fully in scope, no exceptions.** Under Danzell, cloud services are formally defined and cannot be excluded from scope if they hold organisational data or deliver organisational services — and both M365 and AWS clearly do. Apply the shared-responsibility model to know which controls are whose:
- **M365 (SaaS)**: Microsoft owns most of the underlying technical controls (patching the service, physical security, etc.), but you always own user access control — meaning account provisioning/deprovisioning, unique credentials, and critically, **MFA enabled on every account that logs into it**. Missing MFA on a cloud service that supports it is an automatic-fail condition under Danzell, so this is not optional or "best practice" — it's a pass/fail line item.
- **AWS (IaaS)**: you own the lion's day of the controls here — secure configuration of your instances, patching guest OSes and applications, access control into the AWS console and workloads, and malware protection on anything that looks like a server/device. AWS owns the physical infrastructure and hypervisor. Same MFA rule applies to the AWS root and IAM accounts.
- For both, don't just assume the provider "handles it" — where you're relying on Microsoft or AWS for a control, confirm it's a contractual commitment (their trust/compliance documentation), not just an assumption.

**Personal phones for email (BYOD): in scope.** The scoping decision tree is simple: if a device accesses organisational data or services — and reading company email clearly qualifies — it's in scope, regardless of who owns it. The only BYOD carve-out is a device used solely for native phone calls/SMS or purely as an MFA authenticator app, which doesn't apply here since staff are reading email on them. Practically, this means each personal phone used for email needs to meet the secure configuration and malware/unlock requirements — device lock (PIN/biometric/password), and typically some form of mobile device management or configuration profile is the practical way to demonstrate and enforce this across a BYOD fleet, though the standard itself just requires the outcome, not a specific tool.

**Everyone working from home: also in scope, but the boundary shifts.** Home and remote working devices — both company-issued and BYOD — are in scope wherever they're used (home, café, train). The important nuance: your staff's home ISP routers are explicitly OUT of scope — you don't need to assess anyone's home broadband router. Instead, the enforced boundary control becomes the software firewall running on each device itself. If you supply staff with your own routers for home use, those would be in scope. And if you route traffic through a corporate or cloud VPN, the boundary shifts again — to that corporate/virtual firewall, which then needs to meet the firewall theme's requirements.

**What is out of scope here:** effectively nothing in your stack, based on what you've described — you don't have any legacy on-prem servers, no dev/test network mentioned, and no third-party contractor or student devices. Your scope statement will be short: whole organisation, all staff (including BYOD phones used for email), M365 tenant, AWS account(s), home working arrangements, no exclusions.

**One scoping mistake to specifically avoid:** teams in your situation sometimes assume "we're all cloud, so there's nothing to certify" or try to exclude BYOD phones because "it's just email." Both are explicitly called out as common mistakes that lead to fails or invalid scope statements — cloud services can never be scoped out under Danzell, and BYOD used for organisational email is squarely in.

**Bottom line for your gap assessment:** your two biggest workstreams will be (1) confirming and enforcing MFA across every M365 and AWS account — this is your automatic-fail risk — and (2) making sure every BYOD phone and home-working device has basic secure configuration (screen lock, no jailbreak/root, auto-updates) and malware protection in place. Everything else flows from a whole-organisation, no-exclusions scope statement.

Good news: your setup is actually a fairly common pattern for CE, and the scoping rules are clear once you understand the logic. Here's how it breaks down.

The scoping principle
Cyber Essentials scope is defined around "whole organisation" by default. Within that, every device that can access the internet, and every device/service that stores or processes organisational data (including via home working or BYOD), is potentially in scope unless properly segregated. The key test the assessor applies is: does this device connect to the internet and either hold company data or provide a route into company systems? If yes, it's in scope.

Personal phones used for email
Any personal phone (BYOD) used to access company email, calendar, files, or any cloud service is in scope. This applies regardless of who owns the device. In scope means the device needs:
- A passcode/biometric lock (6-digit PIN minimum, or biometric).
- Auto-lock after inactivity.
- The OS kept in vendor support and patched (critical/high patches within 14 days) - this is often the trickiest part with personal Android/iOS devices, since you can't force personal phones to update.
- Malware protection isn't usually required for phones under CE (mobile devices are typically treated as out of scope for anti-malware controls specifically, since built-in mobile OS sandboxing is accepted), but the device-unlocking and patching controls still apply.

If you don't have an MDM (mobile device management) solution enforcing these settings, you're relying on staff self-attestation, which assessors will probe. Many organisations use Intune (bundled with many M365 licences) or a lightweight MDM to enforce passcode and patch-level policies on BYOD, which also makes the questionnaire far easier to answer with confidence.

Everyone works from home
Home working doesn't change scope - it just means "the corporate network" is really "everyone's home router plus their laptop." Under the current CE question set, home-worker routers supplied by the ISP are generally out of scope for the firewall control (you're not expected to reconfigure every employee's home router), but the corporate-owned/managed laptop's software firewall (Windows Defender Firewall, macOS firewall) must be enabled and correctly configured - that's the boundary firewall equivalent for a remote device. If you supply company-managed routers, those would be in scope.

Microsoft 365
M365 is in scope as your primary cloud service. This means:
- Admin accounts: no everyday use of global admin accounts, MFA enforced on all admin accounts (mandatory under current CE requirements) and on all user accounts (MFA is now required for all cloud service accounts, not just admins).
- Secure configuration: unnecessary legacy authentication protocols disabled, appropriate conditional access/security defaults enabled, unused accounts removed.
- Patch management: less relevant here since Microsoft manages the underlying SaaS patching, but your tenant configuration still needs review.

AWS
Your AWS estate is in scope wherever it holds organisational data or provides connectivity into your systems - EC2 instances, RDS databases, load balancers, VPCs, etc. Key points:
- Any EC2/VM instances need supported OS versions, patched within the 14-day critical/high window, host-based firewalls configured, and malware protection where applicable (Linux workloads have some flexibility here depending on assessor interpretation, but Windows EC2 instances need it).
- IAM: MFA enforced on all users, especially root/admin, least-privilege access, root account not used day-to-day.
- Security groups act as your boundary firewall equivalent - default-deny, no overly permissive 0.0.0.0/0 rules on management ports.
- Serverless/managed services (S3, Lambda, managed RDS) reduce your patching burden since AWS manages the underlying infrastructure, but access control and configuration are still yours to secure.

What's likely out of scope
Personal home routers (ISP-supplied, unmanaged), and devices/services genuinely walled off from company data with no access path (e.g., a personal laptop that never touches email, files, or VPN).

Practical next step: build an asset register covering managed laptops, BYOD phones, M365 tenant, and AWS accounts/resources - that register is exactly what the assessor will want to see reflected in your questionnaire answers, and it's the fastest way to spot gaps (unmanaged BYOD, missing MFA, EC2 boxes running unsupported OS versions) before you submit.
Prompt: How fast do we actually have to patch things for Cyber Essentials, and what about our old Windows Server 2012 box?
With Skill
⭐⭐⭐⭐⭐ 5/5 assertions passed (100%)
✅States the 14-day rule with its criteria: apply updates within 14 days when vendor-rated critical or high risk, OR CVSS v3 base score 7.0+, OR no vendor severity detail provided
✅Covers automatic updates: enable them wherever possible
✅Handles unsupported software correctly: Windows Server 2012 (out of support) must be REMOVED, or moved out of scope into a defined sub-set that blocks ALL internet traffic both directions — keeping it in scope is a certification failure
✅Notes the 14-day update questions are automatic-fail questions under the current (Danzell) marking
✅Mentions firmware counts as software (with firewall/router firmware needing make/model listing)
Good question to ask before you submit, because patching timeliness is one of the two areas that can now cause an automatic fail under the current Cyber Essentials question set (Danzell / Requirements for IT Infrastructure v3.3, mandatory for assessment accounts created from 27 April 2026).

**The 14-day rule, precisely.** You must install an update within 14 days of its release when any ONE of these is true:
1. The vendor describes the fix as "critical" or "high risk" severity, OR
2. The vulnerability it fixes has a CVSS v3 base score of 7.0 or above, OR
3. The vendor gives no severity detail at all (no rating = treat it as needing the 14-day turnaround).

Important nuance: if an update bundles several fixes and even one of them meets that bar, the whole update inherits the 14-day clock — you can't cherry-pick around it. Installing every update within 14 days generally is good practice and recommended, but it's only mandatory for updates that meet the critical/high/CVSS≥7/no-detail criteria above. Enabling automatic updates wherever the platform supports it is the practical way most organisations satisfy this without manual tracking.

**Why this specifically matters for your certification:** under Danzell, the two question groups covering this — A6.4 (operating systems and router/firewall firmware) and A6.5 (applications) — are **automatic-fail questions**. That's a change from how the scheme used to be marked; it used to just cost you points/require remediation. Now, if you can't demonstrate the 14-day rule is being met on OS and firmware updates, or on application updates, the assessment fails outright regardless of how strong everything else looks. Firmware counts as software here too, so your router/firewall firmware needs to be tracked and updated on the same clock, and you'll need to be able to list its make and model.

**Now, your Windows Server 2012 box.** This is the part of your question that needs a direct answer: Windows Server 2012 (and 2012 R2) went out of mainstream and extended support with Microsoft years ago — unless you're specifically paying for Extended Security Updates (ESU), it is now unsupported, unpatched software. Under Cyber Essentials, unsupported software is treated very strictly:

- It must either be **removed entirely** from your in-scope estate, or
- **Moved out of scope** into a clearly segregated sub-set (separate VLAN/firewall segregation) where ALL internet traffic — inbound and outbound — is blocked, both ways.

There is no middle ground of "it's old but we've hardened it and left it in scope" — unsupported software sitting inside your certified scope is an automatic certification failure, full stop. It doesn't matter whether it's currently receiving 14-day patches or not, because by definition an unsupported OS isn't receiving vendor patches at all.

**Your practical options for the 2012 box, in order of preference:**
1. **Decommission or migrate** the workload to a supported OS (Windows Server 2019/2022/2025) — the clean, durable fix, and the one I'd push for given this will recur every renewal cycle otherwise.
2. **Pay for Extended Security Updates** if Microsoft still offers them for your version — this technically keeps it "supported" via the ESU program and patchable, but confirm current ESU availability and cost before relying on this, and remember it's usually a stopgap, not a long-term answer.
3. **Air-gap it out of scope**: physically or logically segregate it (dedicated VLAN/firewall rule set) with zero internet traffic in or out, and describe that segregation and justification to your assessor. This keeps it out of your certified boundary but doesn't fix the underlying risk — it just stops it counting against your certification. It's often used as a bridge while you migrate the workload.

Given you're asking about it now, my recommendation: don't try to justify keeping it "in scope but managed" — that path fails. Decide this week whether it's being decommissioned/migrated or properly air-gapped, because whichever you pick changes your scope statement and needs to be reflected in the question set before you submit.

Patch timelines under Cyber Essentials are one of the most precise, non-negotiable requirements in the whole scheme, so it's worth getting exact.

The rule
Under the current Cyber Essentials requirements (as updated by IASME/NCSC), all software in scope must be:
- Licensed and supported by the vendor (i.e., not end-of-life).
- Removed if no longer supported, or isolated so it can't communicate with the internet.
- Updated within the vendor's published timeframes, and in any case:
  - Critical and high severity vulnerabilities (however defined by the vendor, or CVSS v3 score of 7.0+) must be patched within 14 calendar days of the patch being released.
  - Automatic updates should be enabled where available, and devices must be updated within 14 days regardless of whether patching is manual or automatic.
- All patches must come from the vendor - not a third party.

This 14-day window is checked closely by assessors: for basic CE it's evidenced through your questionnaire answers (describing your patch management process), and for CE Plus it's actually tested (the assessor will look for missing patches on sampled devices/systems during vulnerability scanning).

What counts as "in scope" for patching
Every device and every piece of software that's in scope for CE overall: operating systems, firmware where applicable, and all applications (browsers, PDF readers, Office, browser plugins, third-party software) - not just the OS.

Your Windows Server 2012 box
This is a real problem. Windows Server 2012 and 2012 R2 went end of support (extended support ended) in October 2023. Since then, Microsoft has not issued free security patches for it (aside from paying for Extended Security Updates, ESU, which Microsoft has offered as a paid bridge for a few years but which itself has an end date and doesn't run indefinitely).

Under CE rules, any device running software that is out of vendor support is automatically non-compliant unless it is:
1. Upgraded to a supported version, or
2. Fully removed/decommissioned, or
3. Isolated so it has no network path to the internet and cannot be reached from in-scope devices (effectively segregated out of scope) - this is a high bar: it needs to be genuinely unable to communicate with the internet or other networked devices, not just "not used much."

Practically, for a live CE assessment, you have three real options:
- Upgrade the server to Windows Server 2019/2022 (or migrate the workload to a cloud-managed equivalent) before you apply - this is the cleanest and most future-proof route, especially since you'll be recertifying annually.
- Purchase Microsoft's Extended Security Updates (ESU) if you're not ready to migrate immediately - this technically keeps you "in vendor support" for CE purposes, but ESU is a paid, time-limited stopgap, not a permanent fix, and you should treat it as a bridge to migration, not a destination.
- Properly isolate/segregate the box from any network connectivity to the internet or other devices, and document that isolation clearly - assessors will scrutinise this, since "it's just on the internal network" is not sufficient; it needs to be genuinely air-gapped or firewalled off with no route in or out.

What won't work: leaving it connected to your network or internet-facing "because it's not that important" - this alone can fail your certification, since assessors specifically ask about unsupported software during the questionnaire and will flag it in CE Plus testing regardless of business justification.

Bottom line: treat the 14-day patch SLA as a hard operational commitment (build it into your IT process/ticketing, don't just aspire to it), and treat the Server 2012 box as a blocker to resolve before you submit - migrate it, pay for ESU as a genuine bridge, or properly air-gap it. Trying to certify with it live on the network and unsupported is very likely to fail.
Prompt: We passed basic Cyber Essentials last month. What happens in the Plus audit and what trips people up?
With Skill
⭐⭐⭐⭐ 4/5 assertions passed (80%)
✅States the timing rule: CE Plus must be completed within 3 months of the basic certification
✅Describes the audit content: internal (authenticated) and external vulnerability scans, a random sample of user devices (roughly 10%, covering build types), all internet gateways and internet-reachable servers, plus malware and email/browser download defence tests
✅Notes the current retest rules: a failed sample triggers a retest with a NEW random sample, and a second failure revokes the verified self-assessment certificate; answers can't be adjusted once testing begins
✅Lists realistic failure causes: unpatched high/critical vulnerabilities on sampled devices, missing MFA, local admin misconfigurations, unsupported software discovered in scope
❌Notes CE+ is individually quoted (not the fixed basic-tier pricing) and can be remote or on-site
Congratulations on the basic pass. Cyber Essentials Plus (CE+) is the independent technical verification of everything you self-attested to in the basic assessment, and there's a firm clock running now: the audit must be completed within 3 months of your basic certification date. You don't need to redo the self-assessment if it's still within that window, but the auditors will independently test whether reality matches what you declared.

**What actually happens on audit day.** A qualified assessor (remote or on-site — many are now done remotely via screen-share and remote agent tooling) runs:
1. **Authenticated internal vulnerability scans** against a random sample of your in-scope devices — typically around 10%, but the sample is built to cover each distinct build type/image you have (so if you have three different laptop builds, expect devices from each, not just 10% of the total pulled from one type).
2. **External vulnerability scans** of everything internet-facing: all your internet gateways/boundary firewalls and every server reachable by an unauthenticated user from the internet.
3. **Malware protection tests** — confirming your anti-malware (or allow-listing) actually blocks or flags test malware samples.
4. **Email and browser download defence tests** — sending test files/links to see whether your email filtering and browser protections catch known-bad downloads.

**What trips people up, roughly in order of frequency:**
- **Missing patches that were "supposed" to be applied.** The self-assessment says you meet the 14-day rule; the scan finds a critical/high vulnerability (or CVSS ≥7) that's been open longer than that on a sampled device. This is the single most common real-world failure point, especially on devices that were off/asleep during a patch cycle, or on router/firewall firmware that nobody tracks as carefully as OS patches.
- **Devices that don't match the declared build.** If the sampled machine has different software, an unmanaged local admin account, or a stale local password compared to what was declared, that's a discrepancy the auditor will flag.
- **MFA gaps found on testing**, not just declared — e.g., a service account, shared mailbox, or legacy protocol (like an old IMAP/POP connection) that bypasses MFA even though "everyone uses MFA" was true for normal user logins.
- **Malware protection not actually blocking the test file** — out-of-date signature engines, or endpoint protection that was disabled/uninstalled on a specific machine (common on a stale laptop that's rarely used but still in scope).
- **Unsupported software surviving in the sample** — an old application or OS version that should have been removed/updated after the basic pass but is still present on a device that gets sampled.

**The part that's new and worth knowing under the current (Danzell) rules:** if your device sample fails, you don't get to just fix the same devices and resubmit — the retest uses an **entirely new random sample** of devices, not the ones that failed. And if that second sample also fails, it doesn't just fail the CE+ audit — it **revokes your underlying verified self-assessment certificate** too. So a CE+ failure now has teeth that reach back to the basic certification you already passed. Also worth knowing: once CE+ testing begins, you cannot go back and adjust your self-assessment answers to "match" what testing reveals — what you declared is locked in as the baseline being tested against.

**How to prepare in the run-up:**
- Re-verify the 14-day rule right now across every device type, not just spot-check the ones you remember — assume the assessor will find the one exception if one exists.
- Confirm anti-malware/allow-listing is actually running and current on every device, including ones staff rarely use (spare laptops, shared kiosk-style machines).
- Test MFA on every path into your cloud services, including service accounts, legacy auth protocols, and any admin/root accounts, not just standard user logins.
- Make sure whatever you declared as your "build types" genuinely reflects what's deployed — if reality has drifted since you filled in the self-assessment, fix the drift now rather than let the sample find it.

Given the 3-month clock, book the audit slot as soon as you're confident the above is solid — don't wait until the deadline is close, since remediation after a failed sample eats into the window fast.

Congratulations on passing basic Cyber Essentials - Plus is a meaningfully different exercise, so it's worth resetting expectations now rather than at the audit.

What Plus actually is
Where basic CE is a self-assessment questionnaire reviewed by an assessor, Cyber Essentials Plus is an independent technical verification of the same five control themes (firewalls, secure configuration, user access control, malware protection, patch management) - but tested, not just described. You must hold a valid basic CE certificate (no more than 3 months old at the time Plus testing starts) before you can be assessed for Plus, so timing matters if you've just passed basic.

What happens during the audit
1. Scoping call/planning - the assessor (a certification body, sometimes different from the one that did your basic CE) agrees the scope and a representative sample of devices/servers to test, based on your device population (they use a sampling methodology - roughly the square root of each homogeneous group, with minimums).
2. Vulnerability scanning - internal and external scans of in-scope systems, looking for missing patches, weak configurations, and known vulnerabilities exceeding the 14-day patch window.
3. Authenticated device checks - the assessor logs into a sample of your actual laptops/servers with standard user credentials (not admin) to verify: OS/software patch levels, anti-malware is active and up to date, no unauthorised software, account configuration matches your questionnaire.
4. Malware/phishing simulation - typically involves attempting to download a benign test file (EICAR test file) via email and web browser, and sometimes running a script that mimics ransomware behaviour, to confirm malware protection and browser/email controls actually block or flag it.
5. Account separation and privilege testing - confirming standard users can't perform admin actions, and admin accounts are properly separated from day-to-day use.
6. Remote/cloud considerations - if you're cloud-heavy (M365/AWS), the assessor will test cloud service configuration too (MFA enforcement, admin account controls), often via a combination of remote device testing (agent-based or remote desktop) and cloud console review, since Plus moved to accommodate remote/hybrid workforces.

Where organisations commonly trip up
- Patch drift between passing basic CE and the Plus audit - a gap of even a few weeks can let critical patches slip past the 14-day window, and Plus actually checks this rather than trusting a questionnaire answer.
- Local admin rights left on standard user laptops "for convenience" (e.g., developers, IT staff) - Plus testing directly probes for this.
- Anti-malware not actually running/updated on every sampled device, even if it's installed - definitions out of date, real-time protection disabled, or exclusions configured too broadly.
- Unmanaged or forgotten devices - a laptop that wasn't in the asset inventory used for basic CE surfaces during sampling and fails.
- BYOD/personal devices not meeting the passcode, patching, or configuration bar once actually tested rather than self-reported.
- Legacy or shadow IT systems (that old test server, a forgotten VM, a router with default credentials) that weren't declared in the original scope.
- Email/web filtering not actually blocking the EICAR test file or the safe test scripts used to simulate malicious behaviour - often because a security tool is misconfigured rather than absent.
- Firewalls with looser rules in practice than what was described - e.g., temporary rules opened for a project and never closed.
- Account list mismatches - leavers whose accounts weren't disabled, or shared/generic accounts that don't map to a named individual.

How to prepare well
- Re-run your own internal check of patch levels and anti-malware status across the whole device fleet, not just the sample you expect to be tested - the assessor picks the sample, not you.
- Confirm no standard users have local admin rights, and clean up any leftover admin credentials from IT troubleshooting.
- Test your own email/web security controls against the EICAR test file before the audit.
- Refresh your asset inventory to make sure it's complete and accurate, including any devices added since basic CE.
- Treat Plus prep as an operational hygiene exercise, not a paperwork exercise - most Plus failures come from real technical gaps that basic CE's self-assessment format didn't surface, not from documentation problems.

Typical timeline from booking to certificate is a few weeks, and many organisations schedule Plus within the 3-month validity window of their basic certificate specifically so both stay aligned for the next annual renewal cycle.
Prompt: Does Cyber Essentials really come with free insurance? And our customer is an MoD prime — what will they expect from us?
With Skill
⭐⭐⭐ 3/5 assertions passed (60%)
✅Insurance facts right: opt-in with basic CE for UK/Crown Dependencies organisations under £20m turnover with WHOLE-organisation scope — £25,000 indemnity, incident helpline, £1,000 excess, underwritten by AIG and administered by Sutcliffe & Co, cyber fraud excluded
✅States the condition: keep automatically provided vendor updates enabled for critical business software for cover to remain valid, and notes paid uplifts exist
✅MoD context: the DCPP/Cyber Security Model is being superseded by Defence Cyber Certification (DCC, IASME-delivered), with MoD asking defence partners to reach DCC Level 0 by December 31, 2026 — Cyber Essentials remains the supply-chain baseline
❌Mentions PPN 014 as the central-government procurement requirement (CE or accepted equivalents) covering departments, agencies, NDPBs and NHS bodies
❌Advises timeline back-planning for contract bids (certification lead time; CE+ inside its 3-month window)
Two good questions — let me take them in turn, since the insurance answer has real conditions attached and the MoD expectation has changed recently.

**Yes, the insurance is real — but it's opt-in and conditional, not automatic.** When you take out basic Cyber Essentials (not required for CE+, but included with basic CE), you can opt in to bundled cyber liability insurance at no extra cost. The headline terms:
- **£25,000 total indemnity** covering things like incident response (there's a helpline), liability costs, event/breach management, extortion/ransom scenarios, regulatory defence costs and insurable fines, and business interruption.
- **Eligibility conditions**: your organisation must be domiciled in the UK or Crown Dependencies, have turnover under £20 million, and — importantly — your Cyber Essentials certificate must cover your WHOLE organisation, not a carved-out sub-set. If you certified only a segregated part of the business, you won't qualify for the cover.
- **Excess**: £1,000 (rising to £5,000 for US/Canada-related incidents).
- **What's excluded**: electronic theft and cyber fraud are explicitly carved out — so this is not a substitute for dedicated cyber-crime/fraud cover if that's a real exposure for you.
- **Underwriter/administrator**: it's AIG UK-underwritten, administered by Sutcliffe & Co.
- **The condition that actually matters day to day**: to keep the cover valid, you must keep automatically-provided vendor updates switched on for your critical business software. If you're the type of organisation that disables auto-updates for change-control reasons, be aware that could jeopardise the insurance.
- Higher-value uplifts (to £100k or £250k) are available if £25k isn't enough for your risk profile.

So: real, free, and worth taking — but don't market it to your customer as comprehensive cyber insurance. It's a helpful baseline, not a replacement for a dedicated cyber policy if you're carrying meaningful risk (e.g., you process a lot of payment data or have material business interruption exposure).

**On the MoD side — what your customer will expect from you as a supplier in their chain.** The Ministry of Defence has been moving away from the older DCPP/Cyber Security Model framework toward a new scheme called **Defence Cyber Certification (DCC)**, delivered by IASME and launched in 2025. Here's the practical shape of it:
- MoD has asked all defence industry partners (this includes sub-suppliers to primes, not just direct MoD contracts) to reach **DCC Level 0 by 31 December 2026**. If your customer is an MoD prime, they are very likely under pressure to demonstrate their own supply chain — including you — is moving toward that deadline, so expect them to ask about your DCC status or timeline, not just your Cyber Essentials certificate.
- Critically, **Cyber Essentials itself doesn't go away** — it remains the baseline expectation across defence supply chains handling MoD-identifiable information. Cyber Essentials is not being replaced by DCC; think of DCC as sitting alongside/above it for defence-specific requirements, not instead of it.
- Practically, I'd expect your MoD-prime customer to ask you for: (1) evidence of current Cyber Essentials (or CE+) certification, (2) your plan or timeline for DCC Level 0 given the December 2026 deadline, and (3) possibly specifics about how you handle any MoD-identifiable information you're given as part of the contract.

**My recommendation:** don't wait to be asked — proactively tell your customer where you stand on both Cyber Essentials (renewal status, whether it's basic or Plus) and your DCC Level 0 plan relative to the December 2026 deadline. Given DCC is a newly launched scheme, guidance is still evolving, so it's worth confirming the exact current requirement directly with your prime or via IASME's DCC materials before you commit to a specific certification level or timeline in writing.

Two separate questions here - let's take them one at a time.

The "free insurance"
Yes, this is real, but it's more limited than the marketing suggests. When you certify to Cyber Essentials (basic) through most IASME-licensed certification bodies, IASME includes a complimentary cyber liability insurance element as part of the certification package - historically this has been up to £25,000 of cover (the exact figure and terms have varied over time and by provider, so check the current wording from whichever certification body you use). Key caveats:
- It's typically only available to organisations with turnover under a certain threshold (historically around £20 million) - larger companies usually don't qualify for the free cover, though they can often purchase enhanced cover as an add-on.
- It's usually only offered to UK-registered/domiciled organisations.
- It's a modest, entry-level policy intended to soften small-business risk, not a substitute for a proper standalone cyber insurance policy - it typically covers things like incident response costs, business interruption, and liability up to the stated limit, with various exclusions.
- Cyber Essentials Plus doesn't add a different or larger insurance benefit by itself - the free insurance is generally tied to the underlying basic CE certificate.
- It is not guaranteed for every organisation or every certification body arrangement - terms, provider (historically this has been arranged via IASME's insurance partner), and eligibility can change, so get written confirmation of what applies to you at the point of certifying rather than relying on general scheme reputation.

Bottom line: treat it as a genuine but modest bonus, not your primary cyber risk transfer mechanism - if you handle sensitive government or MoD data, you'll likely need proper commercial cyber insurance regardless, sized to your actual risk exposure.

What an MoD prime will expect from you
Being a subcontractor/supplier to an MoD prime brings a materially higher bar than a typical government department contract, for a few structural reasons:

1. Cyber Essentials (and often Plus) as a floor, not the ceiling. MoD contracts frequently reference the Defence Cyber Protection Partnership (DCPP) framework and a risk-based approach called "Cyber Security Model" (which superseded/absorbed elements of the older DEFSTAN 05-138 and the "Defence Cyber Protection Partnership" model). Depending on the risk level of the contract and the type of data you'll handle, you may be required to go beyond basic CE - Cyber Essentials Plus is common, and for higher-risk contracts (those involving Official-Sensitive information, defence-related IP, or higher-impact data), the prime may require alignment with additional standards.
2. Data classification awareness. MoD/defence contracts operate under the Government Security Classifications Policy (OFFICIAL, OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE, SECRET). Even "OFFICIAL-SENSITIVE" data carries handling requirements well beyond generic good practice - expect requirements around data marking, need-to-know access controls, secure disposal, and potentially restrictions on where data can be stored/processed (e.g., no offshore cloud regions, no personal devices for certain data).
3. Supply chain due diligence. Primes typically flow down contractual security requirements (often via DEFCON 658 or similar defence conditions in the contract, and increasingly referencing the Cyber Security Model) requiring subcontractors to demonstrate their own compliance and sometimes to cascade the same requirements further down their own supply chain.
4. Incident reporting obligations. Expect contractual clauses requiring you to report security incidents to the prime (and potentially MoD) within tight timeframes, and to cooperate with any investigation.
5. Personnel security. Depending on the contract, staff with access to certain information may need baseline personnel security standard (BPSS) checks at minimum, and possibly security clearance (SC) for more sensitive work.
6. Physical and system security controls beyond CE's technical scope - things like clear desk policies, controlled printing, visitor management, and secure destruction of media, especially if you're handling any physical documents or removable media related to the contract.
7. Right to audit. Primes and MoD frequently reserve contractual rights to audit your security controls, sometimes going beyond what a CE Plus assessment covers.

Practical next step: ask your prime contact directly (or check the tender's security schedule/annex) which specific standard applies - "Cyber Essentials," "Cyber Essentials Plus," or a defence-specific requirement referencing the Cyber Security Model risk profile - because the answer genuinely varies by contract risk level, and getting this wrong (assuming basic CE is sufficient when Plus or additional defence-specific controls are required) is a common and costly mistake for first-time MoD suppliers.

QC 1000 and your December 2026 integrated audit

Short answer: QC 1000 is a quality-control standard for audit firms, not for your company. It does not add or change any control you have to operate, and it does not change what your ICFR audit tests. The practical effect on you is indirect, through how your audit firm runs its engagements.

What it is
- QC 1000, "A Firm's System of Quality Control," is the PCAOB standard that requires registered audit firms to design, implement and operate a risk-based system of quality control. Think of it as COSO-style risk assessment applied to the audit firm itself: the firm identifies quality risks and responds to them across governance, ethics and independence, client acceptance, engagement performance, resources, information and communication, and monitoring and remediation.
- It takes effect December 15, 2026.
- The PCAOB adopted targeted amendments on September 9, 2026. They rescind the design-only requirement and the External QC Function requirement, and they let firms choose their annual evaluation date. The SEC approved those amendments on November 2, 2026, and the effective date is unchanged.

Does it affect your December 2026 year-end audit?
1. Legal applicability: QC 1000 binds your auditor, not you. Management's 404(a) assessment, your RCM and your ITGCs are unaffected. AS 2201 (the integrated ICFR audit standard) has not been amended by QC 1000, and your COSO 2013 framework remains the framework you assess against.
2. Timing: the effective date is December 15, 2026, which falls inside your fiscal year-end window. Whether it touches your specific audit depends on how the firm implements it for engagements and reports issued after that date. Ask your engagement partner how the firm is applying it. I would not assume a precise cutover treatment without asking.
3. What you may notice (indirect, and firm-dependent, so treat these as likely rather than certain):
   - More formal engagement-quality documentation and review, which can mean more PBC follow-ups and tighter sign-off timelines.
   - Firm-level focus on resourcing, specialists and IT audit staffing. Your ITGC testing team may be asked for clearer evidence of IPE (information produced by the entity) validation.
   - Closer monitoring of the firm's own deficiencies, and so possibly more conservative evidence standards around ITGC reliance.
   None of these changes your obligations. They change how carefully your auditor documents their work.
4. Your ITGC work does not change. You still need:
   - Access: timely terminations, quarterly user access reviews, privileged access.
   - Program changes: approval, testing, and developer/deployer segregation.
   - Computer operations: backup and job monitoring.
   - Program development, for any implementation.
   The quarterly cadences and sample sizes (daily 25, weekly 5, monthly 2, quarterly 2, annual 1) are audit convention, not regulation. Agree the final numbers with your auditor.

Filer status and 404(b)
Whether your auditor attests to ICFR depends on your status, not on QC 1000. Under current law, 404(a) applies to all public companies. 404(b) applies to accelerated filers ($75M-$700M float with at least $100M revenue) and large accelerated filers (at least $700M float) that are not EGCs. Non-accelerated filers and EGCs are exempt. Flag: the SEC's May 19, 2026 proposal would raise the large accelerated threshold to $2B float, exempt all non-accelerated filers from 404(b), and add a roughly 5-year post-IPO on-ramp. Comments closed July 20, 2026, and there has been no final action as of November 6, 2026, so the current thresholds remain operative for this year-end.

What I would do now
- Ask the engagement partner in writing: how is the firm applying QC 1000 to this engagement, and have the timetable, PBC list or sample expectations changed?
- Confirm the year-end timeline: interim testing results, roll-forward, remediation re-test cutoffs, and the report date.
- Close open ITGC deficiencies and finish remediation validation now. A control fixed in December cannot show operation over a sufficient period, whatever the standards say.
- Make sure IPE and key-report validations and SOC 1 coverage (period and bridge letters) are ready.
- Do not pause any ICFR work on account of QC 1000.

This is general compliance information, not legal advice. Confirm details with your auditor and counsel.

QC 1000 and your December 2026 year-end integrated audit

Short answer: QC 1000 is a firm-level PCAOB standard for audit firms. It is not a requirement on your company. It should not change what you have to do for ICFR or ITGC, but you may notice indirect effects in how your audit firm runs the engagement.

What QC 1000 is
- QC 1000, "A Firm's System of Quality Control," was adopted by the PCAOB in May 2024 and approved by the SEC later that year.
- It replaces the legacy QC sections (QC 20 and related) and the "interim" quality control standards.
- It is a risk-based standard modeled on the IAASB's ISQM 1. The firm identifies quality risks, designs responses, monitors them, and remediates deficiencies.
- Its components are governance and leadership, the firm's risk assessment process, relevant ethical requirements and independence, acceptance and continuance of engagements, engagement performance, resources (including technology and intellectual resources), information and communication, and the monitoring and remediation process.
- Firms must make an annual evaluation of the system and report it to the PCAOB on a new Form QC. Larger firms, those that audit accelerated filers or large accelerated filers, have additional requirements. These include designating individuals with specific responsibility (such as a Quality Control Leader) and following specified monitoring and evaluation procedures.
- Related conforming amendments were adopted at the same time, including changes to the engagement quality review standard (AS 1220) and other standards.

Effective date
- The original effective date was December 15, 2025. The PCAOB extended it by one year, to December 15, 2026.
- Firms must have the system designed and implemented by that date. The first annual evaluation is as of a later date (I recall September 30, 2027), with Form QC reporting after that.
- Please confirm these dates against the current PCAOB website. The PCAOB's agenda and board composition have changed, and I am working from memory without live sources.

Does it affect your December 2026 year-end audit?
- Legally it applies to the firm. A December 31, 2026 audit is performed after the December 15, 2026 effective date, so your audit will be done by a firm operating under QC 1000.
- It does not change AS 2201, AS 2110, AS 2301 or your management's SOX 302/404 responsibilities. Management's ICFR assessment criteria (COSO 2013) are unaffected.
- It does not create new deliverables for the issuer.

Practical indirect effects to expect
1. Engagement acceptance and continuance. Your firm may ask more questions or refresh its client risk assessment.
2. Resources and technology. The standard addresses firms' use of technology. Your firm may ask how you use AI or automation in financial reporting and controls, and may document its own tool use more heavily.
3. Engagement quality review. Expect tighter and better-documented EQR involvement, particularly for higher-risk areas such as ITGC reliance decisions.
4. Documentation and timing. Firms may add internal consultation or review steps, which could move timetables or increase requests for PBC items. Raise this early.
5. Communication. Audit committees may hear more about the firm's quality system and its own ICFR-independent monitoring results.
6. Independence and ethics. The standard reinforces independence monitoring, so confirm that your non-audit services (including any advisory work related to ITGC) are pre-approved by the audit committee.

What I suggest
- Ask your audit partner how the firm is implementing QC 1000 and whether any timing or request changes are planned for the year-end audit.
- Confirm the audit committee's pre-approval policy is current.
- No change to your ITGC test plan is needed because of QC 1000. Keep following the planned scope for access, change management, operations, and interface controls.
- Verify the dates and any further amendments or deferrals directly on the PCAOB website before relying on them.

PCAOB's latest inspection publication and what it means for ITGC testing

What it said
The latest publication is the PCAOB Spotlight of October 22, 2026, "Staff Update on 2025 Inspections of Public Company Audits." The headline figures:
- The aggregate Part I.A deficiency rate fell to 23 percent in 2025.
- It was 38 percent in 2024 and 46 percent in 2023.
- The 2025 figure covers 143 firms and portions of 780 audits.

How to read it
- Part I.A deficiencies are significant enough that the firm had not obtained sufficient evidence to support its opinion. The measure blends financial statement audits and ICFR audits, so it is not an ITGC-only number. Do not tell your audit committee that "ITGC audit quality improved by X." The data does not say that.
- It is a good-news trend, but 23 percent still means roughly one in four sampled audits had a significant deficiency. Inspectors are still finding things, and ICFR work remains a recurring area of focus.
- Related context: the PCAOB's 2025 inspection priorities named ICFR quality, generative AI use (at issuers and in audits), and cybersecurity incidents. AS 2201 has not been amended, and it is not on the PCAOB's September 30, 2026 standard-setting agenda. The requirements your auditor tests against have not changed.

What it means for your ITGC testing
1. Expect auditors who document carefully and push back on weak evidence. Years of deficiency findings in ICFR audits have made firms stricter about the following:
   - Evidence that populations are complete (for example, the full list of terminated users or all production changes, reconciled tool extract to deployment log).
   - IPE validation: source, parameters, logic, and completeness and accuracy of any report used in a control, including UARs run off system extracts.
   - Precision of management review controls: what threshold triggers investigation, and what proof the review was done.
   - Reliance on SOC 1 reports: period coverage versus fiscal year, bridge letters for gaps, and CUEC mapping to your own controls.
2. Make your own testing audit-ready. Do not rely on the auditor to catch gaps:
   - Retain evidence in a form that can be re-performed (parameters, screenshots with timestamps, system-generated listings).
   - Test terminations and privileged access continuously. These produce the worst late surprises.
   - Reviewers of UARs should be independent, and revocations should be shown as executed, not just approved.
3. Keep the ITGC evaluation logic correct. An ITGC deficiency is assessed through the application controls and reports it undermines, not as a standalone material weakness. If dependent automated controls are re-validated clean for the period, the failure often lands at a deficiency or significant deficiency. Aggregate related deficiencies hitting the same account or assertion. Classify using AS 2201 Appendix A and Reg S-X Rule 1-02(a)(4).
4. Watch the emerging areas inspectors named: generative AI and automated features in financial systems (treat model or config changes to automated financial controls as in-scope Domain 2 changes) and cyber incidents on financial systems, which can implicate both SOX and the SEC cyber rules (8-K Item 1.05, S-K Item 106).
5. Timing: with year-end close, any remediation needs a sufficient operating window to re-test. A quarterly control needs at least one clean occurrence, and a daily control commonly a 25-item sample over the remediated window. Sample sizes are audit convention, so agree them with your auditor.

Filer status
Whether your auditor attests at all depends on filer status. 404(a) applies to everyone. 404(b) applies to accelerated and large accelerated filers that are not EGCs. The SEC's May 19, 2026 proposal (comments closed July 20, 2026, no final action as of November 6, 2026) would change those thresholds, but current rules remain operative.

Next steps: ask your audit team what their inspection-driven focus areas are for your engagement, and run a pre-audit evidence check on populations, IPE and UARs.

This is general compliance information, not legal advice.

Important caveat: I cannot browse live sources and I do not have a reliable picture of the very latest PCAOB release as of November 2026. I do not want to invent specific statistics, so I am not going to quote numbers for a report I cannot verify. What follows is the pattern from recent PCAOB inspection publications and how it translates into ITGC practice. Please pull the actual document from pcaobus.org (Inspections, "Staff Update and Preview of Observations" and the firm-specific inspection reports) and map it to your own program.

What recent PCAOB inspection publications have consistently said
- Part I.A deficiency rates in audits of ICFR have been a standing concern. The rate of audits with a deficiency in the ICFR area was one of the largest drivers of the overall deficiency rate. The 2024 inspection cycle showed the Part I.A rate falling from the 2022 peak of 46 percent, but it was still high by historical standards. Treat these figures as approximate and check them.
- The most common ICFR-related deficiencies are:
  - failure to identify and test controls that address the risks of material misstatement for relevant assertions
  - insufficient testing of the precision of management review controls
  - insufficient testing of controls over the completeness and accuracy of information used in the control (IPE / system-generated reports)
  - when relying on a service organization (SOC 1) report, failure to assess the report's scope, complementary user entity controls, the period covered, and exceptions
  - failure to evaluate the severity of identified control deficiencies correctly
  - improper reliance on work of others
- On IT specifically, inspectors have cited weak testing of ITGCs where the audit relied on automated controls or IPE, including not testing the relevant ITGCs at all or not testing them for the full period of reliance.
- Staff have also highlighted risks tied to technology and AI, cybersecurity, third-party and cloud providers, and firms' use of tools in audits.

What this means for your ITGC testing (practical implications)
1. IPE and report logic. Document completeness and accuracy for every report used as evidence in a key control. Include source data, parameters, report logic or query validation, and change control over the report. This is a recurring weak spot for both auditors and management.
2. Linkage between ITGCs and key controls. Build and maintain a mapping from each key automated control, IPE, and interface to the specific ITGCs (access, change, operations) that support it. If an ITGC fails, document the compensating or alternative approach and its effect on reliance.
3. Service organizations. Obtain the SOC 1 Type 2 reports, check the period covered against yours, review the scope and subservice organizations (carve-out versus inclusive), map each control objective to your risk, test the complementary user entity controls, and perform bridge-letter or gap-period procedures when the report does not cover year-end.
4. Management review controls. Document the precision threshold, what the reviewer investigates, and evidence of follow-up. Do the same for ITGC-related review controls, such as periodic user access reviews and privileged access reviews. Auditors have been criticized when the reviewer did not evaluate the completeness of the user list or the review was not precise enough.
5. Population completeness for sampling. For access provisioning, terminations, and change tickets, the population must be complete (for example, system-generated from the source). Document how that was validated.
6. Period of reliance and rollforward. If you test at an interim date, plan rollforward procedures. Demonstrate how controls operated through year-end.
7. Deficiency evaluation. For ITGC deficiencies, evaluate the effect on the dependent application controls and the possible magnitude of misstatement, not only the deficiency itself. Include compensating controls only if they operate at the right level of precision.
8. Cyber and cloud. Confirm that your scope covers cloud platforms, SaaS applications that feed financial reporting, privileged accounts and break-glass access, and any recent system migrations.
9. Technology and AI. If you use AI or automation in a financial-reporting control, document governance, change management, and how outputs are validated.

How to use the publication
- Read the staff observations on ICFR and IT, and compare each cited deficiency against your own testing and evidence.
- Ask your external audit team how the observations changed their approach this year, and which ITGC evidence they plan to scrutinize.
- Perform a pre-audit quality check of your ITGC workpapers (a "mock inspection") focused on the points above.

The inspection publication is directed at audit firms, not at management. It does not change management's SOX 404(a) obligations, but it tends to drive increased auditor requests and push-back on documentation, so it is worth acting on early.

Has AS 2201 changed in 2026, and what is on the PCAOB agenda?

AS 2201: no change
AS 2201, "An Audit of Internal Control Over Financial Reporting That Is Integrated with An Audit of Financial Statements," remains unamended. Its top-down, risk-based approach and its Appendix A definitions of control deficiency, significant deficiency and material weakness are as they were. Those definitions line up with SEC Reg S-X Rule 1-02(a)(4), which is why deficiency classifications should cite both. COSO 2013 also remains the current framework, with no successor, only supplemental guidance including generative-AI internal control guidance.

What is on the standard-setting agenda
AS 2201 is not on the PCAOB's September 30, 2026 standard-setting agenda. The topics on it are:
- Comfort letters
- Auditor independence
- Fraud
- NOCLAR (non-compliance with laws and regulations)
- Going concern

Note that some of those topics could touch ICFR work indirectly (fraud, for instance, links to how auditors think about risk). That is an observation about overlap, not a stated plan to amend AS 2201.

Other 2026 developments that people confuse with AS 2201 changes
- QC 1000 (A Firm's System of Quality Control) takes effect December 15, 2026. It governs audit firms' quality control, not your ICFR requirements. The PCAOB adopted targeted amendments September 9, 2026 (rescinding the design-only and External QC Function requirements and allowing firms to choose their annual evaluation date). The SEC approved them November 2, 2026, with the effective date unchanged.
- AS 1000 became effective for fiscal years beginning on or after December 15, 2024.
- The PCAOB's October 22, 2026 Spotlight reported that the aggregate Part I.A deficiency rate fell to 23 percent in 2025 (38 percent in 2024, 46 percent in 2023). This blends financial statement and ICFR opinions.
- The proposal to fold the PCAOB into the SEC was dropped. The PCAOB remains a standalone regulator.
- The SEC's May 19, 2026 proposal on filer thresholds is not an AS 2201 change. It concerns who must obtain an auditor attestation (404(b)). It would raise the large accelerated threshold to $2B float, exempt all non-accelerated filers, and add a roughly 5-year post-IPO on-ramp. Comments closed July 20, 2026, and there has been no final action as of November 6, 2026. Current thresholds remain operative.

What this means for you
- Keep designing and testing to the existing AS 2201 and COSO 2013 expectations. Nothing in the standard has moved.
- The areas that change are applied ones: PCAOB inspection priorities (ICFR quality, generative AI at issuers and in audits, cybersecurity incidents), and AI or agentic features in financial systems (treat model or config changes to automated financial controls as in-scope program changes).
- Agendas can change, so re-check the PCAOB's standard-setting page periodically rather than treating this as permanent.

This is general compliance information, not legal advice. Verify against the PCAOB and SEC websites.

What it means for you
- Plan the year-end 2026 ICFR audit on the existing AS 2201. Do not expect a changed integrated-audit framework this year.
- Watch for technology-related audit procedures. Your auditor may be using more data analytics, and the AS 1105 and AS 2301 amendments mean more attention to the reliability of information provided by you (IPE).
- Management's own assessment under SEC rules (Item 308 of Regulation S-K, SEC 2007 interpretive guidance, COSO 2013) is independent of PCAOB standards.

Next steps
1. Open the PCAOB's "Standard-Setting Agenda" and rulemaking docket pages and check dates and status.
2. Ask your audit firm whether it expects any change in approach.
3. Subscribe to PCAOB updates for any proposals.

Will smaller companies be exempt from 404(b) soon, and should you pause attestation prep?

Short answer: do not pause. The exemption is only a proposal. It is not law.

Current law (operative today)
- 404(a), management's annual ICFR assessment, applies to all public companies.
- 404(b), the auditor attestation, applies to accelerated filers ($75M-$700M public float and at least $100M revenues) and large accelerated filers (at least $700M float). It does not apply to non-accelerated filers (per the SEC's 2020 amendments) or to EGCs (JOBS Act section 103; under $1.235B revenue, up to 5 years after IPO).
- SRC status: under $250M float, or under $100M revenues with under $700M float. SRC status alone does not exempt a company. The revenue test in the accelerated filer definition does the work.

The pending proposal
- On May 19, 2026, the SEC proposed to raise the large accelerated filer threshold to $2B float, exempt all non-accelerated filers from 404(b), and add a roughly 5-year post-IPO on-ramp.
- Comments closed July 20, 2026. As of November 6, 2026 there is no final action.
- A proposal can be changed, delayed or withdrawn, and an adopted rule would need an effective date and transition provisions. Nothing in it applies to your fiscal 2026 year-end.

Why not to pause
1. If you are an accelerated or large accelerated non-EGC filer today, your auditor will issue an ICFR opinion on this year-end. The current rules govern.
2. Even if the proposal is adopted, 404(a) stays. Management must still assess and conclude on ICFR. The documentation, scoping, RCM, testing and deficiency evaluation largely overlap with what an auditor would test, so the work is not wasted.
3. Remediation timing is the real constraint. A control fixed in December cannot show operation, so remediation must finish early enough for a sufficient operating window.
4. Material weaknesses are a disclosure issue regardless of 404(b). About 8 percent of annual reports filed 2023-24 disclosed material weaknesses (KPMG / Audit Analytics, 279 of 3,502), and more than 60 percent of adverse assessments are repeat filers (Baker Tilly, through April 2025). Weak ICFR carries investor, financing and audit-fee consequences.
5. Auditors, lenders and investors may still expect rigorous ICFR.

What to do instead
- Confirm your filer status (float measured at the end of Q2, and the revenue test) and EGC status.
- Run two scenarios: attestation continues; attestation removed in a future year. Keep scoping and testing for the first, and plan any cost reduction for the second only if the rule is finalized.
- Hold the year-end timetable: ITGC remediation validation, roll-forward testing, aggregation analysis, and management's 404(a) conclusion.
- Re-check status before advising on future-year obligations. If you can reduce external cost later, you can do so then.
- Consider whether a voluntary or reduced-scope auditor engagement still makes sense for financing or IPO-readiness reasons.

This is general compliance information, not legal advice. Confirm with counsel and your auditor.

Will smaller companies be exempt from SOX 404(b) soon? Should we pause ICFR auditor-attestation prep?

Short answer: do not pause. As far as I know, there is no enacted change that exempts you from SOX 404(b) auditor attestation. Proposals and discussions exist, but none that I can confirm is final. Verify the current status before making any decision, because I do not have live access to the SEC, Congress, or news sources.

Current rules (as I understand them)
- Section 404(b) requires an auditor attestation on ICFR for issuers that are accelerated filers or large accelerated filers. Non-accelerated filers are permanently exempt (Dodd-Frank section 989G).
- Accelerated filer status depends on public float of at least $75 million but less than $700 million, plus annual revenue of $100 million or more for the 2020 amendments' revenue test. Smaller reporting companies with annual revenues below $100 million are not accelerated filers, so they are outside 404(b). Emerging growth companies are exempt for up to five years.
- Large accelerated filers (public float of $700 million or more) are required regardless.
- Section 404(a) management assessment applies to all non-EGC issuers, and it is not eliminated by any proposal I know of.

What has been discussed
- The SEC under current leadership has signaled interest in revisiting filer categories, scaled disclosure, and the cost-benefit of ICFR attestation. Possible approaches include increasing the public float thresholds for accelerated and large accelerated filer status or revising the SRC definition. Such a change would need an SEC rulemaking (proposal, comment period, adoption, effective date and transition rules).
- Legislation has been introduced over the years (for example, bills to raise the thresholds for accelerated filers). A bill introduced is not a law.
- A proposal published for comment does not change your obligations. Even after adoption, there is normally a transition and an effective date, and the status is generally determined as of the end of the second quarter of the fiscal year (the public float determination date) and measured at year-end for the filer-status transition.

Why not to pause
1. Timing. For a December 2026 year-end, the public float determination was as of June 30, 2026. Any rule adopted now is unlikely to apply retroactively to that determination, so your FY2026 status is almost certainly fixed. Please confirm with counsel.
2. Management still owes the 404(a) assessment, which needs the same documentation, testing, and deficiency evaluation. Most of the 404(b) prep is the same work.
3. Lenders, investors, the audit committee, and your auditor may expect attestation regardless.
4. A pause would be hard to unwind and could cause an unprepared year-end, with the risk of a material weakness or late filing.
5. Any relief, if it occurs, would probably apply prospectively and would save audit fees, not the control work.

What to do
- Confirm your FY2026 filer status with your securities counsel using the June 30, 2026 float and revenue figures.
- Keep the ICFR program on schedule: scoping, risk assessment, ITGC and key control testing, deficiency evaluation, and remediation.
- Track the SEC's regulatory agenda, any proposals, and legislation. Set a decision point for FY2027 planning.
- Talk to your audit committee and auditor. Where you are near a threshold, model scenarios such as moving into or out of accelerated status.
- If you are close to the threshold, consider optional scaled approaches for non-key areas, but keep key controls and ITGCs.

Please verify the current thresholds and any recent SEC action on sec.gov before relying on this.

November-December 2026 SOX ITGC checklist (calendar year-end)

Framing: by now the interim work should be done. November and December are about closing remediation, rolling controls forward to year-end, and building management's conclusion. Cadences and sample sizes below are audit convention, not regulation, so agree them with your auditor. Remediation that lands in December usually cannot show enough operation, so triage first.

Early November (now)
- Deficiency triage: list every open deficiency from interim testing. For each, record owner, root cause, fix date and re-test plan. Anything that can still operate for a sufficient period gets priority.
- Evaluate deficiencies per AS 2201 Appendix A and Reg S-X Rule 1-02(a)(4): facts, likelihood and magnitude, compensating controls (tested before you credit them), and aggregation across the same account or assertion. Evaluate ITGC failures through the application controls and reports they affect.
- Confirm with the auditor: year-end timeline, roll-forward expectations, sample sizes, and any change in scope.
- Confirm filer status and whether 404(b) applies this year. Current thresholds are operative. Flag the SEC's May 19, 2026 proposal, which has no final action as of November 6, 2026.

Access to programs and data
- Run the Q4 user access review for every in-scope system and show revocations executed. Check reviewer independence and completeness of the user population.
- Test terminations across the full year, HR term list against disable dates (24-72 hours is convention). Investigate each exception and review activity logs for post-termination use.
- Re-enumerate privileged access: ERP superuser profiles, DB sysadmin, OS root, service accounts, firefighter logs. Justify each.
- Check SoD rule set and mitigations, especially after any role changes.

Program changes
- Reconcile the change population: tool extract against deployment log, including configuration and master-data-engine changes, and emergency changes.
- Confirm approval before migration, testing evidence, and developer/deployer segregation for the sample.
- Set a year-end change freeze policy and review any late-year changes to automated controls, interfaces or key reports. Treat AI or model configuration changes as in-scope changes.

Computer operations
- Review financially relevant batch job failures and their resolution, backup completion monitoring, and the most recent restore test for in-scope systems.
- Review incidents on financial systems for escalation to finance.

Program development
- If any implementation or migration went live this year, collect charter approval, UAT sign-off, data conversion reconciliations, go-live approval and hypercare logs.

Cross-cutting
- IPE and key reports: re-validate source, parameters, and completeness and accuracy for reports used in controls, especially if reports changed.
- End-user computing: check access restriction, version control and review for in-scope spreadsheets.
- SOC 1: confirm each report covers your fiscal year, get bridge letters for gaps (about three months or less), and confirm CUECs are mapped to owned controls. An unowned CUEC is a gap.
- Cyber: if a material incident touched a financial system, assess both SOX and SEC cyber implications (8-K Item 1.05, S-K Item 106).

Late November to mid-December
- Remediation validation: re-test fixed controls over the operating window (a quarterly control needs one clean occurrence; a daily control commonly a 25-item sample). Document what could not be re-tested in time and treat it as unremediated for conclusion purposes.
- Roll-forward procedures covering the period since interim testing, driven by risk.
- Update the scoping memo for any acquisitions, system changes or new applications.
- Share status with the audit committee: significant deficiencies must be communicated in writing, and any potential material weakness needs early discussion with the auditor, legal and disclosure committee.

Late December and January
- Capture year-end evidence (final access listings, December terminations, year-end batch and backup logs) promptly.
- Aggregation analysis across all deficiencies.
- Draft management's 404(a) conclusion. A material weakness is disclosed in 10-K Item 9A with nature, remediation plan and status, and where 404(b) applies the auditor issues an adverse ICFR opinion.
- Run a lessons-learned review and set next year's calendar. Q1: refresh scoping and update RCMs. Q2: walkthroughs and first testing wave. Q3: second wave and early deficiency triage. Q4: roll-forward and conclusion.

Context: about 8 percent of annual reports for 2023-24 disclosed material weaknesses (KPMG / Audit Analytics, 279 of 3,502), IT access and SoD are recurring themes, and over 60 percent of adverse assessments are repeat filers (Baker Tilly, through April 2025).

Also note QC 1000 takes effect December 15, 2026. It governs the audit firm, not your controls, but ask your auditor whether it changes their timetable or evidence requests.

This is general compliance information, not legal advice.
